I

FRANK LOUI

Grand Master
September 25, 2011 – September 23, 2012

II

FRANK LOUI

Grand Master – 2011-2012
Frank Loui was installed as Grand Master on September 25, 2011.
Frank was raised a Master Mason in 1986 in Fidelity Lodge No. 120
(now San Francisco Lodge No. 120) and served as master there in 1992. He is
affiliated with California Lodge No. 1 in San Francisco, and has served as its
treasurer and secretary.
Frank has served Grand Lodge in many capacities as well, as an inspector
of the 163rd Masonic District for nine years; a member of the Committee of Twenty
and the Annual Communication Activities Committee; a director of both Acacia
Creek and the Nob Hill Masonic Center; and a trustee of the Masonic Homes
of California, the California Masonic Foundation, and the California Masonic
Memorial Temple. He served as senior grand steward in 1996/1997 under Most
Worshipful Allen B. Gresham, and as senior grand deacon in 2004/2005 under
Most Worshipful David R. Doan.
Frank is a member of numerous Masonic organizations. He is a past
venerable master of the Lodge of Perfection at the San Francisco Scottish Rite
and was honored with the rank and decoration of honorary inspector general
of the 33º in 2003. He is currently the personal representative of the sovereign
grand inspector general and general secretary for the San Francisco Scottish Rite
Bodies. He is also a member of the Oakland Scottish Rite Bodies.
Frank is a past presiding officer of all three York Rite Bodies and is a
member of San Francisco Priory 38 Knights of the York Grand Cross of Honor.
He has served the Grand Council of Cryptic Masons as grand bible bearer and is a
member of the Saint Francis, Conclave Knights of the Red Cross of Constantine.
He is a member of Asiya Shrine, the Masonic Rosicrucian Society of the United
States, the National Sojourners - Golden Gate Chapter No. 18 and Heroes of ‘76.
He served as president of the Golden Gate Masters and Past Masters Association
and the Chinese Acacia Club. In June 2012, he was elected an honorary member
of DeMolay International’s Supreme Council.
In community affairs, Frank has served the Saint Monica Men’s Club
and the San Francisco Chinatown Lions Club.
Frank was born in San Francisco, attended California public schools,
and graduated from San Francisco State University with a Bachelor of Arts in
business administration. He and his wife, Jeanie, have been married for 39 years
and have two adult sons, Kevin and Gregory. Their oldest son, Kevin, is currently
serving our country in the United States Army and is on his second tour of duty
in Afghanistan.

One Hundred Sixty-Third
Annual Communication
Friday Afternoon, September 21, 2012
The 163rd Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of the State of California was called to order by Grand Master
Frank Loui on Friday, September 21, 2012.
Worshipful Brother Richard J. Modolo, Master of California Lodge
No. 1 raised the opening session of Grand Lodge. The gavel used to raise Grand
Lodge once belonged to Very Worshipful Brother Levi Stowell, the first Master of
California Lodge No. 1, in 1849, and also the first Grand Treasurer of the Grand
Lodge of California in 1850. Stowell then served as the second Grand Secretary
from 1851 until his death on May 18, 1855. This gavel will be used to raise Grand
Lodge throughout the weekend.
Reception of the Past Grand Masters
The Grand Master welcomed the brethren and directed the Grand
Marshal to present the Past Grand Masters of the Grand Lodge of California at
the Altar. The Grand Marshal then introduced each Past Grand Master, following
which the Grand Master, accompanied by the Deputy Grand Master, personally
greeted each one. The Grand Master asked the brethren to join him in saluting our
Past Grand Masters by the battery of three times three. The Past Grand Masters
were then escorted to seats reserved for them in the auditorium. The Grand Master
then directed the Grand Secretary to send to each absent Past Grand Master the
usual letter of greeting from the Grand Lodge.
Roll Call
The Grand Secretary was asked to call the roll of Grand Lodge Officers,
Past Grand Masters, and Past Grand Officers, and to ascertain if a constitutional
number was present to convene the Grand Lodge of California. The following
were present as indicated by their response to the calling of the roll:

Video Presentation
The Grand Lodge of California premiered a new video entitled “Emblems
of Innocence and Honor: The Masonic Apron.” This ten-minute video looks
at the apron’s origin, its enhancement to a ceremonial vestment with elaborate
decoration, ending with its current state as a piece of uniform apparel. The video
follows the creation of Masonic aprons from the time they were made by hand
in the home to the era of mass production in the factory. Experts and artisans
from across the country will guide us through the history of the Masonic apron.
They include our own Worshipful Brother Adam Kendall, the collections manager
of the Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum; Dr. Aimee Newall, collections
director of the Northern Jurisdiction Scottish Rite museum and library, and
Brother Patrick Craddock, an artisan from Tennessee.
At 4:55 p.m. the Grand Master called Grand Lodge from labor to
refreshment, to be called on again at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday, September 22.

Saturday Morning, September 22, 2012

Brother Fady Zoubi, Master of San Francisco Lodge No. 120.
Introduction of the District Inspectors

auditorium the District Inspectors. The Grand Master thanked the Inspectors for

and presented each of them with a small token of appreciation.
Video Presentation from the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees
Traditionally, the chairmen of the several boards provide verbal reports
during the Annual Communication and a written report appears in the Proceedings
following the Annual Communication. This year, reports are being delivered in
advance and video presentations will be presented throughout the sessions. The
Grand Master directed attention to the video screen for the Report of the Masonic
Homes Board of Trustees. The complete written report can be found in Appendix
J of these Proceedings.

Continuation of Legislation
The Grand Master reiterated the rules governing the proper protocol and
manner of discussion on the various pieces of legislation.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

15

Memorial Service
The Grand Master called on the Very Reverend Joseph H. Ross, Grand
Chaplain, to present a service of remembrance for our departed brethren.
My brethren, we gather here today to remember those among our ranks
who have fulfilled their obligations and completed their time with us. Since our
last meeting one year ago, 334 members of this Grand Lodge have passed to their
eternal reward. They have served this great fraternity to the fullest devoting many
hours to coaching, mentoring, delivering our positive lectures, and performing so
many kind acts in the name of brotherly love, relief, and truth. Our brethren have
laid down their earthly trowels and have ended their toils here on earth. They
are now gathered into that celestial lodge above where the Great Architect of the
Universe, the Ruler and Creator of All, presides.
These departed brethren’s contributions enriched our lives and blazed
a path for each of us to follow that bridges all time and space. I ask each of you
to pause with me now to recall at least one such brother whom you admired.
Remember his example--how he lived the values of our fraternity, how he led with
humility when called upon, and how he followed with devotion and enthusiasm in
all of our efforts. Finally, remember and honor the labor he put forth in perfecting
his ashlar as well as the aid and assistance he provided to you in perfecting your
ashlar, by living a life as admirable and praiseworthy as his.
With brotherly love and gratitude to our brethren who have passed to the
celestial lodge above, we say,
“Soft and safe to thee, my brethren, be thy resting place! Bright and
glorious be thy rising from it! Fragrant be the acacia sprig that there
shall flourish! May the earliest buds of spring unfold their beauties o’er
thy resting place, and there may the sweetness of the summer’s last rose
linger longest! Though the winds of autumn may destroy the loveliness of
their existence, yet the destruction is not final, and in the springtime, they
shall surely bloom again. So, in the bright morning of the resurrection,
thy spirit shall spring into the newness of life and expand in immortal
beauty, in realms beyond the skies. Until then, our dear brothers, until
then. Farewell.” Amen

Very Worshipful Glenn D. Woody, Past Grand Treasurer, delivered a
eulogy for the late Past Grand Treasurer, Joseph W.R. Ashwill.

16

Proceedings of the

Eulogy
Joseph W.R. Ashwill
Joseph Wilbur Richard Ashwill, a Master Mason, born July 2, 1929,
entered into rest February 9, 2012. Age 82 years.
Joe was born in Arthur, Illinois, the son of Fern and Jerome Ashwill. He
had one sister.
The family moved to Indiana during the Depression. Joe graduated from
Connersville, Indiana High School in 1947. He served honorably in the Indiana
National Guard, discharged in 1951.
Brother Joe answered the lure of California in 1957 and spent some time
in sales in the clothing business. It was probably there that he developed his lifelong trait of dressing impeccably.
But, soon the investment business called him and he went to work at
the Pacific Stock Exchange in Los Angeles. He later moved to the brokerage side
of the business and spent some time with a couple of brokerage firms before
joining Wedbush Securities in 1984, where he remained until his retirement on
June 30, 2010.
He married Barbara Pierce in 1985, and they resided in Orange County
and Long Beach until his death.
Brother Joe was raised in Warren Lodge No. 15 in Connersville, Indiana
on May 17, 1954. He affiliated with Bixby Knolls Neptune Lodge No. 699, now
Long Beach Lodge No. 327, in California on March 5, 1975, and served as its
Worshipful Master in 1981.
Our Brother Joe was a member of many Masonic related bodies such as
the York Rite bodies in Long Beach, Al Malaikah Shrine in Los Angeles, High
Twelve, Royal Order of Scotland, Robert The Bruce Association, Red Cross
Of Constantine, National Sojourners, and others. But, his Masonic activity was
centered around the Blue Lodge, California Grand Lodge and the Long Beach
Scottish Rite bodies.
Joe joined the Scottish Rite bodies in Indianapolis, Indiana, in 1954 and
affiliated with the Long Beach bodies in 1980. There he served on their Board
of Governors from 1984 to 2005, was Director of the Work from 1992 to 2005
and served as the Personal Representative from 2007 until his death earlier this
year. He was designated a Knight Commander Court of Honor in 1987 and was
coroneted a 33 Degree Inspector General Honorary in 1993.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

17

At the Grand Lodge level, Joe served as an Inspector from1984 to 1992,
was a member of the then Temple Properties Committee from 1981 to 1986. He
was a member of the Grand Lodge Investment Committee from 1993 to 2008,
serving as it Chairman from 1998 through 2000. Joe served as Junior Grand
Deacon in 1991-1992 and was elected Grand Treasurer in October 2000, serving
for two Grand Lodge years.
Joe was always happy, smiling, affable and thought the best of everyone.
His ray of sunshine in every room and his dedicated service to the Grand Lodge,
Scottish Rite and Masonry in general will be sorely missed.
Soft and safe to thee, My Brother . . .

Most Worshipful Alvin J. Weis, Past Grand Master, delivered a eulogy
for the late Past Grand Master, E. Arthur Haglund.

18

Proceedings of the

Eulogy
E. Arthur Haglund
It is with great pleasure and a high honor that I have been chosen to
present the eulogy for my long time friend and Masonic brother, Edward Arthur
Haglund, the 118th Grand Master of Masons in California and Hawaii who passed
away in Spokane, Washington on October 17, 2011.
“Behold, How Good And How Pleasant It Is For Brethren To Dwell
Together In Unity” -Psalm 133-1. This beautiful passage was well-known to the
great and good man whose memory we here honor.
Art was born into a family of Masons on May 8, 1928 in Havre, Montana
where his father and grandfather were both Past Masters of Havre Masonic Lodge
No. 55. His mother was a member of the Order of Eastern Star. In his youth Art
became Master Councilor of Havre Chapter, Order of DeMolay and holder of the
Chevalier and Legion of Honor Degrees. Another facet of his early leadership
skills was shown by his Eagle Scout award with four palms along with the God
and Country Award.
After graduating from the University of Montana, with a Bachelor
of Science Degree in Business Administration, Art enlisted into the United
States Navy and served on Johnson Island and later at Pearl Harbor Submarine
Base. Returning home he completed graduate school majoring in Production
Management at the University of Washington. All this led him into thirty years
of management positions with Kaiser Aluminum. At the time of his retirement,
he was International Marketing Manager working out of Kaiser Headquarters in
Oakland, California where he traveled worldwide visiting Kaiser’s many plants
around the world.
He met and married his vivacious and lovely wife Barbie, while they
were attending the University of Montana and were blessed with two married
children and two grandchildren. Barbie was a stalwart companion and helper in
Art’s long and successful Masonic endeavors before she died in November 2007.
Art was installed as the 118th Grand Master of Masons in California
and Hawaii in this beautiful Masonic Memorial Temple on October 12, 1983.
His education and professional experience prepared him explicitly for Masonic
leadership which was headlined by his philosophy, “One Mason Can Make a
Difference -You”, which he espoused throughout his year as Grand Master as
he traveled up and down the State of California and the State of Hawaii. By his
enthusiasm, spirit, dedication and persuasiveness he convinced all who heard him
that here was one Mason who did indeed make a difference and convinced others
to follow. Even the smile on his face sent a message of friendship and concern for
those he was conversing with.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

19

Recognizing many of the challenges besetting our Fraternity in the 1980s,
Art instituted programs aimed at achieving quality and excellence in the operation
of individual lodges, including formulating long term goals and the objectives to
accomplish these goals. Working with his Executive Committee, he improved
training methods for the benefit of lodge officers. This was accomplished through
implementing new Fraternal Management Courses, along with the expansion of
the Leadership Workshops for all interested Masons.
Art introduced The Grand Master’s Achievement Award, and during
the 1984 Annual Communications he recognized 61 Brothers for their special
leadership accomplishments. Certainly, Art’s problem-solving and management
development skills accumulated through his many years experience as an executive
in the corporate world were very helpful during his Grand Lodge leadership years.
“One Mason Can Make a Difference -You” were the words he left us and our
departed Grand Master’s entire adult life made a difference to many people and
revolved around the principles of Freemasonry by subscribing to its teachings and
practicing its philosophy. Our California Grand Lodge benefited greatly by his
leadership and by his personal friendship with all of us.
California’s Grand Master Frank Loui and Past Grand Master Alvin
J. Weis traveled to Spokane, Washington to officiate Most Worshipful Art’s
memorial service.
To everything there is a season:
A time for everything under the sun
A time to be born and a time to die
A time to laugh and a time to cry
A time to dance and a time to mourn
A time to seek and a time to let go.
This is the time we remember One who gave meaning to our lives. This
is the time to remember the bonds that tied us together, the love that we shared,
and the memories that remain with us still.
Almighty Father, into Thy hands we commend the soul of our
beloved brother.
At 12:00 p.m. the Grand Master called Grand Lodge from labor to
refreshment, to be called on again at 1:15 p.m.

Coren T. Andrews
Worshipful Brother Coren T. Andrews, past master of East San Diego
Lodge No. 561 and past master of Amity Lodge No. 442, has served Rainbow for
Girls for more than 22 years, including 15 years on the advisory boards for Myrtle
and Infinity Assemblies. He has served numerous terms as Infinity’s Rainbow
Dad and has been chairperson of the Advisory Board for more than 10 years.
Brother Andrews continues to make a variety of contributions to the
Rainbow organization: In San Juan Capistrano, he manages the 4th of July booth;
at Southern Rainbow Camp, he coordinates proficiency exams and performs a
myriad of other assignments; at Grand Assembly, he is often the chief cook; and
at many Rainbow installations and receptions, he serves as a photographer. In
addition, Coren has served as Rainbow’s webmaster for 13 years, creating the
organization’s original website and promptly handling all updates. His devotion
has also reached outside California – he has represented Infinity Assembly
at New Mexico’s Grand Assembly for the past 14 years, completing service
projects and attending other trainings to bring innovative programs to California’s
Rainbow assemblies.
A five year member of the Grand Lodge Youth Orders Committee and
2004 Hiram Award recipient, Brother Coren has been recognized with the Grand
Cross of Color – Rainbow’s highest honor, recognizing several years of exemplary
service beyond the call of duty.
Steven Cooley
Worshipful Brother Steven Cooley, past master of Conejo Valley Lodge
No. 807, has been active in Job’s Daughters since 1988 at the local, state, and
international levels. He is a dedicated mentor for members of Job’s Daughters
Bethel No. 324, Thousand Oaks, where he served as associate bethel guardian
for nine years. For the past 12 years, Steve has chaired the men’s luncheon at
Grand Guardian Council. He has also served as the Grand Guardian Council’s
grand chaplain; as co-chair of the Grand Bethel of California’s variety show; and
as a twenty-one year member of the Mar Monte Guardian Council Association.
Outside Job’s Daughters, Brother Cooley is active in Conejo Valley Chapter No.
632 of the Order of the Eastern Star, where he has served as worthy patron for
three terms. In the Grand Chapter of California, Order of the Eastern Star, Steve
served as the 2011 grand sentinel.
Brother Cooley’s charitable spirit is reflected in his eight-year term as a
member of the Board of Directors for the Hearing Impaired Kids’ Endowment Fund,
and has been California Job’s Daughters’ liaison to the HIKE Fund since 2002.
HIKE is the philanthropic project of Job’s Daughter’s International, providing
hearing devices for underprivileged children. Steve has also been involved in
philanthropic efforts through his work as a Mason: A Hiram Award recipient,

Richard P. Harlan
Worshipful Brother Richard P. Harlan, an inspector of the 810th Masonic
district and past master of San Bernardino Lodge No. 178, has been involved with
DeMolay for nearly 25 years, receiving both the Chevalier and Legion of Honor.
Richard is a member of San Bernardino Chapter, Order of DeMolay.
He served as a chapter dad for more than 10 years, and continues to act as a
key chapter advisor. A four year assistant eastern league administrator and two
year web master, Brother Harlan was recognized with the Guild of the Leather
Apron, equivalent to an advisor of the year award, in 2002. He has also served as
Inland Empire’s district governor, a deputy member of the International Supreme
Council, and as Southern California Jurisdiction’s communication chairman – a
position he has held for the past four years.
A dedicated Mason, Brother Harlan has been a member of the San
Bernardino Building Association since 1996 and has served several terms as its
president. Richard is also actively involved in several appendant bodies: He is
a longtime member of the San Bernardino Scottish Rite where he has served as
master of Kadosh, wise master of Rose Croix, and, currently, as venerable master.
He is also a member of Order of the Eastern Star, Tri-Star No. 211, and is actively
involved in York Rite as a member of Keystone Chapter No. 56 ; Valley Council
No. 27 of Cryptic Masons; and St. Bernard Commandery No. 23.
Charles R. Wilson
Brother Charles R. Wilson, a member of North Butte Lodge No. 230 in
Gridley, has been involved with DeMolay for more than 40 years, including a
term as superior divisional master councilor in 1975. He has earned the Chevalier,
Cross of Honor, and Legion of Honor.
Brother Wilson’s many contributions to Northern California DeMolay
have revitalized the services offered by the organization. To assist youth with
public speaking engagements, he developed the Northern California DeMolay
Public Speaking Training – an innovative program providing real-time coaching
to youth leaders, greatly improving their speaking skills and self-confidence. A
director of the DeMolay Foundation and a member of the scholarship committee,
Charlie has devoted countless hours to mentoring scholarship recipients. He

also volunteers as a musician at installations, conventions, and other DeMolay

Brother Wilson embodies the principles of DeMolay and is a wonderful
example of what a Master Mason should be; his dedication and selflessness will
inspire the next generation of DeMolay and Masonic leaders.

education for generations to come.

43

Grand Master’s Message
Good afternoon, brethren. I am pleased to welcome the delegates and
members of the Grand Lodge of California Free and Accepted Masons to this
163rd Annual Communication of our Grand Lodge.
For 163 years, we have traveled from the north and from the south, from
the mountains and from the valleys, to unite as a fraternity. Welcome back. Thank
you for trusting me with this great honor, as your 146th Grand Master. I hope I’ve
served you well.
To our guests from other jurisdictions, we are glad to have you here this
weekend. Thank you for your friendship, and your support.
I’d like to recognize Worshipful Paul L. Owyang, the master who
appointed me to my first leadership position in 1988. I’d also like to recognize
Worshipful Edward P. Margherio, my first supervisor as District Inspector in 1993.
These two individuals started my leadership position within our gentle craft.
I stand before you now to fulfill one of my final responsibilities as your
Grand Master: a report on the condition of our craft.
California is blessed with scores of devoted Masons. As I traveled this
state, I had the chance to meet you and your families. At every lodge, I saw men
who have put the fraternity at the center of their daily lives, who have made it
part of their dinner table conversations and community service. You don’t do it
for fame or fortune or recognition. You do it because it’s the right thing. All year
long, you inspired me.
Over the past 12 months, I represented the Grand Lodge by presiding
over eight cornerstone ceremonies, seven lodge anniversaries, and 12 installations.
I visited with our remarkable youth orders at all four jurisdictional meetings, even
a Job’s Daughters Leadership Retreat at Camp Hammer. We traveled to eight
other Masonic jurisdictions, including Louisiana, South Carolina, and Wyoming,
and represented California Masonry at the Western Conference of Masonic Grand
Lodges and the Conference of Grand Masters of Masons in North America. I was
privileged to bestow a 50-year pin and eleven Diamond Jubilee pins.
This year, I instituted Veritas Lodge U.D. and chartered Golden
Compasses Research Lodge. On the other hand, seven charters were arrested for
various reasons, from lack of officers to financial irresponsibility. I was pleased
to restore two of those, Texas Lodge No. 46 and Santa Clara Valley Daylight No.
844. We will continue working with the remaining five lodges, Sublime Benicia
No. 5, Santa Lucia No. 302, Foothill No. 305, Valle de France No. 329, and Chino

44

Proceedings of the

Valley No. 427. Some of you have been asked to help rebuild these lodges. Thank
you for showing true leadership in the face of serious challenges. There’s a lot at
stake. If a lodge folds, that community no longer has a Masonic presence. And
our communities today need Masons more than ever. Let’s help get these lodges
back on track.
I want to share another piece of Masonic news, which is both negative
and positive. This past June, the lodge building of Crescent No. 45 in Crescent
City was destroyed by arson. The building was lost, along with all of their records.
On July 2nd, although the building site was still warm from fire, the lodge held
their stated meeting in the parking lot, under the guidance of the fire department.
The Grand Lodge of Oregon stretched forth their hand and invited them to hold
subsequent meetings at Brookings, Oregon, less than 20 miles away, until they
rebuilt their home. I attended that first meeting in Brookings on August 6th. We
had 104 in attendance that evening, with members from Crescent City and several
lodges from Oregon. Two Past Grand Masters from Oregon and their current
Senior Grand Deacon attended. That Senior Grand Deacon is Worshipful Arthur
Borland, a past master of Three Great Lights in Menlo Park. Worshipful Borland is
in attendance this afternoon. Let’s give our neighbor, the Grand Lodge of Oregon,
a big hand of appreciation and thank you. In the weeks since, Crescent Lodge
was able to move into a new temporary building, closer to home in Crescent
City. But they will not soon forget the brotherhood and graciousness of our
northern brethren.
As to the general condition of the craft, we are steadily replenishing our
numbers. We conferred 4,252 degrees this year. We had the most affiliations since
2000. The Great Architect was kind to us this year, and the number of deaths was
the lowest since 1935. Our total losses were at 3,777 – still higher than our total
gains, but we continue to narrow the gap.
Over the past five years, it has become clear that our fraternity is in
a period of regrowth. A few years ago, Most Worshipful Larry Adamson stood
here to deliver his Grand Master’s Message. He predicted that, by the end of this
decade, our gains would at last overtake our losses, and we would be in a period
of true growth. I share his confidence. There is a new wave of young men out there
who understand and value what we offer. They are seeking us out. And we are
meeting them halfway. 163 years ago, we offered brotherhood, relief, and truth.
We still do. But today, we are offering it in more modern ways.
We are three years into our fraternity’s 2010-2015 strategic plan. For
proof of how we are evolving, look no further. Our course is plotted under
five priority areas: Member experience; Masonic education; Leadership and
management; Beyond the lodge; and Philanthropy. We’re taking huge strides in
all of them.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

45

We rolled out a new application, and added new applicant information
sections to freemason.org. We developed a new applicant investigation process,
which we’ll introduce to the fraternity this fall. We’ll also introduce a new,
web-based candidate education program. We held the 2012 California Masonic
Symposium in two cities – which made it possible for a record 436 members
to attend. With UCLA, we cohosted our first International Conference of
Freemasonry. We created a training program for the adult leaders of Masonic
youth orders. In the field of care giving, we’re developing new aging care options
for members who choose to age at home.
We redesigned our leadership retreats to make them more collaborative,
including combining masters and wardens for the first time. The new design
focuses on leadership development and building a vibrant lodge culture. We
updated the Lodge Management Certification Program to be a webinar series,
making it more productive and interactive. We developed a new LMCP course to
specifically address improving the member experience.
Many of you witnessed these advances firsthand: In total, 1,280 brothers
and their ladies attended this year’s leadership programs.
With two years left, we still have our work cut out for us. We are
working on Web and mobile apps for Masonic education; an online accounting
and reporting system for lodges and hall associations; and improvements to ritual
instruction. Through the Masonic Homes, we’re doing important work in memory
care. We intend to be a leader in this field, just as the Masonic Center for Youth
and Families has positioned us as a leader in the field of youth psychology.
At the lodge level, a number of you have embraced the strategic plan.
Thank you. You deserve an enormous amount of credit. Any progress has been
on your watch, and by the hard work of Grand Lodge committees and staff. But
I’ll level with you. Just as many lodges have stood by and watched. Change is
not easy. But those lodges have been unwilling to put in the work, or stray from
business as usual. Ask yourself: Are you doing your part? If the answer is no, the
time is now. Have a conversation with your lodge leaders. Print out the strategic
plan. Measure your lodge by it every month. Rise to your potential.
I am proud to share the most recent update of our Raising A Reader
project. The goal was to bring Raising A Reader’s literacy program to California
kindergartners for the first time. Kids who can’t read at grade level struggle in
every subject in school, and often drop out altogether. They never reach their
potential, or get the opportunities they deserve. California is ranked near the
bottom of the U.S. for child literacy. By partnering with Raising A Reader, we set
out to change that.
At last count, you raised more than $505,868, thanks to contributions by
151 lodges and 1,377 individuals – an astounding number; the highest individual
participation we’ve ever had for a Grand Master’s Project. There’s still time
to contribute.

46

Proceedings of the

Your generosity will have long-term effects. Thanks to your contributions
so far, we will bring Raising A Reader to about 5,000 students. We are targeting
the lowest-performing classrooms for the greatest impact. The program runs for
five years on its initial investment. And our work has just begun.
Members asked for a statewide program in support of public schools.
This is it. Raising A Reader will be our fraternity’s project for years to come.
Together, we can turn the page for child literacy in California.
For my first 21 years of life, I only lived three and a half blocks from
Grand Lodge. I graduated from high school in this auditorium and on this stage.
When I attended SF State, it was three blocks from the Scottish Rite from where
I am currently working. At the time, I didn’t realize how important Masons were
to my education. Now, I know the whole story. When California was first settled;
during the teacher shortage of 1920; and many times since; the Masons stepped
forward and gave public education a hand. The schools need us again. And once
again, we have stepped up.
In closing, when we gather every year at Annual Communication, it’s
worth asking: Why are we Masons? Why do we put in the time, when time is so
precious? In the grand scheme of things, why do we matter?
The Masonic scholar Margaret Jacob, one of our partners at UCLA,
would give one answer. She would talk about our influence on democracy around
the world. A widow in Stockton would give another answer. She would say that
the Masons took care of her when she got sick. And a student at Jose Ortega
Elementary School? The Masons helped him learn how to read.
My point is that we don’t do this for ourselves. The great things Masons
do – the things that go down in history – do not occur inside the lodge. They might
start there. But ultimately, they are measured in our communities, our country, and
our world.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

47

Connect – Communicate – Commit
My thanks to my executive committee for their tireless work. To Most
Worshipful M. William Holsinger, who is retiring as grand treasurer, for his
invaluable service. To the Grand Family for all the support they showed Jeanie
and me, and the sacrifices they made for the fraternity. To every board president
and member; to every committee chair and member; for volunteering precious
time and talent behind the scenes. To the Grand Lodge staff in San Francisco,
Union City, and Covina for advancing our fraternity and taking on our causes as
their own. And most of all, to my family and to my wife, Jeanie. You have stood
by me and supported me, rearranged your year for me, and have been patient and
understanding without fail.
To every brother in this room: Thank you for the extraordinary privilege
of leading this fraternity. This year, I lived a dream. It wouldn’t have happened
without you.

Respectfully submitted,
Frank Loui, Grand Master

Report of the Deputy Grand Master
2012/2013 Grand Lodge Budget
John F. Lowe, Deputy Grand Master

As your Deputy Grand Master, it is my duty to prepare and present to
you a budget for the upcoming fiscal year. First let me say that I am grateful for
the support of the brethren who adopted the per capita proposal I submitted at the
2011 Annual Communication.
Since that time, I have been refining the budget while monitoring current
income and expenses as well as our membership activity. Earlier this year, I
discussed the budget further with the Masters and Wardens at our retreats. Their
input over the last two years has been very helpful. I have also worked with the
Grand Lodge Finance Committee, our Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary and our
finance staff to be sure that we are operating in an efficient and responsible way.
As a result of this teamwork, I now place the attached budget before you for
consideration at the upcoming Annual Communication.
Our strategy with this budget has been to control costs without reducing
services and programs. I am proud to say, that with the help and input from a lot
of our members and our staff, we have achieved that.
Revenue for the next fiscal year is estimated to be $2,636,088, which is
approximately 3.4% more than the 2011/12 fiscal year, mostly due to an increase
in the dividend from the Nob Hill Masonic Center. The summary of changes in
revenue from the current year is as follows:
The actual per capita collected will decrease by approximately $20,000
and income from applications will decrease by approximately $12,000 however
income from investments will remain the same. The dividend from the Nob Hill
Masonic Center will increase by $87,000.
Expenses for the next fiscal year are estimated to be $2,608,540, which
is approximately 3.3% more than the 2011/2012 fiscal year. The main factors that
contribute to the increase are as follow:
Lodge insurance will increase by 6.5%, wages will increase by 2.5% and
health care premiums by 8.7%. Items subject to inflation are planned to increase
by 2%.
The projected net revenue after expenses is $19,183.
I thank you, again, for your previous support and ask for your support
now as we consider this budget for our coming fiscal year.

John F. Lowe, Deputy Grand Master
Revenue Analysis
The Grand Lodge has several sources of income. Historically, the primary revenue source has been per-capita and
degree fees. The Grand Lodge Endowment Fund was created in 1992 and generates investment income. To better
manage those monies, a four and a half-percent spending policy has been instituted, calculated on a rolling five-year
valuation to ensure the preservation of the fund principle. The Grand Lodge may have other income like interest on
bank accounts and other financial instruments from time to time. In 2004, the California Masonic Foundation included
in its mission the funding of Masonic education and leadership training programs and now provides a grant for those
purposes. In 2005, the delegates of the 156th Annual Communication adopted a $30 application fee to be paid to
Grand Lodge by all applicants for degrees and out-of-state affiliations. The Grand Lodge manages different service
bureaus throughout the state and receives reimbursement for those expenses. The Grand Lodge also manages the
investments of its related entities and receives reimbursement equal to the cost of those services. The Grand Lodge is
the sole shareholder of the Nob Hill Masonic Center Inc., and may receive dividends on the profits of the corporation.

Installation Address

John F. Lowe
Grand Master of Masons in California, 2012-2013
In 2005, I stood before this fraternity to deliver my Grand Oration. I
talked about the importance of constancy and quoted Benjamin Franklin, who
said, “Without Steadiness or Perseverance, no Virtue can long subsist.”
Seven years have passed, and I am humbled to stand before you now as
grand master. I am proud to say that in those seven years, we have been constant.
We have shown steadiness and perseverance. We have kept our eyes laser-focused
on our goals. And here we are today, beginning the 164th year of our Grand Lodge.
I have had my eyes on this particular milepost for some time.
Seven years ago in that same Grand Oration, I talked about our strategic
plan. I called it “the constancy of purpose to guide our craft.” We have since
completed that plan, and drawn up a new one. Our current strategic plan, for 2010
through 2015, is a mandate from our members. It’s bold. It’s uncompromising.
It’s something to be proud of, and built for future generations of Masons to use
as a compass.
We have drilled down to five priorities: Membership experience,
leadership development, Masonic education, beyond the lodge, and philanthropy.
Using these priorities, we have attached our goals to new mileposts, even further
off on the horizon. Once again, with steadiness and with perseverance, we are
gaining on them.
We added world-class Masonic education, including a second
Symposium location and an international conference with our partners at
UCLA. We’re developing new interactive, Web-based candidate education. We
introduced a new application form and are preparing to roll out a new applicant
investigation process. While in the past our lodges were schools of government,
lodges today are schools of leadership. So while we overhauled many of our
officer leadership development programs, we didn’t stop there. With the goal of
rejuvenating leadership throughout the fraternity, we have initiated The Masonic
Leadership Project, which will explore and define what leadership means today
to all California Masons. We’re planning improvements to ritual instruction.
And we’re creating more ways to connect lodges and individuals with Masonic
Outreach resources.
These are just a few examples of the goals we are reaching, and surpassing.
With every accomplishment, we embody our vision: For the Masons of California
to be a relevant, respected organization, both inside and outside the fraternity.
To be engaged in the worldwide principles and fellowship of Freemasonry. To
make that profound difference in the lives of our members and in California’s
communities that you mandated to be the prime directive in all that we do.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

75

Seven years ago I asked you, “Will you, each day, brighten a part of
your community?” Today, I ask you again. My theme as grand master is Beyond
the Lodge: Serving our communities. Supporting our public schools. Making a
profound difference in California.
These goals are all part of the promise we made when we became
Masons. Fulfilling them is not always easy. But we didn’t become Masons to
do what’s easy. We became Masons to make a difference. We became Masons
to lead.
That’s who we are. Masons do what’s right, even when it takes a lot of
work. We rise to the challenges of the times we live in. Let each of us gather up
our working tools, and set to work on the tasks at hand.
Another key element of our work has been an annual Grand Master’s
project. In recent years our Grand Lodge has used this platform to accomplish
amazing things for our communities.
When we began drafting the current strategic plan, you asked for a
statewide commitment to public education. Inspired by that charge, we’ve focused
on literacy --- and our partnership with Raising A Reader is that commitment.
We took our queues from meetings with school and educational leadership from
across the state and set out on the path to do something big for public education.
Our strategic plan has provided us with the path forward. Rather than
develop a Grand Master’s project each year, we are able to use the strategic plan
to guide our work, and to make a difference. We needed something big. We must
step in where no one else can, or will. Brethren, literacy, along with engaging
and strengthening families, remains as critical today as ever. That’s why we will
call our program the fraternity’s project – not the Grand Master’s project --- and
Becky and I couldn’t be more thrilled. We now have the continuity to address
large problems over multiple years. Imagine what we can accomplish.
Our partnership with Raising A Reader has already improved hundreds
of lives– and over the course of the next several years, it will help thousands more,
eventually reaching more than 50,000 California students and families directly.
Masons have always valued knowledge --- and the freedom that comes with it.
Our commitment to literacy ensures that the system of public education we have
championed for more than 150 years will grow stronger for future generations.
Raising A Reader is not only about literacy – it’s also about engaging
families in need. Research tells us that families that read together are stronger.
Period. Active engagement and involvement in a child’s education solidifies
that child’s chance at success – both in academics and in life. Reading to a
child improves everything from vocabulary skills to self-confidence. But most
importantly, it strengthens that critical relationship between a child and a family
member. That’s what our partnership with Raising A Reader helps create. Stronger

76

Proceedings of the

families, strong schools and stronger communities. Let me say that again. We will
help build strong families – which help create strong schools --- which serve to
strengthen our communities.
Parents and caregivers today face a growing number of challenges. Even
in these complex times, most families are eager to dedicate time to reading and
bonding with their children. But competing priorities – unavoidable realities and
responsibilities – often get in the way and rob them of those opportunities. It’s up
to us to do all we can to help deserving families statewide face these challenges
head on and provide them with the tools they need to succeed in the most difficult,
but most rewarding, role of their lives.
Study after study has proved it; Raising A Reader is built upon it: In
literacy, and in learning, family is the foundation.
We all know the importance of family; we became Masons to be
better fathers, husbands, and sons. We know that families are at the heart of our
communities, and that strong schools are built on strong communities. Let’s make
literacy our legacy, and our gift to the children of California.
This year, I ask you to stand beside me in support of this mission, and
work beside me with the same steadiness and perseverance that you have already
shown. I ask you to go beyond the lodge, and leave a lasting impact on California
and Masonry. We have visibility unlimited to our goals on the distant horizon, and
the compass of virtue to guide us always towards true north.
Brother Winston Churchill once said, “If you have knowledge, let others
light their candles with it.”
My brethren: Now is the moment to step out beyond the lodge, and
spread that light.

Report of the Senior Grand Warden
Per Capita Recommendation for 2013-2014
John L. Cooper III, Senior Grand Warden

As your Senior Grand Warden, I am responsible for preparing and
presenting to the Grand Lodge a proposal for the per capita assessment that will
be collected in 2013 to fund the Grand Lodge fiscal year for the period November
1, 2013 through October 31, 2014.
Beginning with my term as Junior Grand Warden, I have worked with
the Executive Committee, the Finance Committee and the Grand Lodge staff to
develop projections of the income and the necessary expenses for the 2014 fiscal
year. Earlier this year, I was able to share our plans with the Masters and Wardens
who attended the spring leadership retreats. I really appreciated the comments I
received during and following the retreats.
The proposal that I enclose for you seeks to maintain programs
and services of our Grand Lodge while planning for certain efficiencies and
improvements.
After decades of serious decline, membership in our fraternity is moving
toward stabilization. We project that we will have a net loss of members in 2013,
but it will be one of the smallest losses in the last 40 years. Our strategic plan is
helping us shape our future to be a more effective and relevant fraternity.
Earlier this year, you received information about Intacct, a web‐based
accounting and reporting solution for lodges and hall associations. The program
will be implemented this coming year with some 50 lodges on board before the
end of the year. It is expected that as many as 200 additional lodges will join the
program in 2013 and more in 2014. With our fraternity working together in this
important area, we will increase consistency and continuity in the way we account
for our finances, and we will simplify the process so it is less of a burden on our
lodges and our hall associations. This initiative includes relieving lodges from
having to make financial reports to the Grand Lodge and the state and federal
government. In 2014, the Grand Lodge will complete the required forms 1099 and
199 (the federal and state financial returns) for all lodges, whether or not they are
using the Intacct system as their own local financial accounting system. In order to
fund this service, I have allocated approximately $50,000 to support the system.
In preparing a draft budget for the 2013/14 fiscal year, I have considered
the factors that will increase per capita, as well as those factors that will mitigate
the necessary increase.

80

Proceedings of the
The factors that will increase per capita are:
•

Membership loss. We project a total loss of 1,555 billable
members, which represents a loss in revenue of $54,425.

•

Insurance. Premiums for our lodge insurance will increase
by 6%.

•

Labor costs. Wages are held to a 3% increase. Health care
premiums will increase costs by an additional 3%.

•

Professional fees: The support for the Intacct system is $50,549.

•

Inflation. Items subject to inflation are expected to increase
by 2%.

The factors that will help offset the per capita increase are the following:
•

Nob Hill Dividend. We project that the dividend from the Nob
Hill Masonic Center will be $189,750, which is $44,537 more
than the previous year.

•

Cost savings. We have identified a number of expenses that
can be held at or near last year’s levels without any factor for
inflation. You will notice that the expenses in many categories
are nearly the same as the budget presented by the Deputy
Grand Master.

These factors allow us to present a balanced budget, with a per capita
of $37.50.
However, as you heard earlier today, the members of this Grand Lodge
decided that Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons will now pay dues,
and, in turn, the lodge will make a per capita contribution to Grand Lodge for each
Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Mason. This will have the effect of lowering
the per capita assessment for all Masons. Taking into account the total number of
Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons now on the rolls of our lodges, and
considering a rate of dues remissions for these Masons at the same rate as Master
Masons, we will add 9,340 Masons to the per capita assessment. This means the
necessary per capita for the 2013/14 Grand Lodge year will be $32.00.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

81

I know that Freemasonry means as much to you as it does to me. We
want to continue to make advancements even in uncertain economic times. I have
worked diligently with many others to insure that the increase will be justified by
improvements in our fraternity. I strongly support lodge and hall involvement in
the new accounting system. I believe our leadership development, membership
development, and masonic education programs are essential to our future. Your
support for the adoption of this per capita proposal, will allow us to maintain the
programs and services of our Grand Lodge with a reasonable and responsible per
capita, and we will also greatly improve our accounting and reporting systems.
Thank you for your support of the 2013/14 per capita proposal!

PER CAPITA

There are several factors that affect Per Capita, membership levels, insurance, labor costs and professional fees
are the primary factors. The membership analysis for the 2013/2014 fiscal year projects a total loss in
membership of 1,555 members. While this is one of the lowest losses of members in decades, the membership
decline will result in lost revenue of $54,425 or $1.08 in additional Per Capita. The professional fees supporting
the Intacct Project represent another $1.00 in Per Capita. Insurance, and modest labor increases along with
inflation of approximately 2% accounts for the additional Per Capita. All other things being equal, the Per Capita
would have to be increased by $3.38 to cover the effect of all of these factors discussed here. Due to
improvements in the Nob Hill Masonic Center operations, the Nob Hill Masonic Center dividend will result in a
revenue increase of $44,537, an $0.88 Per Capita reduction. These factors allow us to present a balanced
budget with a Per Capita of $37.50. However, during the 163rd Annual Communication meeting, the members of
the Grand Lodge of California decided that Entered Apprentices and Fellow Craft Masons will now pay dues, and,
in turn, the lodge will make a per capita contribution to Grand Lodge for each Entered Apprentice and Fellow
Craft Mason. This will have the effect of lowering the per capita assessment for all Masons. Taking into account
the total number of Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons now on the rolls of our lodges, and considering
a rate of dues remissions for these Masons at the same rate as Master Masons, we will add 9,340 Masons to the
per capita assessment. This means the necessary per capita for the 2013/2014 Grand Lodge year will be $32.00.

Report of the Grand Treasurer
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The overall financial condition of the Grand Lodge is strong. The Grand
Lodge, our Constituent Lodges, and we as individuals continue to deal with a
sluggish economy, a challenging employment market, and a volatile investment
market. While these factors affect the financial activities of the Grand Lodge, just
as they do for all of us, the Grand Lodge has met the challenge through diligent
efforts of the Grand Lodge officers, board and committee members and our staff.
The Grand Lodge Investment Committee carefully monitors the Grand
Lodge investment portfolio and has made changes in the portfolio to better
reflect the current economic times with an eye ever toward improving the return
on the portfolio without sacrificing safety. For the coming year, they have again
recommended the percentage of distribution to be taken from the portfolio for
budgeting for the 2012-2013 year to remain at 4.5%; and that recommendation
has been adopted by the Grand Lodge and each of the other entities participating
in the investment pool.
The Grand Lodge Insurance Committee through the expertise of its
members continues to keep the Grand Lodge and its various entities well protected
against loss at the lowest possible premium costs.
The Finance and the Audit Committees of the Grand Lodge continue to
perform their duties in an efficient manner, overseeing the financial affairs of all
related entities. The audits of all entities were completed with no audit comments
regarding weaknesses in internal controls.
We are fortunate to have an efficient and dedicated staff in the Grand
Lodge office – in particular the finance department under the very capable
leadership of Chief Financial Officer, Thomas Boyer. Their dedicated handling
of our financial affairs, together with the thoughtful foresight of our predecessors
in establishing healthy reserves which now generate income to fund much of our
annual programs, enable the various entities to provide consistent programs and
services to their constituents.
I must also make mention of the Executive Committee, consisting of
the Grand Master and the progressive elective line. In addition to their regular
meetings to discuss the direction and progress of Grand Lodge programs and
activities, they hold a separate monthly meeting to review the finances, comparing
budgeted income and expenses to actual, that they might take appropriate and
timely remedial action if indicated. It should also be noted that any surplus at the
end of the fiscal year is not carried over into the next year’s budget, but rather it
is transferred to the Grand Lodge endowment fund. The result is that each Grand
Master begins his year with a zero balance with only the budget for his year to
work with.

88

Proceedings of the

The detailed information I am going to give you today is for the ninemonth period from November 1, 2011 (the beginning of our fiscal year) through
July 31, 2012. It should be noted that the information for this nine-month period
is unaudited and has been prepared internally by our finance department staff. The
official proceedings of this Communication will contain audited financials for the
entire fiscal year ending October 31, 2012.
As of July 31, 2012, your Grand Lodge had assets of $6,962,597 and
liabilities of $3,588,858, for total net assets of $3,373,739. These assets were some
.3% higher than at the end of our October 31, 2011 fiscal year. Keep in mind that
most of the assets you might attach to the Grand Lodge are not actually owned by
the Grand Lodge itself and do not appear in these numbers. I am referring to major
assets such as this facility which is owned by the California Masonic Memorial
Temple Association, our Masonic Homes at Covina and Union City which are
owned by the Masonic Homes of California, Acacia Creek at Union City, and the
assets of the California Masonic Foundation, all separate corporations.
The last several years have been volatile ones in the investment markets.
The investment accounts of the Grand Lodge were down 11.4% for the twelvemonth period ended July 31, 2012.
For the nine months ended July 31, 2012, the total income was
$1,763,245, while total expenses were $1,579.877. While the net excess as of
July 31, 2012 of income over expenses is some $183,368, it should be noted that
approximately 20% of the total year’s expenses occur in the last three months of
the fiscal year. The current projection is that the Grand Lodge will end the fiscal
year on October 31, 2012 with a slight surplus.
The nine-month expenses were divided in the following manner: 21%
for fraternal matters (such as the annual communication, travel expenses of the
elected and appointed officers, and the insurance for the Constituent Lodges); 24%
for appropriations and programs (such as various Lodge Support Committees,
the Freemason magazine, Membership and Leadership Development, Masonic
Formation, and committees such as Policy, Jurisprudence, Investment, Ritual and
Trial Review), and 55% for General and Administrative items (such as salaries
and benefits, accounting and auditing, investment management fees, legal fees
and general office operations).
During this year, I was privileged to serve as a member of a task force
originally appointed by Most Worshipful William J. Bray III, which was charged
with the duty to study the subject of Life Membership Funds. The Committee,
chaired by Past Grand Treasurer, Very Worshipful Glenn Woody, has worked
diligently to develop legislation to clarify the existing program and to present some
new concepts for your consideration in the form of Resolutions 12-03 through 1209. The Life membership Fund can, and should be, a valuable investment tool
for Constituent Lodges that, if properly administered, can provide an avenue

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

89

for members to provide a perpetual source of income to their lodge that will
continue even after their death, and at the same time will relieve the member of
paying dues for the balance of his life. I urge you to give serious consideration to
these Resolutions.
Early in this year, the Grand Secretary requested that I assist him in the
disposition of the assets of Covina Lodge No. 334, whose charter was revoked at
the 2011 Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge. The results of our efforts
will be included in the report of the Grand Secretary.
I want to acknowledge the many dedicated brothers who serve on the
various Boards and Committees of this Grand Lodge, and its related entities.
Their dedication and hard work they devote to the affairs of this Grand Lodge is
extraordinary and they deserve our thanks.
The staff of this Grand Lodge is dedicated and as a symphony orchestra
is dependent upon its conductor, so our Grand Lodge staff is dependent upon our
Grand Secretary. Ten years ago I saw the potential in this man and first appointed
him to the office of Assistant Grand Secretary. Since that time he has exceeded
my greatest expectations. To Very Worshipful Allan Casalou we owe our most
sincere thanks.
Finally, my Brethren, as you know, I have chosen not to stand for reelection for next year. I began my service to Grand Lodge 43 years ago as a member
of the Public Schools Committee, and over the years I have been privileged to be a
part of this vibrant, ever advancing Grand Lodge. It is with every confidence that
I turn the post over to Worshipful Ray Schmalz, who I anticipate you will elect
tomorrow. He has served on the Investment Committee for the past four years and
currently serves as the Vice Chairman of that Committee. Ray brings a wealth of
knowledge and experience in financial and investment management to the office.
I can’t begin to thank each of you enough for having permitted me to
work with you and for you during this year now concluding. This Grand Lodge
is exemplary, and it is an honor to be a part of such a great force for good in
today’s world.
Respectfully submitted,
M. William Holsinger, PGM, Grand Treasurer

Report of the Grand Secretary
Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge,
I am pleased to present this, my fifth report, to you as your
Grand Secretary.
Lodge and Membership Information
As of today, there are 338 chartered lodges in our jurisdiction, including
two lodges under dispensation and five research lodges.
Our membership at the beginning of the fiscal year was 57,250. For the
2012 fiscal year, we had 2,271 gains, and 3,735 losses. The ending membership on
June 30, 2012, was 55,357. While we still recorded a net loss of 1,464 members,
this is the smallest loss of members in this jurisdiction since 1966. It is also worth
noting that our rolls include 8,475 Entered Apprentice Masons and 1,789 Fellow
Craft Masons. Our database also includes 25,019 active Masonic widows. A more
detailed report of membership activity, together with a number of Lodge by-law
amendments, life memberships, and veteran’s awards is included in my written
report to be distributed in the Proceedings.
Summary of Accomplishments
There were a number of accomplishments during the year that I would
like to share with you today, but because of the amount of business in my report,
I must save them for the written report. I do want to mention one of them though.
This summer, our Grand Lodge received two national awards from the
Association of Media and Publishing, an association of nearly 1,000 membership
organizations in the US, including organizations like Rotary International, Habitat
for Humanity, trade associations, and alumni organizations. The California
Freemason magazine received a bronze award for general excellence in design
and content. We also received a silver award for Media Innovation and Social
Media Strategy. This is the ninth consecutive year that the Masons of California
have received one or more communications awards from AMP.
Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges
It is my responsibility as the Grand Secretary to keep the Grand Master
informed on matters pertaining to the recognition of foreign Grand Lodges and
to present to you in the form of a motion the recognition of certain Grand Lodges
which meet our criteria therefore.

94

Proceedings of the

Section 409.010 of the California Masonic Code permits our Grand Lodge
to recognize any Grand Lodge that is regularly formed by lodges which trace their
origin to regular and legitimate Ancient Craft Masonry; hold undisputed sway as
the acknowledged sole or concurrent supreme power in Ancient Craft Masonry in
the territory in which they claim jurisdiction; confine their authority and exercise
thereof to the three degrees of Craft or Symbolic Masonry; and subscribe to the
General Regulation of Freemasonry.
We are aided in the evaluation of Grand Lodges seeking recognition by
the Commission on Information for Recognition, a committee of the Conference
of Grand Masters of Masons of North America. We are honored in California
that our very own Past Grand Master, Most Worshipful William J. Bray III, is a
member of that important Commission.
Three Grand Lodges have written to our Grand Lodge seeking
mutual recognition.
The Grand Lodge of Albania
The Grand Lodge of Albania was formed from three Lodges working
under the auspices of the Grand Orient of Italy on October 14, 2011.
The Grand Lodge of Moldova
The Grand Lodge of Moldova was formed on October 16, 1999, from
seven Lodges working under the auspices of the Regular Grand Lodge of Italy,
and later authorized by the Grand Orient of Italy.
The Grand Lodge of Tahiti
The Grand Lodge of Tahiti was formed from three Lodges working
under the auspices of the French National Grand Lodge on December 21, 2011.
It is the opinion of the Commission on Information for Recognition that
each of these Grand Lodges meets the requirements for recognition. Therefore, I
move that the Grand Lodge of California grant mutual recognition to the Grand
Lodge of Albania, the Grand Lodge of Moldova and the Grand Lodge of Tahiti.
Motion ADOPTED.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

95

The Grand Lodge of the Valley of Mexico
At the 2003 Annual Communication, the Grand Lodge of California
suspended recognition of the Grand Lodge of the Valley of Mexico because
that Grand Lodge had invaded the territory of the Grand Lodge of the State of
Baja California. We have been informed by the Grand Lodge of Baja California
that this issue has been resolved. Therefore, I move that the Grand Lodge of
California restore recognition with the Grand Lodge of the Valley of Mexico.
Motion ADOPTED.
Dispensations and Charters
In accordance with §801.065 of the California Masonic Code, Oasis
Lodge U.D. has petitioned this Grand Lodge for a Charter. Grand Master Bray
granted a dispensation to Oasis Lodge on September 15, 2011. In reviewing
the records of this Lodge and from the information provided by the District
Inspector, it has been determined that Oasis Lodge has met the requirements of
the petition. Accordingly I move that a Charter be issued to Oasis Lodge U.D. and
that it be entered into the Registry of this Grand Lodge as Oasis Lodge No. 854.
Motion ADOPTED.
Also in accordance with §801.065 of the California Masonic Code,
Veritas Lodge U.D. has petitioned this Grand Lodge for a Charter. Grand Master
Loui granted a dispensation to Veritass Lodge on May 24, 2012. In reviewing the
records of this Lodge and from the information provided by the District Inspector,
it has been determined that Veritas Lodge has met the requirements of the petition.
Accordingly I move that a Charter be issued to Veritas Lodge U.D. and that it
be entered into the Registry of this Grand Lodge as Veritas Lodge No. 855.
Motion ADOPTED.
At the last Annual Communication, the members adopted a resolution
to revoke the Charter of Covina Lodge No. 334 and directed the Grand Secretary
to dissolve the lodge and preserve the assets for a future lodge in the community
of Covina.
Over the last twelve months, the lodge and hall association have been
dissolved and the assets have been consolidated. The assets received total
$2,462,969. Of this amount, $137,192 was from existing bank accounts and
investments and $2,325,777 came from the sale of the Masonic temple at 170
School Street in Covina. During the year, there were $17,217 in additional
receipts and $31,815 in expenses, mainly associated with the operation of the
hall association. The total assets on hand as of August 31, 2012, were $2,448,371.
These funds are being held in trust for a future lodge in the community of Covina.

96

Proceedings of the

All of the permanent records of Covina Lodge and items of Masonic
significance have been preserved as part of the Grand Lodge archives. Other
items have been sold or given to lodges and Masonic organizations in the Los
Angeles area.
It is rare that a lodge is dissolved and it is a large undertaking – one that a
Grand Secretary cannot do alone. A number of people assisted with the dissolution
of Covina Lodge. Our Grand Treasurer, Most Worshipful Holsinger, was very
instrumental in consolidating the financial assets of the lodge and hall association
and was key in the sale of the temple. He also made a number of personal trips
to Covina transporting back to the Grand Lodge many records and Masonic
items. Worshipful Brother Adam Kendall led all of the efforts to inventory the
records and personal property of the lodge and to preserve and distribute them as
necessary. Finally, Worshipful Brother Richard Watson, a Past Master of Covina
Lodge, was invaluable in every step along the way. To each of these brothers and
to all those who assisted with this project, I extend my appreciation.
Appreciation
As I conclude my report, I also wish to extend my appreciation and
gratitude to the 338 lodge Secretaries and 155 Assistant Secretaries in this
jurisdiction whose dedicated work is the backbone of our lodges and of our Grand
Lodge. I also wish to thank our Assistant Grand Lecturers and District Inspectors
who, in addition to their Ritual duties, work very diligently on a number of
administrative matters throughout the year.
It has been a real privilege and an honor to work alongside our Grand
Treasurer, Most Worshipful Brother Bill Holsinger. Bill and I have worked
together for this Grand Lodge in one capacity or another for more than a decade,
including two terms he served as Grand Treasurer. One of the best aspects of
Freemasonry is the great men we meet, befriend, admire, and cherish. In my life,
Bill is at the top of that list. He is retiring from office this year, but his life will
continue to be a model for Masons everywhere.
Lastly, I want to thank our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Brother Frank
Loui. Frank has been a great leader for our fraternity and a very good mentor to
me. He always knows how to relieve the pressure when it arises. He knows how
to keep things simple, straight-forward, and positive. His friendly face and happy
demeanor in our office has been a boost to our staff who count him and Jeanie
among their friends and family.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

97

Thank you, Most Worshipful, for your leadership, your mentorship, and
your dedicated service to our Craft.
And thank you, my brothers, for the opportunity to serve and work
with you.
Respectfully submitted,
Allan L. Casalou, Grand Secretary

Appendix F

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

121

Report of the Grand Lecturer
Most Worshipful Grand Master and Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
As required by §404.250 of our Masonic Code, the Grand Lecturer is
required to “Render to Grand Lodge at each Annual Communication a full and
detailed account of his services during the year, and to set forth, with respect to
ritual, the condition of the Lodges”, I offer the following report.
It has been a pleasure and a very high honor to serve as your Grand
Lecturer this year and is a memory I will cherish for the rest of my life. My
journey over the rough and rugged road of life is still in progress, and this year
has been one of the most educational and rewarding years of my life. I thank you
for the opportunity to serve as Grand Lecturer for this Dynamic and Progressive
Grand Jurisdiction.
In accordance with the wishes of our first Grand Master in 1850, the ritual
committee has worked very hard to ensure a “uniform system of work that should
characterize the Lodges within California.” For over 160 years the manner in which
good men became Masons in California has remained relatively consistent. In
September 2010, the Grand Master allowed Craft lodges the option of returning to
the ancient tradition of wearing white gloves during meetings and Degrees as well
as adopting Chambers of Reflection as “educational opportunities” for Candidates
prior to the “official” start of the First Degree. During this same period, Craft
lodges began to focus on taking more time to get to know each candidate prior
to their initiation as well as improving the educational opportunities provided to
each candidate between his degrees by requiring additional instruction and testing
beyond the minimum Basic Masonic Education program required by our code.
In order to determine the quality of our uniform system of work, your
Grand Lecturer held 15 Ritual Committee meetings and traveled about 4,088
miles in order to supervise two Inspector Ritual Conferences and eight Master
Mason ritual exemplifications covering all three degrees in all ten Divisions.
What I observed was that in every case lodges continued to make good
men Masons by performing ritual performed that was directly proportionate to
the overall health and/or the educational culture of the lodge. Healthy lodges
with an active membership committee, where harmony reigned supreme and
which possessed an ongoing educational culture for not only the candidate
but also for the other members of the lodge, demonstrated “ownership” of the
ritual experience and produced high quality and uniform ritual. Conversely,
struggling lodges with little membership growth, little educational opportunities,
and/or membership dissention, demonstrated lesser ritual skills. Although both
healthy and struggling lodges made good men Masons, the quality of the lessons
imparted to the candidate through our ritual differed significantly. Lodges that
took “ownership” of the maintenance of their lodge health traditionally conferred
a higher quality of uniform degree work where the candidate and the sideliner
received the maximum educational benefit.

122

Proceedings of the

It became obvious to your Grand Lecturer that in order to have quality
ritual, lodges first needed to be “healthy”. When lodge officers take ownership
of the quality of their ritual they do so as a team, the essence of a healthy lodge.
Successful lodges that perform uniform ritual learn the lessons such a performance
has to offer: Discipline to a commitment to excellence, Partnership development,
Teamwork, Confidence/Self-Esteem building, Self-reflection/Introspection,
Mental health that leads to extended physical health, Organized presentation of
our heritage and other educational lessons whereby we retain enough knowledge
of our past to improve our future, Progressive leadership improvement, Patience
development, and above all Pride in a job well done.
So the Ritual Committee also asked the question, “What can we do
to assist struggling lodges to become healthy lodges where they would take
ownership in the maintenance of their health and ritual performance?”
To address this question the Ritual Committee reviewed the manner in
which the ritual was taught in California and explored all available alternatives. To
assist in this endeavor, the Ritual Committee also conducted a survey of all Lodge
officers, Officers Coaches, and Inspectors. In summary, what you told us was that
you wanted programs that would better prepare Officers’ Coaches for their duties,
provide ritual consistency, and make District Officer Association meetings and
Schools of Instruction more interesting and meaningful. At the direction of the
Grand Master, a special task force has been developed consisting of the Grand
Lecturer and other ritual enthusiasts who will spend the rest of this year and into
next year attempting to make your wishes come true.
Ritual Competition - At this time I would like to congratulate and thank
each lodge that participated in this year’s ritual competition. A total of 50 lodges
competed in the competition with the scores from the best team in each Division
used to identify the “Best Ritual Team in California” for 2012. Each competing
lodge demonstrated the teamwork necessary for the development of not only their
ritual skills but also the improvement of their administrative and social skills. At
this time I would like to recognize those lodges that received the distinction of
being the best ritual team in their respective Divisions as well as the lodge that
came in first place in the State as the best ritual team in California Masonry:
