The lodge with the highest combined score for memory and floor work
was Torrance University Lodge No. 394 with a score of 1,629 out of a possible
1,640 points or an overall score of 99.3% and earned the title of “Best Ritual Team
in California” for 2012. Congratulations to you all on a job well done!
Finally, the Ritual Committee offers its most sincere thanks to two
Assistant Grand Lecturers who will be leaving us this year: Worshipful
David Perry who continues his Masonic journey as the Junior Grand WardenRecommendee, and Worshipful Jack McEnterfer, who continues his Masonic
journey by sharing his outstanding ritual skills at his very successful weekly ritual
school at Bellflower lodge. I thank both of you for your service to our Craft and
wish you continued success into the future.
In conclusion, it is my hope that in the future more lodges will make
the supreme effort to “take ownership and pride” in the quality of the ritual
performed in their Lodge. There are three rules to obtaining quality ritual: The
first is “Repetition”, the second is “Repetition”, and the third is, you guessed it,
“Repetition. No amount of instruction by me, the Assistant Grand Lecturers, the
Inspectors, or your Officers Coaches can improve ritual performance until the
Lodge members themselves make that all important choice to work as a team to
take ownership of the quality of their ritual development and through repetition
improve the ritual experience within their lodge.
Thank you for your confidence in, and your support of, your
Grand Lecturer.
Respectfully submitted,
Jack M. Rose, Grand Lecturer

Appendix G

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

127

Grand Chaplain’s Message

by The Very Reverend Joseph H. Ross
Most Worshipful Grand Master, our Past Grand Masters, our Masonic
youth leaders and members, distinguished and honored guests, family and friends:
We are grateful to be gathered here today and honored by your presence
at this celebration of Masonry and the young people who have chosen to be a part
of our Masonic family.
Today, it is my privilege to address all of you and to share my thoughts
on the divine blessing of leadership that God has bestowed upon this fraternity, its
members, and its youth.
What is leadership? And more importantly, what does it mean to be a
Masonic leader inspired by the divine principles embodied in the teachings of
our craft?
Certainly, Masonic leaders are those who live with integrity and practice
honesty and transparency in all their actions before man and God. They are faithful
to their ideals and loyal to their families, brothers, and friends. Masonic leaders
demonstrate courage while facing the tough decisions that leaders are called upon
to make and exhibit confidence in the abilities of others to succeed even when
success may be hard or seem far off. They exhibit an unswerving commitment
to all that they undertake to do. Masonic leaders enliven their followers with
positivity, energy, and enthusiasm. They serve willingly and with humility. They
are compassionate and sincere in all situations. It honestly seems that God is
their companion wherever they go, no matter their company, regardless of the
ruggedness of the road they travel.
Our Grand Master this year, Frank Loui, is such a Masonic leader, as are
the many Past Grand Masters who join us today. They have served and shared
with all of us their talents and their leadership. But there are others here who also
deserve recognition like our former, current, and future Grand Lodge Officers.
Certainly, the inspectors and Masters of lodges must be acknowledged for their
efforts too. They are all important and esteemed Masonic leaders who live and
practice the values of our craft.
Yet, it seems to me that the most important leaders in this room are
the young men and women of our Masonic Youth Orders. They represent the
blessings to be bestowed upon our fraternity and our communities in the days and
years to come. They exude the enthusiasm that is needed to inspire all of us to be
more involved and better leaders, brothers, and men. These young people are also
Masonic leaders who share and practice our Masonic values.

128

Proceedings of the

And the second most important leaders in the room? The many brothers
I see when I look out across this auditorium who demonstrate their leadership by
serving as advisors, coaches, and mentors for these young people. They are the
epitome of Masonic leadership and are represented today by those being honored
with the Grand Master’s Youth Support Award. They are the ones who greet and
welcome the youth. They dedicate their time to teaching and sharing. They care
about those who come to them to learn and grow.
Let each of us commit ourselves to being Masonic leaders like these
young men and women and their adult advisors are. If we do, perhaps fewer of our
Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts will slip out the back door of our lodges
unnoticed. It is never too late. Even those of us who are nearing our senior years
can be leaders. In fact, we may be the best since we can share whole lifetimes
of experiences.
Let me share a few of the kernels of wisdom that I have harvested from
a lifetime of experience and that have become important to me:
•

A gentle person turns away wrath, but harsh words stir up anger

•

Remember that a man has three names—the name that he
inherits; the name that his parents give to him; and above all,
the name he makes for himself

•

A winner recognizes his God given talents, works hard to
develop them into skills, and then uses them to accomplish
his goals

•

Finally, always remember to praise loudly and blame
very softly.

I believe these to be grains of Masonic wisdom and leadership as well.
My brother, leadership is a divine blessing. And as I look out across this
auditorium I know that our fraternity has been given an immeasurable amount of
that divine blessing.
Most Worshipful Loui, brethren, and guests, thank you for allowing me
this opportunity to speak to you today.
Our Heavenly Father, thank you for the multitude of blessings you have
given us, especially our youth and their adult advisors. Continue to guide them
and our soon to be installed leaders and help them to show the way. Watch over
each of us as we depart this place later today so that we may all return here in your
presence and enjoy the fellowship of one another once more. All this we say and
ask in your Holy Name. Amen.

Grand Oration
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Most Worshipful Past Grand Masters,
fellow officers of the Grand Lodge, distinguished visitors and Brethren;
As your Grand Orator, I have the distinct honor, privilege and pleasure
of addressing you, the Grand Lodge of Free & Accepted Masons of California,
upon a matter of profound importance to the Craft. Before doing so I want to
thank our Grand Master, the Most Worshipful Frank Loui, for giving me this
once in a lifetime opportunity. And on behalf of the other Grand Officers
may I add, Most Worshipful Sir, that this has been a most memorable year in
California Freemasonry.
My brethren, today freedom is under attack. Of course that is nothing
new, for history records that freedom has rarely been given to mankind. When
it has arrived it has more often than not resulted from a vicious and brutal fight.
“Let my people go!” Moses demanded of Pharaoh, whose heart we are
told hardened and stayed that way until the Red Sea splashed in upon his valiant
soldier sending them all to their death. Centuries later with the flick of a long
ask from his famous cigar Winston Churchill responded to a complaint that the
enemies surrounding his tiny island were about to destroy freedom – he said,
“You have enemies? Good . That means you have stood for something, sometime
in your life.” On January 6, 1941 President Franklin Delano Roosevelt stood on
the floor of the US Congress and delivered his famous “Four Freedoms” speech.
Predicated upon the profound belief that God did not make man for bondage,
President Roosevelt stirred a Nation gripped by a relentless war that was raging in
Europe by reminding everyone what was at stake – nothing less than free speech,
the freedom of religion freedom from want and freedom from fear. He said,
“Freedom means the supremacy of human rights – our support goes to those who
support those rights – our strength is our unity of purpose.”
Although President Roosevelt was speaking to a Nation made up of
men and women of all faiths coming from all backgrounds, he might as well
have been standing at the lecturn in a Masonic Grand Lodge delivering those
same words. For, at each and every turn, Masonry has struggled mightily to
support each and every one of the freedoms he mentioned that day in 1941.
Our Masonic exceptionalism is embodied in its members – Masons united for a
common purpose.
This year, our Grand Lodge commenced an assault upon one of the
gravest threats to the freedom of future generations of our children – childhood
literacy. Knowledge and its signal importance to attaining and preserving freedom
lies at the core of Masonic ritual. At the heart of our cherished mysteries lies
a legend about three unworthy craftsmen laboring at the construction of King
Solomon’s Temple who conspired to extort a secret from our Grand Master
Hiram Abiff.

134

Proceedings of the

We refer to them as Ruffians. Albert Pike defined called them symbols
of the greatest enemies of individual welfare and social progress ever to exist:
kingcraft, priestcraft, and the ignorant mob-mind. Of those three the most terrible
enemy is the ignorant mob-mind, for it is easily inflamed, hard to restrain and ever
willing to wreak havoc wherever peace and freedom prevail.
This year, Grand Master Loui’s theme was “Connect, Communicate,
Commit.” It became a call to action for all California Masons to get up out of
their easy chairs, roll up their sleeves and get busy with the hard work of reversing
the deplorable state of childhood literacy – to fight against the onslaught of the
ignorant mob-mind. The state of California had sunk to 47th out of our 50 states
in childhood literacy and statewide bureaucrats were using that statistic to decide
how many prisons would be required to warehouse the thousands of ignorant
children whose destiny was crime and imprisonment.
It was time For Masons to “Connect” with our school children,
“Communicate” with their teachers, and “Commit” to making a difference - to
build our children into monuments of success; good citizens who will one day
become builders of a better world. It was time for California Masons to take a
stand; to say “enough is enough”, link arms with our public schools and lay a new
cornerstone upon which the future of our free society would be rededicated.
As Masons we instinctively knew why we must act – we knew our
history – we knew that without our Masonic ancestors neither we nor any other
people anywhere would ever enjoy two of the most important freedoms any
human being could ever hope to embrace: the freedom to practice the religion of
our own choice, and the freedom to acquire knowledge through a system of public
schools that are not owned lock stock and barrel by one ideology or one theology.
We also knew that the work to ensure those freedoms is as much a work to be done
today as it was years ago.
It was a Mason – Horace Mann – the man educators today refer to as the
Father of the Public School Movement – who laid the first cornerstone whereupon
this Nation would erect the best institutions of learning and make them accessible
to every child in the land. Today, because of Horace Mann’s belief in Masonic
exceptionalism, the primary source for educating our children from kindergarten
through high school is our public schools.
Since Masonic Ritual is the root of Masonic wisdom what exactly does
it tell us about the importance of Connecting with our children; Communicating
with their teachers; and Committing to improving how they read? We need
only recall the Middle Chamber lecture in the Fellowcraft Degree to discover
the answer.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

135

You remember the ritual; you probably even remember the Mason who
first delivered the lecture to you and have never forgotten the impact it made upon
you; and you know as you sit here this morning the importance of studying the
seven liberal arts and sciences – grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, geometry,
music and astronomy. Remember that special feeling you had inside - here was
something for you to dive into – Masonry was pointing you in the right direction
- and you read, you studied and you became better informed – unhindered by
ideology – uninhibited by theology – and blessed because you were a Mason.
And the best thing was that you could take advantage of what Masonry
asked you to do because of something you probably had taken for granted most
of your life - you could read. But brethren, that special gift – the gift of reading
- should never be taken for granted – it must be nurtured; fed; challenged; and
helped every step of the way until each and every child masters that art.
This past Masonic year your Grand Family had the privilege of visiting
several public schools to perform our very ancient and inspirational cornerstone
ritual. We met some of the most dedicated teachers, administrators, school board
trustees and community leaders – men and women whom we discovered shared
our goals. You wouldn’t know the names if I recited them, but every single one of
them possessed a common characteristic – they didn’t seek acclaim or applause –
they simply wanted to connect, communicate and commit provide their students a
chance to grow up and become the best they could become.
I particularly remember our time in Ceres, California – a wonderful
typical town of that part of California where I was born - the San Joaquin Valley
– the agricultural belt that proudly feeds the world. No less than 200 students
from Cesar Chavez Jr. High sat quietly, attentively listening to our cornerstone
ceremony. The Superintendent, principal and members of the school board were
there. So, too, were members of the City Council, the Chief of Police and the
Fire Chief. Those students didn’t come from wealthy homes. They didn’t wear
the best and most expensive sneakers. They didn’t have the latest IPods dangling
from their ears. Their mothers and fathers worked hard to put food on the table.
They didn’t have easy lives but they had something money could never buy. They
had caring adults who gave them a new school; caring adults who showed up to
support them in their activities; and caring adults who silently promised that no
child would ever be left behind.
You might think that school children who witness our cornerstone ritual
walk away bored to tears. If you thought that you would be wrong. This past year
I witnessed first-hand something that I thought I already knew from raising three
sons and one daughter and from herding around nine grandchildren: children
of every age have inquiring minds the size of enormous sponges that soak up
everything they hear – even our cherished cornerstone ritual.

136

Proceedings of the

At the conclusion of one of our ceremonies, a young man walked up to
me and stood looking at me without uttering a word. Finally after staring at each
other in complete silence for several awkward seconds, I asked: “Did you like
the ceremony?”
The boy nodded his head – “Where did it come from?” he asked.
I was tempted to tell him to ask our Grand Lecturer, Jack Rose – but
decided to tackle the job myself. “A long time ago,” I began, “men who built
buildings like your school understood the importance of laying a solid foundation
before placing bricks, stones or anything else on top. The foundation begins
with something called a cornerstone – just like the one we were depicting
this afternoon.”
What followed was a brief conversation that connected some of our
Masonic ritual and its rich symbolism to something the boy easily understood:
before we can become what we dream of becoming, we have work to do – we
have things to learn - we have a foundation to lay.
That lesson was also on display in a different way. This year California
Masons started coming to grips with how best to implement Grand Master Loui’s
project – “Raising a Reader.” It was and is a project taken straight from the pages
of your Strategic Plan to make a profound difference in public education.
Writing in his epic work “Morals and Dogma”, Albert Pike taught us an
important truth: men and women working together accomplish things that one
man or one woman can never hope to accomplish. It is a truth that informs us that
when Masons join hands with their communities they can move mountains – or,
“raise a reader.”
From as far north as San Francisco to the southern tip of San Diego,
California Masons assembled in committees called “Public School Advisory
Councils”. Their goal was to identify the objectives of Grand Master Loui’s
project, to assess the talent necessary to implement those objectives, and to rebuild
childhood literacy in partnership with our public schools and the community.
It was and continues to be nearly as difficult a task as the building of
King Solomon’s Temple – which as you recall required the efforts of 70,000
Entered Apprentices, or bearers of burden; 80,000 Fellowcraft, or hewers on the
mountains and in the quarries; 3,330 masters or overseers of the work; and three
grand masters working together as a team. We didn’t bring such huge numbers
of men to bear, but the resolve of those who participated was just as determined.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

137

“If you build it, they will come!” became a common refrain. And build
it they did. From the bottom up Masons laid the cornerstone consisting of several
councils of local Masonic leaders. The bricks consisting of school districts and
communities were added next. To all of this a fine mortar was added consisting
of the extraordinary Dr. Holly Kreider and the excellent people at Raising A
Reader. In the end a partnership was built, one whose breadth you can discover
for yourself by going to www.raisingareader.org. You can read about the extent
of the commitment Masonry has made to stamp out ignorance and build a better
future for our children, our country and our world. You, my brethren, are a part of
something big: you are part of an enormous dedicated effort to make a profound
difference; to take our Masonic values out of the lodge room and into the classroom
so that thousands of children can live life to its fullest extent.
There is a familiar adage: “from little acorns big oaks grow.” Life is a
blessing, my brethren, even when things are tough. But the Great Architect has
appointed one remedy for all the tough times we and our children must endure - a
contented spirit. I was reminded of that just about the time I allowed myself to
wonder whether or not our partnership would actually work. The reminder came
in the form of a lesson from one of my grandsons – he actually thrives on putting
puzzles together.
His name is Harrison and he is 9 years old. I wanted to give Harrison a
special gift and selected a puzzle of the world made up of a thousand pieces. I was
certain that it would take hours if not days for him to put it together. After ripping
the gift wrap from the box he disappeared for what I was sure would be the rest of
the day. Within an hour he came back and announced that he was done.
“Come look, Grandpa,” he said grabbing me by the hand and leading me
to the bedroom.
To my complete surprise he had everything in place just exactly the way
the world really fits together.
“How did you do that so fast?” I asked.
“It was really pretty easy,” Harrison replied. He picked up one of the
puzzle pieces and showed me the reverse side. On it was a picture of a man
and a woman. “There are people on the opposite side of every piece,” Harrison
explained. “I put the puzzle together upside down. All I had to do was put the
people together and the whole world came together at the same time.”
The light bulb turned on in my head – Harrison made it seem easy. I
realized then and there that with our Masonic values – our Masonic determination
– and our Masonic exceptionalism – all we had to do was reach out, connect
the pieces to the puzzles in our communities and we would make a profound
difference – and we did; and we always will.

Grand Master’s Decision
Grand Master Loui’s Decision No. 1
Modifications to Lodge Life Membership Programs
There is legislation pending before this Annual Communication which
would modify some of the rules applicable to our Lodge life membership
programs. I have been asked whether Grand Lodge may modify these rules with
respect to amounts now in our Lodge Life Membership Funds or whether these
new rules may only apply with respect to amounts received from future sales
of life memberships. Each life membership is really a contract between the life
member and his Lodge. How does that contract restrict our ability to make future
changes in our Lodge life membership programs?
Lodges have been allowed to have life membership programs since the
Nineteenth Century. Prior to 1931, the Lodge, with the approval of the Master,
could invest the Life Membership Fund in any securities approved by the Master.
In 1931, the law was amended to limit the investment of the Life Membership
Fund to bank deposits and securities legal for investment by banks under the
laws of the State of California or the Territory of Hawaii. In 1951, the law was
amended again to extend the list of permissible investments for Lodge funds,
including those in the Life Membership Fund. That broadened rule, as it has been
modified since, is now found in Section 809.130 of the Code.
These prior modifications of our law were effective with respect to
amounts already part of a Lodge’s Life Membership Fund, and there is no evidence
of concern at the time that any such modification would be an impermissible
alteration of the terms of an implied “contract” between the life member and the
Lodge. This contract is simple: the purchasing member pays the Lodge a fixed
sum and the Lodge promises the purchaser that he will never again pay dues. The
Lodge does not promise to hold the life membership payment in trust and pay the
purchaser’s dues from the fund. The Lodge only promises that the member will
never again be required to pay dues even if the assets in the Life Membership
Fund are no longer sufficient to pay his dues. Thus, the life member has no interest
in the Life Membership Fund or how it is invested.
Based on this history and my understanding of how a life membership
works, it is my decision that all the terms of the Lodge Life Membership program
can be changed so long as no one who is then a life member is ever again required
to pay dues.
If you agree with this interpretation of our law, I ask you to vote “yes”
for Grand Master’s Decision No. 1.

142

Proceedings of the

If you approve this decision, the following narrative will be added
to the appendix of the California Masonic Code in which the Grand Master’s
interpretative decisions are recorded:
Interpretation of Sections 809.150 and 809.320 of the California
Masonic Code.
Modifications to Lodge Membership Programs
(2012 G.M. Decision No. 1)
All the terms of the Lodge Life Membership program can be changed
so long as no one who is then a life member is ever again required to pay dues.
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Currently pending before this Grand Lodge are several Resolutions
dealing with changes to Life Membership Funds. Without stating his opinion on
the wisdom of any of these changes, Grand Master Loui has correctly reasoned
that there is no prohibition against changing provisions of the California Masonic
Code with respect to funds currently in Lodge Life Membership accounts. Each
life membership is a contract between the life member and his Lodge. The terms
of the contract are simply that in exchange for the payment of a set amount, a
Lodge member will remain a member of that Lodge without ever again having to
pay annual dues. Once the life membership is paid for, those funds belong to the
Lodge and the member has no personal involvement in how those funds are to be
maintained or invested. Accordingly, the manner in which those Life Membership
Funds are invested, allocated or transferred by the Lodge, as permitted by our
Code, may be changed from time to time by revising the provisions of our Code
with the consent of Grand Lodge.
Grand Master Loui’s decision that the terms of a Lodge life membership
program can be changed, so long as no one who is then a life member is ever again
required to pay dues to his Lodge, is an accurate interpretation of the intent behind
our Code provisions regarding Life Membership Funds.
This Decision is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Decision APPROVED.

Grand Master’s Recommendation
Grand Master Loui’s Recommendation No. 1
Removes the Grand Lodge Committee on Fraternal Support Services
from the List of Standing Committees
In 2002, the Fraternal Support Services Committee was added as a
Standing Committee of the Grand Lodge to provide information about services
that are offered through the Masonic Homes of California, the California Masonic
Foundation, the Grand Lodge and Masonic Service Bureaus. Over the years, the
need for this service has changed. Today, the Grand Lodge and its charitable
entities maintain a coordinated plan for communication including the use of the
California Freemason magazine, the Leader, websites and other communications.
The California Masonic Foundation has formed public schools advisory councils
around the state, and the Masonic Homes of California has additional plans for
lodge outreach.
The past efforts and accomplishments by the members of this committee
are to be commended and should not be diminished by this recommendation. The
needs for the services have simply changed. In an effort to keep the Committees
of Grand Lodge to the necessary minimum, and with the full support of the
Executive Committee, I recommend that the Committee on Fraternal Support
Services be removed from the list of Standing Committees of the Grand Lodge.
Should a future Grand Master find the need again for such a committee, our Code
already gives him the authority to appoint it as a Special Committee.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made
to the Code. Section 406.005 of the Code would be amended to read as marked:
§406.005. STANDING COMMITTEES.
The members of standing committees (other than those who serve ex-officio) shall
be appointed by the newly installed Grand Master at each Annual Communication
before the close thereof. A member ceases to be a standing committee member
by death, removal by the Grand Master (other than those members who serve exofficio), resignation, ceasing to be a member of a Constituent Lodge or suspension
or expulsion as a Mason. In the event of any vacancy on any standing committee
other than the Executive Committee or Ritual Committee, the Grand Master may
appoint a successor for the balance of the current term. All standing committee
appointments (other than those who serve ex-officio) shall expire at the close of
the next succeeding Annual Communication.
The following are standing committees of the Grand Lodge: Annual
Communications Activities, Audit, California Freemason, Compensation,
Executive (all of whose members serve ex-officio), Finance, Fraternal Support
Services, Investments, Jurisprudence, Lodge Support, Masonic Properties,
Policy and General Purposes, Ritual (all of whose members serve ex-officio) and
Trial Review.

Resolution No. 11-02
Increases Lodge Refreshment Revolving Fund
The proponents of this Resolution seek to increase the maximum amount allowed
in the refreshment revolving fund from $500 to $2,000.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, a Lodge may establish a revolving fund, consisting of not
more than $500, for the use of its Stewards or Junior Warden, as the Master may
determine, in providing refreshments for all regular lodge functions; and
WHEREAS, when several events that require refreshment coincide in
the same month, such as stated meetings, degrees, installation and special events,
the $500 amount is inadequate to cover these expenses; and
WHEREAS, to comply with the California Masonic Code, the Junior
Warden would need to acquire funds directly from the Master or Treasurer, or pay
these expenses out of pocket and be reimbursed; and
WHEREAS, increasing the amount permitted in the refreshment
revolving fund from $500 to $2,000 would allow for additional funds when
needed for the month; and
WHEREAS, during normal months, a smaller amount could be
deposited in the refreshment revolving fund.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 809.120 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.120. LODGE REVOLVING FUNDS.
A Lodge may establish two revolving funds. One such fund, consisting of not
more than $500 $2,000, may be established for the use of its Stewards or Junior
Warden, as the Master may determine, in providing refreshments for all regular
Lodge functions. One such fund, consisting of not more than $500, may be
established for the use of its Secretary for his incidental expenses. Each such
revolving fund may be replenished monthly on presentation of receipted vouchers
and shall remain subject to provisions of this Code.

Proceedings of the

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to increase the maximum
amount allowed in a Lodge refreshment revolving fund from $500 to $2,000.
The proponents argue that when several events coincide in the same month, such
as stated meetings, degrees, installation and special events, the $500 amount is
inadequate to cover all expenses.
In 1974, the maximum amount permitted in the revolving fund was
$250. In 1990, the maximum amount was increased to the current $500. Although
the increase sought by this Resolution is proportionately much higher than the
previous raise, it does take into account not only the fact that many Lodges today
have more social events than in the past, but that inflation is taking its toll on
all of us.
The purpose of having this revolving fund is so a Lodge can provide
refreshments for its members without knowing in advance the amount that will
be needed. A dollar limit is placed to cap the amount of discretionary spending
without a prior vote of the members. This would not change how much a Lodge
is allowed to spend per month; it simply defines how much the Junior Warden or
Stewards are allowed to spend without a prior vote of the Lodge. Currently, Junior
Wardens and Stewards must spend their personal money for expenses that exceed
$500 and request reimbursement at a subsequent Stated Meeting.
This Resolution, if passed, would not require that any Lodge use the full
$2000 nor would it change the total amount a Lodge could spend on “Social and
Fraternal” expenditures. While those expenditures remain capped at 30 percent of
total income, the Lodge would have more flexibility in carrying out social events.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this

Resolution NOT ADOPTED.
Resolution No. 11-06
Restores the Historic Role of Entered Apprentices and Fellow Craft Masons
The proponents of this Resolution seek to have most Lodge business conducted
in a Lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons and to allow Entered Apprentice and
Fellow Craft Masons to speak but not vote on any matter before the Lodge.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, before 1842, lodge business was conducted in the Entered
Apprentice Degree; and
WHEREAS, this practice gradually changed after that time as a result of
the Morgan Affair and the subsequent Anti-Masonic movement; and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

149

WHEREAS, Section 807.020 of the CMC now provides that all business
except the examination of candidates in the lecture of Entered Apprentice and
Fellow Craft degrees, the conferring of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft
degrees, and the consideration of relief of a worthy Mason shall be done in a lodge
of Master Masons; and
WHEREAS, California is the only one of the ten western United States
that still conducts business in the Master Mason degree only; and
WHEREAS, Section 804.860 of the CMC states that an Entered
Apprentice or Fellow Craft is not entitled to vote or speak on any matter before
the Lodge; and
WHEREAS, all Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons are
Masons under the jurisdiction of a Lodge and are subject to all the rules and
regulations of Freemasonry.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 804.860 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.860. ADDITIONAL RIGHTS OF AND PROHIBITIONS ON
ENTERED APPRENTICES AND FELLOW CRAFTS.
An Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft may sit in the Lodge in which he has
received the degree or degrees when open in a degree taken by him, while he
conducts himself with due order and propriety. He may speak but may not vote on
any matter coming before the Lodge. He may advance after satisfactorily passing
a strict examination in a tiled Lodge. He may visit another Lodge working in a
degree taken by him, with the consent of the Master of his Lodge and the consent
of the Master of the Lodge visited, if accompanied by a Master Mason who has
sat with him in a tiled Lodge and vouches for him.
He shall not pay dues. and is not entitled to vote or speak on any matter before
the Lodge.
He may be buried with Masonic honors upon the request of his family, unless he
was a demitted, withdrawn, suspended or expelled Mason at the time of his death.
Neither he nor his widows or orphans are entitled to relief from the Lodge.
He shall not exercise any control over Lodge funds for charity or for
other purposes.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 807.020 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:

150

Proceedings of the

§807.020. ADDITIONAL REGULATIONS APPLICABLE TO MEETINGS.
A.

Sunday Meetings. No Stated or Special Meetings of a Lodge shall be
held on Sunday except for the annual Installation of Officers or funeral
services. If the Stated Meeting of a lunar Lodge falls on a Sunday, the
Stated Meeting shall be held on the following day.

B.

Work to be Done in Lodge of Master Entered Apprentice Masons. All
business, except the examinations of candidates in the Candidate’s
Lecture of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft and Master Mason
degrees, the conferring of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft
and Master Mason degrees, and the consideration of relief of a worthy
Mason, shall be done in a Lodge of Master Entered Apprentice Masons.
A Lodge of Master Masons may be called down for the examinations
of candidates in the Candidate’s Lecture of the Entered Apprentice and
Fellow Craft degrees.

C.

Quorum. A Lodge shall not be opened, nor shall any work be done
or business transacted, except by, or in the presence of, and under the
continual direction of the Master, the ranking Warden, the Grand Master
or the Grand Master’s designated representative. No Lodge shall transact
any business with fewer than five members of the Lodge present except
the conferring of degrees. The Tiler is present while he is at his post in
the Tiler’s room.

D.

Presence of Charter. No meeting shall be conducted by a Lodge unless
the Charter of the Lodge is present. A photocopy of the Charter may
be made under the direction of the Grand Secretary at the request
and expense of the Lodge. The Grand Secretary shall attach thereto a
certificate with the seal of Grand Lodge affixed that the copy is a true
copy of the Lodge’s Charter. The copy may be used by the Lodge instead
of the original Charter at any time.

E.

Presence of Flag. The Flag of our country shall be displayed at all
meetings of a Lodge. At the annual election of officers, and at such other
meetings as may be deemed desirable by the Master, the Flag shall be
formally presented at the Altar and received in the manner prescribed in
the Ritual. The Altar of a Lodge shall not be decorated with any flag.

F.

No Smoking. Smoking is forbidden in the Lodge room at all times when
the Lodge is in session.

G.

No Adjourned Meetings. There shall be no adjourned meeting. Each
meeting of a Lodge must be closed when the business proposed for
transaction has been concluded.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

151

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of Resolution No. 11-06 seek to have most Lodge
business conducted in a Lodge of Entered Apprentice Masons and to allow
Entered Apprentice Masons and Fellow Craft Masons to speak but not vote on
any matter before the Lodge. Similar proposals have been presented in the past
to determine whether our Grand Lodge would change its long standing custom
and rule of conducting business only in the Master Mason Degree. All have been
rejected by this Grand Lodge.
The proponents are correct in indicating that in the formative years of
Freemasonry, Lodge business was conducted in the Entered Apprentice Degree
because Entered Apprentices made up the bulk of the membership in the Fraternity.
Fellow Craft Masons and Master Masons were rare. During the 1840’s, many of
the Grand Lodges in the United States revised their rules to require Lodges to hold
Stated Meetings only in Lodges of Master Masons. The change was instituted to
encourage all Masons to become Master Masons. Lodges in other countries may
meet in the First Degree where several years are required to advance through the
Degrees. However, in recent years our Grand Lodge has adopted changes in our
proficiencies whereby we have shortened the time and difficulty for advancement.
As Masons, we are taught that Masonry is a progressive moral science
taught by degrees only. Upon completion of the three degrees, the candidate
becomes a Master Mason and is informed that he is now entitled to all the rights
and privileges therein. Until he becomes a Master Mason, he does not pay dues
nor is he entitled to vote or speak in the Lodge. This proposal does not provide for
the Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft to pay dues and/or vote while participating
in the business of the Lodge. It would also prohibit the Lodge from conducting
Fellow Craft or Master Mason proficiencies at the Stated Meeting.
While it is desirable for a candidate to participate and learn as much as
possible about the Fraternity, he can do so by spending time with his coach or
Mentor while the Stated Meeting or other meetings are in progress. Presently,
nothing prohibits Entered Apprentice Masons or Fellow Craft Masons from
attending and participating in non-tiled functions of a Lodge or in the Degree that
he has been through.
This Resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to require Entered Apprentice and Fellow

WHEREAS, Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts are Masons under

to comply with all the rules and regulations of Freemasonry and are subject to the
disciplinary processes of the fraternity; and
WHEREAS, an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft Mason remains
active on the roster of the Lodge even if he does not advance and even if his
degree fees have been forfeited; and
WHEREAS, Section 804.860 of the CMC states that an Entered
Apprentice or Fellow Craft shall not pay dues; and

many of the benefits of the Lodge including receiving a bulletin or Trestleboard,
attending social events, education classes and other programs and services that
utilize lodge funds;

Apprentice or Fellow Craft Mason to contribute to the costs of these programs
and services; and
WHEREAS, the adoption of this resolution will lower the Grand

Apprentices and Fellow Crafts as well as Master Masons.

Masonic Code be amended as marked:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

157

§804.820. RIGHT TO BURIAL.
It is the right of every Mason, other than a demitted, withdrawn, suspended or
expelled Mason, to a Masonic memorial service or burial with Masonic honors.
The foregoing notwithstanding, a demitted Master Mason has the right to a
Masonic memorial service or burial with Masonic honors if he dies within a year
after receiving a Demit.
It is the duty of the Lodge to bury an eligible Mason of that Lodge, wherever
he may have died, and an eligible Mason of another Lodge in this or any other
Jurisdiction who dies within the vicinity of the Lodge. If such deceased Mason’s
financial circumstances require it, the Lodge shall pay the necessary expenses of
the burial, even if the deceased Mason’s Lodge refuses to reimburse the Lodge
for such expenses. The Lodge shall reimburse any other Lodge for the reasonable
expenses incurred by it in suitably burying one of its deceased Masons. No Lodge
shall fix in advance the amount to be paid for such burial.
When financial circumstances require it, it is also the duty of the Lodge to pay all
the necessary expenses of the burial for one of its deceased member’s widow and
orphans dependent upon her and to reimburse any other Lodge for the reasonable
expenses incurred by it in suitably burying them. No Lodge shall fix in advance
the amount to be paid for such burial.
A Lodge may, in its discretion, conduct Masonic funeral or memorial services for
a member Mason of the Lodge suspended for non-payment of dues, if there is no
other Masonic offense established against him, but it shall not pay the expenses
of the burial.

Demit or discontinuing multiple membership may only obtain a refund of his dues
paid in advance if he has returned his dues receipt in such Lodge with his request
for a Demit or Certificate of Discontinuance of Multiple Membership. There shall
be no refund of a life membership to a member who dies, is issued a Demit or
discontinues his multiple memberships.

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 809.360 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.360. REMISSION OF DUES.
If recommended by the Charity Committee, a Lodge, without giving the name of
the delinquent Masons members except to the Secretary, may remit to December
31st of the current calendar year the accrued dues of those of its Masons members
who are unable to pay.
The Charity Committee should review the situation of a Mason member whose

remitted to December 31st of the current calendar year. A Lodge shall not remit

except as herein provided.

of taking care of himself, or a member who is a resident of the Masonic Homes of

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 809.370 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.370. SUSPENSION FOR NON-PAYMENT OF DUES.
If a Mason member has not paid his dues during a period of 12 months, the
Secretary shall notify him that he will be suspended for non-payment of dues
unless at the Lodge’s next Stated Meeting either his dues have been paid or
sickness or inability to pay is shown as the cause for the failure to pay. The notice
shall be given either by certified mail, return receipt requested, postage prepaid,
addressed to his last known address, or by actual service of notice, duly certified
by the Tiler. If all dues due and payable have not been paid by the time of the
Lodge’s next Stated Meeting, he shall be declared suspended by the Master, unless
for special reasons shown the Lodge shall remit his dues or grant him further time
for payment. No worthy brother who is unable to pay his dues shall be suspended
for non-payment of dues.
No Mason member who has attained the age of 80 years or who has attained an
aggregate number of years in age and years as a Master Mason in good standing
equaling 120 or more shall be suspended for non-payment of dues without a
written report to the Lodge from the Member Retention Committee evidencing

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

163

when and where the committee interviewed the delinquent Mason member, why
the delinquent Mason member has not paid his dues and whether the delinquent
Mason member has the ability to pay his dues. A copy of this report shall be
provided to the Grand Secretary at least thirty days before the vote may be taken
on the suspension.
A Mason member shall not be expelled from Masonry for non-payment of dues.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 809.380 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§809.380. RESTORATION OF A MASON MEMBER SUSPENDED FOR
NON-PAYMENT OF DUES.
A Mason member suspended for non-payment of dues:
A.

Shall be automatically restored if, within two years, he pays any arrearage
due at the time of his suspension, together with such further dues as
would have accrued against him had he not been suspended, to the date
of his payment, unless such arrearage and dues have been remitted by his
Lodge; and

B.

May make a request to his Lodge for restoration if he has not paid
them or had them remitted by his Lodge for the period of two years.
The Mason member shall not be restored except by a two‑thirds vote
by ballot of all the members present at the next Stated Meeting after the
request for restoration is presented. As a condition of his restoration, he
shall pay any arrearage due at the time of his suspension, together with
such further dues as would have accrued against him had he not been
suspended, to the date of his payment, unless the arrearage and dues have
been remitted by his Lodge. A petition denied may be renewed at any
future Stated Meeting.

The Secretary shall immediately notify the Grand Secretary of the restoration.

§809.560. SOCIAL AND FRATERNAL EXPENDITURES.
A Lodge may expend Lodge funds for the following purposes, subject to the

A.

limitation not expended in one year may be carried forward to future

§1404.940. REVERSAL BY GRAND LODGE.
Whenever a verdict is reversed and set aside by Grand Lodge and a new

The suspended or expelled Mason shall be immediately entitled to all of

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Resolution would require Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft
Masons to pay Lodge dues which includes the assessed Grand Lodge per capita.
The proponents of this legislation point out these Masons enjoy many Lodge
benefits but do not help offset the costs that the Lodge and Grand Lodge incur
on their behalf. Adoption of this Resolution would spread the expenses of Grand
Lodge and the constituent Lodges over a larger base.
Requiring Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts to pay dues would not
entitle them to all of the privileges of being members of the Lodge. However, as
they currently enjoy the most costly benefits, such as receiving a monthly bulletin
or Trestleboard, attending social events, education classes and other programs
and services that utilize Lodge funds, it would put them on an equal footing with
Master Masons in terms of their financial support of the Lodge.
While requiring Entered Apprentices and Fellow Craft Masons to pay
dues is a change in current law, it is consistent both with economic reality and
with our Masonic principle that Masons, unless destitute, should not be a financial
burden to their Brothers.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.

Resolution No. 11-08
Removes Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts from
Lodge Rolls After Five Years

The proponents of this Resolution seek to remove an Entered Apprentice or Fellow
Craft Mason from the Lodge rolls five years after his fees and contributions have
been forfeited.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, many California Lodges carry on their books a significant
number of Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons who have exhibited no
intention to advance to higher degrees; and
WHEREAS, after three years of no response to requests of these Entered
Apprentice and Fellow Craft Masons to encourage them to continue, their fees
and contributions are considered forfeited; and
WHEREAS, in most cases, contact can no longer be made with these
brothers because of change of residence without notification to the Lodge and
being unable to trace said brothers by any of the standard methods available to
the Lodge.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 804.690 of
the California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§804.690. FORFEITURE OF FEES AND CONTRIBUTIONS.
When a candidate does not present himself qualified for the Fellow Craft and
Master Mason Degrees within a period of three years from the date of his initiation
as an Entered Apprentice, the Master shall appoint a committee of two or more
members of the Lodge to investigate and report back to the Master the reasons why
the candidate has not presented himself for advancement. If the candidate does
not supply any explanation satisfactory to the Lodge, the Master shall direct the
Secretary to forward to such candidate by certified mail, return receipt requested,
postage prepaid, deposited in the U.S. Post Office, addressed to him at his last
known address, a notice advising him that unless he shall present himself qualified
for advancement, on or before a specified date (at least 60 days in advance), his
fees for the unconferred degrees and all of his previous contributions shall be
declared forfeited.
On the date specified, the Master shall declare the fees and contributions forfeited
unless further time shall have been granted by a vote of the Lodge.
A candidate thus denied advancement shall be considered only as an Entered
Apprentice or Fellow Craft of the Lodge with the right to apply for the remaining
degree or degrees, and again paying the fees and contributions therefor, subject to
investigation and election, the same as any other candidate.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

167

If, after five years from the date his fees and contributions were declared forfeited,
he has not applied for the remaining degree or degrees, the Lodge may issue
him a Demit.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend section 804.690 of the
California Masonic Code regarding forfeiture of fees and contributions when a
candidate for degrees fails to advance.
The proponents seek to add a provision that after five years from the
forfeiture, the Lodge may issue the candidate a Demit. This would remove the
individual from the Lodge rolls.
This Resolution appears to add a natural succession in the forfeiture
process and simplifies the record keeping of the Lodge.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.
Resolution No. 11-10
Creates a New Classification of Historic Lodges
The proponents of this Resolution seek to provide a classification of special
purpose Lodges for the preservation of our historic Masonic heritage.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
Whereas, the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State
of California has, or has had, a Masonic presence in many historic communities
in this State; and
Whereas, the loss of a Masonic Lodge in these communities often
means the loss of historic buildings that are important to the heritage of California
and to the Fraternity; and
Whereas, the chartering of special-purpose Lodges in these historic
communities will serve as a means of maintaining these historic buildings; and
Whereas, these special-purpose lodges could serve as a means of
maintaining historic buildings that might otherwise be lost to Freemasonry, and to
our heritage in California.
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that a new Section 816.000
be added to the California Masonic Code to establish a classification of specialpurpose Lodges for the preservation of our historic Masonic heritage, to read
as follows:

168

Proceedings of the
CHAPTER 16
HISTORIC LODGES

§816.000. HISTORIC LODGES.
Historic Lodges are a special classification of Constituent Lodge with authority to
preserve historic buildings owned, or leased by them, together with any historic
paraphernalia, and/or to preserve a historic connection to a community. Historic
Lodges shall be subject to all provisions of this Code applicable to Constituent
Lodges, except as follows:
A.

The word “Historic” shall be included in the name of the Lodge;

B.

Membership:
1.

Shall consist exclusively of Master Masons in good standing
of Constituent Lodges or of Lodges under the jurisdiction of
Grand Lodges recognized by this Grand Lodge;

2.

Shall cease if a member loses such status; and

3.

May be voluntarily severed at any time by resignation;

No member of a Historic Lodge shall, by reason of that membership
alone, be considered a member of a Constituent Lodge for any purpose
of this Code.
C.

Only Master Masons in good standing of a Constituent Lodge shall hold
office and vote;

D.

Grand Lodges recognized by this Grand Lodge, their Lodges and
Masonic Organizations in this or any other Jurisdiction, composed
exclusively of Master Masons under the jurisdiction of this Grand
Lodge or any other Grand Lodge recognized by this Grand Lodge,
may become “Subscribing Members,” entitled only to receive bulletins
and publications;

E.

Receipts for dues must accompany a Petition for Dispensation, but
no Demit or Request for Demit shall be received or issued by a
Historic Lodge;

F.

The provisions of this Code requiring certain recommendations,
notifications and certificates from an Inspector dealing with qualifications
of officers and membership in a Lodge seeking a Dispensation or Charter
shall be deemed complied with if an Inspector designated by the Grand
Master certifies to the standing of the petitioners, the provision for a
suitable Lodge room and the qualification of the officers for their duties.
The Dispensation and Charter shall be issued without charge;

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

169

G.

The provisions of this Code dealing with the qualifications of Master,
Senior Warden, Junior Warden and Senior Deacon shall not apply to
the officers of Historic Lodges. When the Master-elect or a Wardenelect or a Senior Deacon appointed is not a Past Master of a California
Lodge, before he can be installed he must produce a certificate from the
Inspector of the district in which the Historic Lodge is situated certifying
to the proficiency of such officer in the opening and closing ceremonies;

H.

They shall not:
1.

Confer degrees,

2.

Be liable for the relief of a member, his wife, widow or orphan,
and a member of a Historic Lodge shall not be eligible for
admission to the Masonic Homes of California unless he is a
member in good standing in a Constituent Lodge, or

3.

Be entitled to representation in Grand Lodge or any
vote therein;

I.

Historic Lodges shall be exempt from the contributions levied by
Grand Lodge on Lodges, and applicants for membership in Historic
Lodges shall be exempt from the contributions levied by Grand Lodge
on applicants;

J.

No officer or former officer of a Historic Lodge shall, by reason of that
position alone, be a member of Grand Lodge. Sections of this Code
dealing with the title of Past Master shall not be applicable to one who
has served as Master of a Historic Lodge only, and the Master of a
Historic Lodge shall not, upon death or completion of his term of office,
by reason of that fact alone, become or be known as or designated as a
Past Master, and shall possess none of the rights, powers or privileges of
a Past Master of a Lodge;

K.

Their Stated Meetings shall be held at least once annually. By a vote
of its members, the Lodge may change the place, date and time of a
Stated or Special Meeting to something other than what is fixed in its
Charter or Bylaws. The meeting place must be safe and suitable for a
tiled Lodge meeting in this Jurisdiction as determined by the Inspector
of the district in which the Historic Lodge is situated. Business may be
transacted immediately following the opening of any Stated Meeting.
Members shall be given notice of any change to the place, date and time
of Stated Meetings;

L.

The forms of Petition for Dispensation, Petition for Charter, Charter
and Uniform Code of Bylaws shall be used or adopted insofar as the
provisions may be applicable to such Lodges;

M.

They shall have no judicial powers;

170

Proceedings of the

N.

The giving of notice of receipt of applications for membership and
the referral of applications for membership to a committee of three for
investigation and report thereon provided for elsewhere in this Code are
dispensed with, and applications for membership may be voted on at the

O.

Suspension of a member for non-payment of dues shall not affect his

P.

R.

They may provide complimentary memberships to Junior Wardens,
Senior Wardens or Masters of a Constituent Lodge.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to create a new classification
of Special Purpose Lodges for the preservation of our Masonic heritage. Such
Lodges, to be known as Historic Lodges, would have the authority to preserve
buildings with historic Masonic significance owned or leased by them. Historic
Lodges would consist of Master Masons in good standing who are members of
California Lodges or of Lodges under the jurisdiction of Grand Lodges recognized
by this Grand Lodge.
Historic Lodges would not confer degrees but rather would obtain
members by affiliation only. They would be required to meet a minimum of
once annually to transact business. Historic Lodges would be exempt from per
capita and the officers would be exempt from the usual qualification requirements
except they would be required to demonstrate their proficiency in opening and
closing ceremonies.
However, there is no statement in this Resolution that indicates who
would be responsible for the liabilities of such Lodges.
This Resolution is not consistent with the policy and General Purposes
of this Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.

§806.000. COMMITTEES.
A.

The Master and Wardens shall be a Charity Committee, and shall have

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 807.020 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

175

§807.020. ADDITIONAL REGULATIONS APPLICABLE TO MEETINGS.
A.

Sunday Meetings. No Stated or Special Meetings of a Lodge shall be
held on Sunday except for the annual Installation of Officers or funeral
services. If the Stated Meeting of a lunar Lodge falls on a Sunday, the
Stated Meeting shall be held on the following day.

B.

Work to be Done in Lodge of Master Masons. All business, except the
examination of candidates in the Candidate’s Lecture of the Entered
Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees, the conferring of the Entered
Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees, and the consideration of relief of a
worthy Mason, shall be done in a Lodge of Master Masons. A Lodge of
Master Masons may be called down for the examination of candidates
in the Candidate’s Lecture of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow
Craft degrees.

C.

Quorum. A Lodge shall not be opened, nor shall any work be done
or business transacted, except by, or in the presence of, and under the
continual direction of the Master, the ranking Warden, the Grand Master
or the Grand Master’s designated representative. No Lodge shall transact
any business with fewer than five members of the Lodge present except
the conferring of degrees. The Tiler is present while he is at his post in
the Tiler’s room.

D.

Presence of Charter. No meeting shall be conducted by a Lodge unless
the Charter of the Lodge is present. A photocopy of the Charter may
be made under the direction of the Grand Secretary at the request
and expense of the Lodge. The Grand Secretary shall attach thereto a
certificate with the seal of Grand Lodge affixed that the copy is a true
copy of the Lodge’s Charter. The copy may be used by the Lodge instead
of the original Charter at any time.

E.

Presence of Flag. The Flag of our country shall be displayed at all
meetings of a Lodge. At the annual election of officers, and at such other
meetings as may be deemed desirable by the Master, the Flag shall be
formally presented at the Altar and received in the manner prescribed in
the Ritual. The Altar of a Lodge shall not be decorated with any flag.

F.

No Smoking. Smoking is forbidden in the Lodge room at all times when
the Lodge is in session.

G.

No Adjourned Meetings. There shall be no adjourned meeting. Each
meeting of a Lodge must be closed when the business proposed for
transaction has been concluded.

H.

Good Standing Requirement. No member may make a motion, second
a motion, speak on a motion, vote on a motion, recommend anyone for
membership or ballot on membership at a Lodge meeting unless he is

176

Proceedings of the
then a member in good standing of that Lodge. He must present a current
dues receipt to the Tiler to demonstrate that he is a member of the Lodge
in good standing or be verified by the Master, Senior Warden, Junior
Warden, Secretary or Assistant Secretary as a member of the Lodge in
good standing.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to modify the California Masonic
Code in several areas regarding Masons not in good standing. These changes can
be summarized as follows:
1. Require the Secretary to notify each member annually of the
consequences of not being a member in good standing.
2. Require that a Mason be in good standing to serve on a Lodge
committee, make a motion, second a motion, speak on a motion, vote on a motion,
recommend anyone for membership or ballot on membership at a Lodge meeting.
3. Require any Mason desiring to speak, vote, or otherwise participate in
a Lodge meeting to present a current dues receipt to the Tiler or be vouched for
by the Master, Senior Warden, Junior Warden, Secretary, or Assistant Secretary as
being in good standing.
The first change (annual notification of the consequences of not being a
member in good standing) is consistent with Grand Lodge policy of encouraging
member retention and does not impose an undue burden on a Lodge.
The second change (limitation of the rights and privileges of a member
not in good standing) must be viewed as directed primarily at a member who
is not in good standing but has not yet been suspended, because, according to
Section 804.155 of the California Masonic Code, a suspended member is already
deprived of all rights, privileges, and benefits as a Mason and prohibited from any
Masonic communication until legally restored.
Currently, a Brother who is not in good standing but has not yet been
suspended may not serve on a Grand Lodge committee, receive an award from
Grand Lodge, apply for dispensation to open a new Lodge, affiliate with another
Lodge, transfer his membership to another jurisdiction, apply for a Demit, serve
as a Lodge officer, vote in Lodge elections, prefer Masonic charges, be recognized
as a Past Master, or be eligible for admission to the Masonic Homes. He is not
otherwise restricted from participating in Lodge.
This Resolution would place further restrictions on such a Brother’s
activities in Masonry, such as not serving on a Lodge committee or balloting
on membership. This proposed change is consistent with the other restrictions
already placed on a Brother who is not in good standing. It is the policy of Grand
Lodge that a Brother who wishes to be active in his Lodge should pay his dues.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

177

The third change (requiring a member to present a current dues receipt
or be vouched for) is intended to enforce the restrictions of this Resolution. In
practice, the Master and Secretary should know which Brothers are not in good
standing and can enforce this requirement as needed. Requiring a Brother to
present a current dues card on request is not unreasonable.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
Resolution ADOPTED.

This Resolution would require that the Installing Officer and Master of
Ceremonies be certified before being permitted to preside at a Lodge Installation.
The proponents point out that a majority of our installations are held with our
families and the public present and should be an impressive ceremony by which
our fraternity is cast in only the most positive light. When the ceremony is done
poorly, it can be embarrassing to Lodge officers and their guests and reflect
negatively upon the fraternity.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

181

It has long been the policy of this Grand Lodge to require that all Masonic
ceremonies, particularly those open to the public, such as funerals, be presented
in the best manner possible. This proposal would not guarantee perfect work at
an Installation; but it does insure that those who preside at this most important
ceremony have proven their ability to perform the work in a proper fashion.
We make every effort to maintain a high standard of ritual work while
in Lodge; we should do the same in public. It is important to remember; we have
very few opportunities to highlight our Fraternity in the public eye.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this

Resolution No. 11-15
Allows Grand Lodge to Use the Same Auditor for

The proponents of this Resolution seek to allow Grand Lodge to use the same
auditor for more than five consecutive years.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
Whereas, a Grand Lodge Committee on Audit was added to the
California Masonic Code with the requirement that the firm acting as auditor be
changed every five years; and
Whereas, neither the California Non Profit Integrity Act of 2004
applicable to California non-profit organizations nor the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of
2002 applicable to U.S. public companies requires that the audit firm be changed
every five years; and
Whereas, it may not be in the best interests of the Grand Lodge or its
related entities to change the audit firm every five years.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 406.015 of the
California Masonic Code be amended as marked:
§406.015. AUDIT.
The Committee on Audit shall consist of not less than three or more than seven
members. Any other provision of this Code to the contrary withstanding, the
Committee on Audit shall consist solely of members of the Grand Lodge. At
least one member of the Committee on Audit should have sufficient education

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Current Masonic Law requires that the Grand Lodge outside auditing
firm must be changed every five years. This Resolution seeks to amend the Code
by deleting the five-year limitation. In its place, the Resolution would require the
Grand Lodge Committee on Audit to review annually the outside auditing firm
and, if it deems it appropriate to retain the same firm for more than five years, to
report that fact to Grand Lodge together with the reasons therefore.
It is common for an entity to change auditors every so often so as to lessen
the possibility that a less than arms-length relationship might develop between
the auditor and the entity it audits. The auditors might become too trusting of
management and not remain truly independent.
Offsetting these concerns is the efficiency and resulting lower costs
that come from the people involved, both on the audit side and the management
side, learning to work well together over a period of years. Grand Lodge has
great confidence in its current financial staff, in its ability and in its integrity. It
also has great respect for its outside audit firm and the principals who have been
working on its accounts. More importantly, the Grand Lodge Audit Committee is
comprised of experienced, career accountants and auditors who are very diligent
in overseeing the audit process and the people involved.
The proponents of this Resolution point out that neither state nor federal
law require nonprofit organizations to change their auditors every five years. As
the policy considerations for the current five-year limitation are not of concern
at this time, there is no logical basis for requiring a change in auditors every five
years simply for the sake of change.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution are seeking to cause the Master-elect
to kneel and pray aloud during the installation ceremony. They rightly point out
that we are often reminded of the benefit of prayer and they cite that the Grand
Master-elect does kneel and pray aloud before being installed Grand Master.
Our ritual, ceremonies and social gatherings usually begin by invoking
the aid and blessing of Deity; however, nowhere is a man required to pray aloud.
In the Entered Apprentice degree the Senior Deacon prays for the candidate. In
the Third Degree the candidate is directed to pray either audibly or silently. By the
time a man is installed Master he should not need to be instructed when or how to
pray. Regarding the Grand Master Elect praying, Grand Lodge ritual differs from
that of the constituent Lodges and thus sets no precedent.
This Resolution is not consistent with the policy and general purposes of
this Grand Lodge.

186

Proceedings of the

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
The proponents of this resolution seek to modify the Installation ritual
for constituent Lodges by requiring the Master-Elect to kneel at the altar and, in
an audible tone of voice, deliver a prayer just as the Grand Master-Elect does
during the Grand Lodge Installation ceremony.
The installation ceremony for the Grand Lodge of California and the
installation ritual for constituent Lodges, which was developed from a John
Barney version of the Preston Webb ritual work, have served both entities well
for over 162 years.
To prevent confusion by some members of the public, who believe our
fraternity to be a form of religion, public events by constituent lodges do not
include displays of religious activity by anyone other than a brother who delivers
the invocation in accordance with our teachings and sometimes a benediction on
behalf of the lodge.
The Installation ceremony for Grand Lodge is designed to be slightly
different from that of the Installation Ritual for Constituent Lodge in order to
reinforce the differences between the two and to remind the Craft of the supreme
authority invested in the office of Grand Master and the need for him alone to be
the one who prays for the wisdom to govern Masonry within California.
We must remember that our rituals are not stand alone activities that
are presented independently. They are, however, activities that are interdependent
upon other related activities. Just as each degree conferral forms the foundation
for the following degree, so does the institution ceremony for a new lodge form
the foundation for the Installation ritual.
The Installation ritual for the constituent lodge stems from the ceremony
used by the Grand Master at the Institution of a new lodge. In that ceremony,
the Grand Master instructs the new Master, Wardens, and members as to their
respective duties and responsibilities and concludes with instructions to the new
Master to strictly conform to all edicts of the Grand Lodge or General Assembly of
Masons, one of which is for the Master to ensure the Installation of his successor.
To install his successor the Craft established a specific installation
ritual which retained much of the language and ceremony used by the Grand
Master during the Institution of the lodge. Consequently, just as the Grand Master
installed the new Master into his office, so does the new Master imitate the Grand
Master when he ensures the installation of his successor: Thus, the mantle of
authority is uniformly passed from the Grand Master to the new Master and then
to each new Master through eternity. The Institution ceremony does not require
the Master to kneel at an altar and deliver an audible prayer, consequently, neither
does the Installation ritual.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

187

Additionally, the recommended verbiage changes the current ritual
verbiage by adding some words and deleting important words as in the following:
Current ritual:
I.O.
Brother Master of Ceremonies, you will now present the
Brother who has been elected to discharge the important duties of Master of
this Lodge.
RESOLUTION VERBIAGE (words eliminated / words added):
I.O.
Brother Master of Ceremonies, you will now present the Brother
who has been elected to discharge the important duties of Worshipful Master of
this Lodge, first causing him to kneel at our Altar.
CURRENT RITUAL:
M.C.
Worshipful Sir, I take pleasure in presenting to you, Brother
__________, who has been duly elected to serve as Master of this Lodge.
RESOLUTION VERBIAGE (words eliminated / words added):
M.C.
Worshipful Sir, I take pleasure in presenting to you, I have the
honor and pleasure of presenting Brother _______________, who has been duly
elected to serve as Worshipful Master of this lodge.
The current Installation ritual has not proven to be a burden over the
years to the Fraternity in general or the lodge in particular; therefore, the Ritual
Committee does not support this resolution.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

know the work and lectures of their current position as well as the Master’s work
and lectures of the previous office; and
WHEREAS, Resolution No. 2008-05 as adopted omitted the requirement
for the Senior Warden to be proficient in the Master’s work and lecture of the

WHEREAS, qualification consistency should be the goal for

WHEREAS, this resolution is a house cleaning measure meant to

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 805.530 of

§805.530. CONDITIONS TO INSTALLATION OF THE SENIOR
WARDEN-ELECT.
Before a Senior Warden‑elect can be installed, there shall be presented to the
Installing Officer a Certificate of Qualification of the Grand Lecturer, the Assistant
Grand Lecturer of the division in which his Lodge is situated, or the Inspector of
the district in which his Lodge is situated, certifying that:
A.

He has personally examined the Senior Warden‑elect and that he is
qualified to give the Senior Warden’s work of the Entered Apprentice,
Fellow Craft and Master Mason Degrees, and the Master’s work and
lectures of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft Degrees;

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to clarify the section of the
California Masonic Code involving the qualifications of the Senior Warden.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

189

Prior to the adoption of the Fourth Edition of the California Masonic
Code in 2006, section 25080–A required the Senior Warden elect to be proficient
in “the work and lectures of the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees.”
That language was carried over into the new code in section 805.530. In 2008,
section 805.530 was amended to make it clear that the Senior Warden-elect had to
be proficient in the Master’s work and lecture of the Fellow Craft degree as well
as the Senior Warden’s work of all three degrees. However, Resolution 08-05
inadvertently deleted the long-standing requirement that the Senior Warden-elect
also be proficient in the lecture of the Entered Apprentice degree.
Resolution 2012-02 corrects the Code by making it clear that a Senior
Warden-elect must be proficient in the Senior Warden’s work of all three degrees
as well as the lectures of both the Entered Apprentice and Fellow Craft degrees.
It has long been the policy of this Grand Lodge that the Senior Warden
be proficient in the work as well as the lectures of the Entered Apprentice and
Fellow Craft degrees so that he could, if the need arose, take the chair of the
Junior Warden for the presentation of degrees. This Resolution makes it clear that
the Senior Warden elect must be so qualified.
This Resolution is consistent with the policy and general purposes of this
Grand Lodge.
