Report of the Strategic Planning Committee
Masonic Homes of California
July 2011-June 2012
In May 2011 the Masonic Homes Board identified four strategic
priorities in addition to the traditional services offered at their Union City and
Covina campuses and through Masonic Outreach Programs: continuing-care- athome; outreach to lodges; support for youth and families and memory care. Since
that time, the Strategic Planning Committee has worked with the board and with
staff to ensure these initiatives advance through research and development and
that the board as a whole continues to provide leadership in developing the longterm strategic vision of the Masonic Homes of California.
The Strategic Planning Committee continues to serve as a sounding
board where initiatives and ideas are brought for review and discussion. As
Chair, I am proud that the members of the Strategic Planning Committee (John
L. Cooper III, Michael J. Cornell, John W. Herring and Stuart A. Wright) have
all given considerable time and energy not only to their direct committee work
but to serving as board leaders involved with these specific strategic initiatives.
I am pleased to report that with their help and the dedicated work of our staff,
we have made significant progress. We are now in the process of hiring a project
coordinator for our continuing-care-at-home initiative, designed to sustain the
highest degree of independence and quality of life possible for members within
an active family and community network that allows them to successfully live in
their own homes. Trustee John Heisner and Sabrina Montes, Director of Outreach
Services, partnered with Jim Kurupas, AGL for Division IX and lodge leaders in
the San Diego area to develop a lodge outreach program that extends the benefits
and expertise available through Masonic Homes in partnership with local lodges
creating support networks for vulnerable members. Draft curriculum to train local
leaders is now under review and initial vetting of local resources available to these
networks is underway. After initial development in the San Diego region, Masonic
Homes intends to implement similar programs across California. In addition to
the cutting-edge work taking place at the Masonic Center for Youth and Families,
the only program of its kind in North America offering holistic, multi-disciplinary
assessment and treatment of youth with behavioral and psychiatric needs, the
Homes is partnering with the Grand Lodge Communications Department to create
a parenting blog to provide much needed information to parents and families
across California. The Masonic Homes is also exploring avenues to develop
networks of support for Masonically-affiliated families across the state to connect
them with local service providers and to capitalize on the opportunities provided
through telemedicine which allows clients to access medical specialists through
the Web without having to travel from their own communities.
Over the past nine months, as part of our exploration of how best to
address the growing need for state-of-the-art memory care, we established
strategic partnerships with leading educators and researchers in the University of

254

Proceedings of the

California system, Community Colleges, private universities, Kaiser Permanente
and the California Institute for Nursing and Health Care who recognize, as we
do, that greater emphasis must be placed on training nurse leaders in the fields of
geriatric and long-term care nursing in order to sustain quality, person-centered
memory care programs. Initial discussions are now beginning about the design of
training to practice programs for nursing students, graduate research opportunities
developing meaningful outcome studies and evaluation metrics and avenues for
emphasizing the importance of person-centered geriatric and long-term care
within the nursing curriculum.
In addition to the input and direction the Strategic Planning Committee
gives to these evolving strategic initiatives, we support the board in examining
its own governance practices and determining how to establish policies that more
clearly articulate the ends the Masonic Homes seeks to accomplish on behalf of
our membership and our communities and how to exercise its authority more
effectively, holding itself and the management of the organization accountable for
achieving these ends in ways that align with our fundamental mission and vision.
This work has proven challenging at times to our board, including the members
of our committee, as we recognize the need to shift from a familiar focus on
specific projects which are the responsibility of our executive management, to
a broader perspective on framing the ends of the organization and then holding
our executives accountable for achieving them. This policy governance model
furthers the review of the structure of the Strategic Planning Committee begun
over a year ago, as we realize our primary aim must be to support the board
in shaping its strategic policies rather than assist management with the direct
implementation of particular programs. To that end, we have engaged our trustees
in meaningful discussions about how best to provide information and resources
to inform their discussions about memory care and how to structure board
meetings so that our trustees can define meaningful ends statements that give the
necessary direction to our executive leadership who then bring their expertise
to bare in creating programs to achieve these ends. The Strategic Planning
Committee recognizes that the evolution in our governance practices is part
of a wider effort by all the Masonic-entity boards to elevate our understanding
so that we can collaborate more effectively in achieving the strategic priorities
established by our membership and the Masons of California who seek to make a
profound difference in the lives of every member and in the communities to which
we belong.
I want to recognize the outstanding contributions of the members of
the Strategic Planning Committee and their dedication and commitment to the
Masonic Homes of California, the residents and members that we serve and to
our craft.
Respectfully submitted,
Fred L. Avery, Chairman
John L. Cooper III
John W. Herring
Michael Cornell
Stuart A. Wright

Report of the Board Development Committee
Masonic Homes of California
July 2011-June 2012
It is my honor and pleasure to present the annual report of the Board
Development Committee of Masonic Homes of California.
The Committee is charged with various responsibilities, including
developing and updating board orientation; planning continuing board education;
fostering best governance practices; reviewing compliance with civil and Masonic
regulations; engaging with the craft to identify qualified candidate to recommend
to the Board and the Grand Master; review the Bylaws; and prepare and review
an annual Board self-assessment.
The Committee began the year with the development of a plan for the
year, which included all of its responsibilities. Early in 2012, the Board of MHC,
along with all of the boards and major committees of Masons of California, began
an exploration of the Policy Governance model developed by John Carver. The
Committee assisted the Board in this exploration, and most of the annual Board
retreat in May was dedicated to learning more about and developing the systems
needed to adopt and implement Policy Governance.
As the interest in the model began to grow, the Committee temporarily
set aside its action plan for the year since it understood that many of the Board and
Committee processes in place would be amended, sometimes drastically, if Policy
Governance were to be adopted. As of this writing, the Committee is assisting the
Board to develop the agenda for a special meeting in July, 2012 during which the
Board will complete the work it started in May.
It has been a privilege to serve the fraternity. I thank the dedicated
members of the Committee who have so ably served this past year.

John L. Cooper III

Respectfully submitted,
Gary Charland, Chairman
John W. Herring

John R. Heisner

Report of the Executive Vice President
I am pleased to once again introduce the management reports on each of
our service lines by its executive or director and to report on some of the unifying
themes that guide our work each and every day. The residents and clients of
Masonic Homes of California are blessed with a committed and capable executive
team, guiding an equally committed and capable workforce.
Resident-Centered Care and the New Philosophy of Care
I have been reporting for two years on the implementation of our new
philosophy of care (that is, moving from a primary focus on care toward an
emphasis on the empowerment of residents and clients to fulfill their highest
potential). This past year we have purposefully converged that philosophy with
a related movement in our skilled nursing section, Resident-centered Care. In
short, resident-centered care pivots care and services around the preferences and
life choices of each resident, whenever possible, rather than the convenience of
the facility. Thus, to use a simple example, residents who prefer evening instead
of morning baths would be accommodated. It is a good direction, but one that
is surprisingly difficult to fully implement. Even the best of caregivers can
sometimes get in a routine that seems most “efficient” rather than what a given
resident would prefer. It’s a mind shift that takes time to become woven into daily
work. I expect in future reports to apprise you of our progress in this change of
work culture in our skilled nursing section.
Excellence in Service
In past reports I have outlined our improvements in service excellence.
In the past year we have entered a new and more complex phase, challenging
ourselves with a higher standard of effort. In the past year we have:
•

Hired a new Risk Management consulting firm, steeped in the field of
health care, retirement living, and senior service to assess our program
with a fresh set of eyes. We have asked the firm to be thorough and
candid. We expect that report at the time of this writing, and it will form
the basis for action plans to be implemented over the next year. We are in
the midst of budget season, and so any major improvements that require
additional resources will be considered.

•

Commissioned a detailed and frank third party assessment of our
dementia program on both campuses, with a special focus on Traditions,
our dementia care center in Union City. We received that report in May,
2012, and staff has been hard at work implementing action plan to address

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

257

the findings. We have already made several major improvements, and
have included the more systemic improvements into the operating and
capital budget proposals for FY 2013.
•

Hired a new Quality Assurance and Program Improvement (QAPI)
director, Barbara Gallardo, in April, 2012. Barbara will be taking our
current Quality Assurance program to a higher level, at first to meet new
requirements under licensing and certification, but more fundamentally
to help us imbed continuous quality improvement in the culture of
Masonic Homes. We will start by helping the nursing staff improve
in clinical areas, but we have already embarked upon smaller projects
that have little to do with nursing. We expect that all departments will
ultimately be included in the QAPI program.
Strategic Initiatives

We have made significant strides in the development of the four strategic
initiatives of MHC: dementia care/memory support; care at home; lodge outreach;
and youth & family services. I urge you to read the report of Fred Avery, Chairman
of MHC’s Strategic Planning Committee, in these proceedings. Under Fred’s and
President David Doan’s leadership, we are poised to address our future as we
continue to evolve to meet the needs of the fraternity.
Community Recognition
Finally, I am pleased to report that Masonic Homes of California was
awarded the Tom Kitayama Business Service Award by the New Haven Schools
Foundation, in recognition of MHC’s leadership in advancing the cause of and
helping to raise funds for the school district, which has, like all districts in
California, experienced several years of drastic budget cuts.
I thank you for the opportunity to address the fraternity. It has been
an eventful year, and the coming year promises to be even more exciting. I feel
privileged to be a part of it.
Respectfully submitted,
Melvin Matsumoto, Executive Vice President

Report of the Executive Director/Administrator
Masonic Home at Union City
July 2011 – June 2012
The Annual Report is presented on behalf of the residents and staff of the
Masonic Homes at Union City. We would like to also express our appreciation to
the Board of Trustees and Masonic Lodges for their support of this community.
Here are the major activities and achievements in the last year.
Activity and Programming
The Outdoor Lodge was initiated by the Siminoff Daylight Lodge No.
850 on Saturday, June 2nd.
We initiated a Woodlands/Habitat Restoration project in partnership
with Tri-CED, a local organization and the largest nonprofit recycling company
in the State of California. The project includes restoration of our hillsides with
flora it had a hundred years ago; on-site waste management System to achieve
zero wet waste and improve our carbon footprint; and organic composting for the
entire campus.
Masonic Home of Union City in partnership with Acacia Creek was
winners of the ‘Golden Sneaker’ for the second year in a row. The Walk to
Wellness is a significant highlight of the Wellness initiative. The combined total
this year was 85,300,192 steps in May, with more than 275 staff, residents and
volunteers participating on 21 teams.
In response to the Memory Care initiative, an action plan was developed
and initiated utilizing recommendations of a consultant and a new position,
Program Specialist, was created to focus on staff education and program
development in the area of dementia care and memory support.
Much work has been performed on Disaster Training including continued
training with CERT classes and evacuation chairs with residents & staff; and
floor-to-floor and full building evacuation drills throughout the campus.
In keeping with the new philosophy of care, several programs have been
put into place:
•

‘Know your Numbers’ program – staff visits all residents the first week
of the month and offer to check their weight, B/P, and other vital signs.

•

‘Vertical’ is a program to assist resident with balance issues. Sessions
include assessing rooms for hazards, balance exercises, review
of medications.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

259

•

‘Neurobics’ is a 6 week course to enhance memory and brain health with
strategies and mental games.

•

‘Nourish’ a program about nutrition in the older adult with emphasis on
making good choices.

•

‘My Stress Solutions’ learn to harness your stress levels.
Other major activity includes:

•

Scrabble Tournament in September 2011 was a resident inspired and
led event.

•

Tomatopalooza, an enjoyable event in August, showcased a variety
of dishes with tomatoes, grown in the MHC garden, as the primary
ingredient

•

A Cookie Expo and Tree Trimming Party was held with residents and
staff baking cookies to share and all helped decorate the tree in the
Auditorium.

•

The Annual Tree lighting was held on December 13th was enjoyed by 900
visitors. Ninety-seven year old Mrs. Betty Ehly lit the tree with Santa.

•

Annual Arts & Craftsman show was extended to a two day event and
artists demonstrated their talents in a ‘Living Art’ area of the show.

•

An Around the World Wine Tasting Event encouraged study (different
countries), fun (wine tasting from around the world with appropriate
snacks), socializing between MHC and Acacia Creek, visiting of
seldom visited places at MHC and exercise (walk around campus to get
to stations).
Capital Additions and Replacements

New vehicles were purchased to upgrade the fleet: a 32 passenger bus;

All three floors of the Sedam Building were given a much needed facelift
with new paint, carpeting and baseboard.

The Grider Gym, originally opened in 1996, has been completely
remodeled including new, senior friendly equipment which allows each
resident to track her/his progress electronically.

Proceedings of the

Report of the Administrator
Masonic Homes of California at Covina
July, 2011 – June, 2012
On behalf of the residents and staff of the Masonic Homes at Covina,
we are pleased to present the following Annual Report highlighting the successes
and challenges of the past year. We would like to also express our appreciation to
the Board of Trustees and our Masonic Lodges for their dedication and support
of our community.
During the past year we served a senior population which averaged 75
residents. The population represented a resident mix of 57% Independent Living;
35% Assisted Living and 8 % Skilled Nursing. We had 15 admissions; 10 deaths
and 2 transfers to the Union City Campus.
Our waiting list included thirty-four prospective residents representing
twenty-six households. The average waiting period for admission was
approximately eleven months. Our staff is committed to call each prospective
applicant monthly to inquire on their well-being: physically, emotionally and
financially. Referrals to our Masonic Outreach Program are made if services and
support are needed.
Our senior community offers a “Continuum of Care” model that provides
a full spectrum of care and services. Residents are treated with respect and dignity
while partnering with staff to define what quality of life means to each individual.
Activity and Programming
As a resident-centered, mission-driven community, and in keeping
with the tenets of Free Masonry, the Masonic Homes of California promotes the
quality of life by empowering our members, their families and our community to
live well, and have active, meaningful and rewarding lives.
During this past year our focus has been on “Wellness”. At the conclusion
of our “2011 Wellness Challenge, Pound for Pound Program,” residents and staff
had a total weight loss of 158 pounds. As a result we donated 158 pounds of food
to our local food bank.
We are now focusing on our “Wellness Challenge for 2012.” This year
residents and staff are being encouraged to “Try Something New.” Each week
there is a scheduled program that either a staff member or resident will instruct.
The scheduled programs include Cooking with Spices, Flight Simulator, learning
how to use and be safe on Facebook, SKYPE with family and friends, Tips &
Tricks to achieve Great Photography, and more!

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

271

Our “Partners in Care Program” was a success this year. The workshop
is designed for those with chronic conditions to self-manage and be empowered.
The program provides tools to improve their quality of life. Our two resident
trainers facilitated the class teaching ten other residents the program.
This year we partnered with Mt. San Antonio College’s Older Adult
Program to provide a “Brain Fitness” class for our residents and seniors in our
community. Mt. San Antonio College has teamed with San Diego State University,
California Community College, Educators of Older Adults and a neuro–scientific
software company to offer this Brain Fitness Program. This program has proven
successful in empowering cognitive functions of seniors through participation in
scientifically designed computer delivered brain exercises, which will improve
processing speed information, vision, hearing, both long and short term memory
and reaction time. The residents who attended this class feel they have improved
in all these areas.
Our residents are involved in community volunteering. Residents
volunteered at the Citrus Valley Hospice Facility, Covina Police Department,
Badillo Elementary School, Joslyn Senior Center and the California Science
Center. We also have many resident volunteers on campus; working in the general
store, teaching ceramics, conducting tours, working in the gift shop, greeting
guests at the front gate, gardening, photography, New 2 U clothing store, and
publishing our monthly resident newsletter.
Our resident committees include; Resident Council, Health Services,
Dietary Services, Active Living, Disaster Preparation, Building & Grounds,
Housekeeping and Spiritual. During the past year we had a total of 15,025
volunteer hours from our residents.
On June 16, 2012, our campus enjoyed our 7th successful “Summer
Festival. The “Summer Festival” joins together our Masonic Lodges and Eastern
Star. The Grand Master’s Summer Festival theme for the event was Hawaiian. We
had over 400 guests attend this event.
Our campus retreat program continues to grow. This year we enjoyed
the fellow-ship with DeMolay, Job’s Daughters, Rainbow Girls, Inspector
Development Academy and IDA.
Our Campus is proud to be a training site for the University of Southern
California Social Workers, East San Gabriel Occupational and Technical Program
for Certified Nurse Assistant and Chaffey College for Activity Leaders.
We have many Masonic affiliated groups along with our surrounding
community organizations visiting our campus. These groups use our facilities
for meetings and retreats throughout the year. Some of the events held on
campus included; Lodge BBQ’s, Polling Destination for 4 precincts, California
Census Bureau, Charter Oak School District, and the Chamber of Commerce to
name a few.

Report of the Vice President of Masonic Outreach
and Youth Services
Masonic Homes of California
July 2011 – June 2012
Masonic Center for The Masonic Center for Youth and Families
(MCYAF) was opened in February 2011 to help youth between the ages of 4 and
17 who struggle with behavioral, academic, emotional or social difficulties and
who could benefit from a developmentally appropriate treatment. We serve the
youth and we serve their families.
Since opening, we have served over 120 youth. In caring for these 120
children we have cared for their families, for future generations of those families
and our communities. Youth who were at the brink of expulsion are now bringing
home their report cards with pride; families who were fractured, now sit at the
table to enjoy dinner together; and on the stories go.
We start with understanding – not labeling. We talk with parents and
guardians and those who interact closely with the young person in a variety of
settings –teachers, coaches, babysitters and relatives. We want to understand
where and how the young person flourishes and where and how they struggle.
Assessment psychologists complete extensive cognitive, personality and
neuropsychological testing to understand the details about the youth’s functioning
and capacities.
The treatment team comes together to review the findings of the
testing and the information gathered from interviews with family, friends and
professionals. From this discussion, we develop a treatment plan that considers
the young person in the context of their family and daily realities. A treatment plan
that incorporates all that we know and have observed about the young person:
their sly sense of humor; their deep anxiety and vigilance; their hopelessness;
their dreams.
We know that a young person who struggles with emotional and
behavioral difficulties can be helped through a relationship with a thoughtful and
caring professional so we offer individual psychotherapy for the youth and/or the
parents as well as couples and families counseling. The terms of the treatment are
dictated by the needs of the youth and family.
We brought together a group of internationally-recognized providers
– the best in their fields – and we developed a unique and integrated approach
to treatment. In so doing, we recognize an obligation to use our experience to
show what’s possible when you invest wisely in youth and families. So we are
working with top researchers across the country – including the Yale Child Study
Center and the Anna Freud Centre in London – to demonstrate our outcomes and

278

Proceedings of the

publish our findings. The name of Masonic Center for Youth and Families will be
synonymous with excellence, innovation and our values in professional circles
and in our communities and schools.
Through MCYAF, California Freemasons are insisting on innovative and
high quality of care for our youth. Such a commitment speaks to the strength of
our organization and our deep and active commitment to the health of our children
and our communities. We look forward to the years ahead to serving more of our
fraternal family and other’s in the name of Freemasonry.
Respectfully Submitted,
Steffani Kizziar, Vice President of Masonic Outreach & Youth Services

Report of the Director
Masonic Outreach Services
July, 2011 – June, 2012
CHILDREN’S SERVICES- Family Resource Center
Upon closure of the Masonic Homes Children’s Residential program in
2009, we began serving our residents through case management and financial
support. During this third year of the Transition Program, we provided financial
and non-financial case management to 8 children and their families, who still need
on-going support. At the end of this school year, 3 of these children graduated
from high school. Two of the graduates have been approved to receive a Masonic
Homes Scholarship and the third will pursue a Masonic Homes Scholarship
in 2013.
In 2012-2013, the Transition Program we will serve 5 children and their
families. Of these, 2 will need out-placement support and 3 will need financial
case management, with nominal financial support to help meet their educational,
extracurricular and clothing needs. The 5 children are those in most need of our
continued support, due to their vulnerable family environments. These children
continue to make positive strides in their lives with our on-going support and
guidance. Next year, we will have 1 high school senior, 3 high school juniors and
1 high school sophomore. Two of these children have Masonic affiliations.
The Masonic Homes Scholarship Program continues to offer scholarships
to alumni of the Children’s Program. Scholarships are provided for up to 5 years
toward undergraduate studies; up to 2 years toward Master’s programs; and up to 5
years toward Doctoral programs. Additionally, scholars are able to attend schools
of their choice throughout the United States. The scholars receive scholarships
based on the type of school and their full-time or part-time status. A hallmark of
this program’s success has been the case management support that is provided
to ensure students access school support services, and successfully navigate
through college on their way to becoming independent adults. All scholars must
maintain a GPA requirement and re-apply for scholarship annually. This has
led to strengthening the students’ accountability for their own performance and
commitment toward their education. During this past school year, one scholar
graduated with a Masters’ degree and another graduated with a Bachelors’ degree.
For the upcoming 2012-2013 school year, the Scholarship Program will serve
18 students. It is truly gratifying to witness the success of our former alumni, as
they pursue a higher education and complete college to better themselves and
their futures.

280

Proceedings of the

MASONIC FAMILY OUTREACH SERVICES – Family Resource Center
In October 2009, we began providing financial and non-financial case
management to members and their families under the age of 60, currently known
as Masonic Family Outreach Services. There are eligibility requirements for
financial support as well as time limits for such support. Financial support is
short-term and intended to act as a bridge from economic hardship toward selfsufficiency. All financial clients agree to partner with their Care Manager toward
this goal and must also apply and access any public benefits for which they qualify.
Case management support is extended to the entire Masonic family, with
no eligibility requirements or time limits. Case management services are broad,
flexible and able to serve families in their own communities. Our support includes
identifying resources for families struggling with today’s complex issues, as
well as assistance with applying for public benefits and other programs. Our
Care Managers provide support that meets the member’s individual needs. The
Masonic Assistance line provides information-referrals to all callers in need of
community resources. We are able to serve callers with a wide range of needs and
across different age groups. This past year, 20 members received direct financial
assistance and another 86 members received on-going case management. On
average, MFOS serves 20 clients per month with case management and 6 clients
per month with financial case management.
MASONIC SENIOR OUTREACH SERVICES
Many of our elderly brethren and their wives and widows continue to
experience economic difficulties related to living longer than planned and their
increasing care needs and costs. Additionally, we are seeing other members seek
early retirement due to loss of employment and health related issues. As a result,
we are serving more members through our MSOS program this past year than in
the previous year. This year, 248 members received direct financial assistance
through our MSOS program; another 44 received ongoing case management
services; and approximately 275 members received information and referrals.
The generous support of Masons, who give to our annual fund, helps ensure that
we are always in a position to the meet the increasing and diverse needs of our
fraternal family.
We believe creation of one central number, the Masonic Assistance line,
as the single point of inquiry for all Masonic Assistance Programs has made it
easier for callers to obtain information about any of our programs. The Masonic
Assistance line telephone number is printed on the new dues cards, so that it
is readily available. MOS has continued to expand its outreach efforts this year
by conducting lodge presentations throughout the state, but also through the
Lodge Outreach Initiative. This strategic initiative is focused on strengthening
our partnerships with our lodges by formalizing our communication process and

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

281

developing trainings materials and tools that will be utilized by our lodge leaders
as they fulfill their fraternal obligation of providing relief to their members. The
Lodge Outreach Initiative is in its initial stages of development and MOS is
currently partnering with the San Diego Masonic Leadership to identify, develop
and test its goals and objectives.
The Masonic Outreach Services Department has continued to improve
the delivery of our services, while expanding our programs and outreach efforts
into our lodges. We are excited about the potential impact on our members and
delivery of services as we embark upon on our strategic initiatives. Through
our collaborative and innovative work together, we believe that we will be
better positioned to meet the needs and interests of our members, across the
generational spectrum.
Respectfully submitted,
Sabrina Montes, MSW, Director of Masonic Outreach Services

Report of the Directors of the
Acacia Creek Retirement Community
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:
Most Worshipful Grand Master, officers and members of the Grand
Lodge, Brothers all, I am pleased to report to you that the Acacia Creek Retirement
Community, now in its third year of operations in Union City, has made great
strides toward increasing occupancy. In July of last year Chuck Major began his
new role as Acacia Creek’s Executive Vice President. Chuck brought an extensive
record of success in stabilizing retirement communities and meeting occupancy
and financial objectives. He launched a series of marketing initiatives to encourage
deposits and move-ins even as the housing market remains soft.
As a result of these initiatives move-ins began materializing in January
of this year. Acacia Creek has projected occupancy to increase from 71 Residents
occupying 52 apartments to 101 Residents in 75 apartments by the end of this
current fiscal year attaining over 50% occupancy. Tours have increased from an
average of 20 a month to 130 a month. Deposits continue to be acquired through
aggressive marketing events and an expanded outreach program. Currently, there
are 22 10% depositors who are expected to become Residents within the next
two years. These statistics compare favorably with the experience of market-rate
continuing care retirement communities nationwide against whom we benchmark.
The application process to renew our Provisional Certificate of Authority
(PCOA) from the Department of Social Services has been submitted for 2013.
We anticipate its renewal based upon the success of the marketing programs and
continued trend of increasing occupancy.
The annual Resident Satisfaction Survey scores have reached new heights.
The Residents’ involvement in the decision making process of the community
has given them a sense of ownership and personal pride. Involvement in our
“Successful Aging” programs through Masterpiece Living and subscriptions to
the Dakim Brain Fitness Program have seen dramatic increases in participation as
Residents become aware of the opportunities to maintain a healthy lifestyle. The
Residents are the best sales people in the community and are always involved in
the sales process. They interact with prospects at marketing events and share their
dinner table with interested parties who are overnight guests experiencing the
lifestyle of the community. The absorption of non-Masons into the Acacia Creek
community has been as smooth as we had anticipated. In fact, it has resulted in
two new petitions for Masonic degrees from among the eight new male nonMason residents.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

283

A quote from a letter the Board received recently from Past Grand Master
Ron Sherod tells the story:
“Your staff is unequaled. Everyone here has a happy face and a wonderful
and positive attitude. We are in our third month of residence and not one

attractively presented. We Masons are indeed proud of our home and

Staff satisfaction has been validated through their annual survey and by

In conjunction with the Masonic Homes Board and staff we are looking

The Acacia Creek Board has been engaged for the past several months in
aligning our efforts with the other Grand Lodge Entities in adopting a new policy
governance model designed to enhance board efficiency and effectiveness and
provide greater accountability of our operations. The Board Members of Acacia

It’s been an honor and pleasure to serve as President of the Acacia Creek

Report of the Trustees of the
California Masonic Foundation
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.&A.M. of California:
Continuing to build on the momentum gained over the last two years,
your California Masonic Foundation expanded the profound impact that the
Masons of California have had on public education and student careers this past
year. Through the Strategic Plan initiatives of literacy, Investment in Success,
and the Public Schools Advisory Councils, the fraternity has set new levels of
involvement in our communities and in our classrooms. In addition to overseeing
a wide array of support programs, the Board also took a major step to improve its
governance process by adopting the Carver Policy Governance Model.
Strategic Initiatives
Excellent progress was made this year in furthering implementation of the
two strategic initiatives assigned to the Foundation – support to public education
and increasing Lodge involvement in the community. In addition, our relationship
with the State Board of Education deepened by hosting a second successful
reception, this time in San Diego. This event allowed the local school districts to
meet and converse with Superintendent Torlakson. The number of Public School
Advisory Councils throughout the jurisdiction was doubled to a total of six. Each
held a Public Schools Month Kickoff celebration in April which highlighted our
70 scholarship recipients and our statewide literacy program, including total
monetary donations of over $775,000 to these efforts. Considerable community
and media interest was generated by these highly successful events.
Literacy
Major steps were taken this year to expand our strategic partnership with
Raising a Reader, the finest, nationally recognized program for early childhood
literacy in the country. Special branding and messaging was developed this year,
including a new logo reflecting the major support from the Masons of California.
This logo will be appear on the side of the red book bag that is the cornerstone
of the program – that bag filled with the wonder of reading and a world of
comprehension that is given to each student in the program every week.
A major step forward also occurred this year with the designation by
Grand Master Loui and the Executive Committee of Raising a Reader as the Grand
Master’s Project for at least the next three years. The unparalleled commitment

Middle School Math
The transition from elementary school arithmetic to the abstract concepts
of mathematics embodied in algebra and geometry can be extremely challenging
for most students. Finding a meaningful and impactful way to improve the ability
to make this transition continues to be elusive. Dialogue continued this year with
educators on a number of fronts, but no clear, nationally recognized, program has
emerged to meet the need and expectations of the Foundation. Continued research
and evaluation next year should result in a recommended approach for the Board
to consider.

286

Proceedings of the
Investment in Success

This year was the second for the Foundation’s revised scholarship
program. The expansion from three to six Public Schools Advisory Councils
and the addition of the Alameda/Contra Costa region allowed an increase in the
number of students evaluated and scholarships allocated. Seventy students were
initially awarded $490,000 this year (See Attachment A). These recipients were
nominated by their school principals and counselors and went through a rigorous
interview and evaluation process by the Advisory Council members in their area.
Most of these students live in challenging environments with many family issues
and limited possibilities for a college education. Yet these students consistently
showed the drive to succeed, a vision for their future, and the commitment to
better themselves and to give back to the community. You can be proud that, with
the help of the Masons of California, they have been given a chance for a better,
more productive life.
In addition, the Foundation began a partnership with the GLOW
Foundation, an effective organization that helps external entities interface with,
and support, public school systems. The Foundation plans to utilize GLOW to
interface with school district officials and statewide partners to help identify
candidates for the Investment in Success scholarships next year.
Public Schools Advisory Councils
The effort to increase community involvement at the local lodge level
was bolstered by the addition of three more Councils this past year – South Bay,
Orange County, and the Inland Empire. All six Councils were challenged to
accomplish three things; coordinate and conduct a Public Schools Month Kickoff
event in April, interview and select recipients for the Investment in Success
scholarships, and to reach out to the lodges in their area to raise funds for the
Grand Master’s Project, Raising A Reader.
Each Council performed admirably and successful Kickoff events were
conducted around the jurisdiction, with attendance by the Executive Committee
and Foundation Trustees. The Councils worked closely with their local school
districts to define the scholarship candidates and to conduct the interview and
selection process. Personal presentations of the scholarship award were made
where possible to further highlight the student’s accomplishment while publically
reinforcing the Fraternity’s commitment to public education. Council members
also visited Lodges to make presentations about Raising A Reader and seeking
monetary support for the Grand Master’s Project. The Board thanks the Chairmen
and members of all six Councils for their tireless work on behalf of the Foundation.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

287

Teacher of the Year
The Foundation continued its major sponsorship this year of the California
Teacher of the Year program. The annual state banquet was held in Sacramento
and the five Teacher of the Year finalists were celebrated. Your Grand Master and
the Foundation were present and the Masons of California were recognized for
their strong support. Each of the five was individually honored in a celebration
within their own community where the Foundation presented monetary awards
and gifts to each. In addition, California was honored to have one of the five
become a finalist for National Teacher of the Year. Subsequently, California was
further honored when Rebecca Mieliwocki, a seventh grade teacher from Burbank
was named the 2012 National Teacher of the Year. We will hear from Rebecca
personally at this Annual Communication.
Other Programs
The Foundation continued to underwrite our existing leadership
development, Lodge growth and Masonic education programs; including
the Masters and Wardens Leadership Retreats, Lodge Certification Program,
Inspector’s Development Academy, Masonic Formation, the Institute for Masonic
Studies and the Masonic Symposium. In addition, our Heritage sites, historic
article preservation, Library and Museum, and CMMT maintenance were funded.
The Foundation was approached this year by the California Rainbow
Foundation with a proposal to manage their scholarship endowment fund to
achieve greater returns by leveraging the Foundation’s Grand Lodge resources.
The Foundation approved the proposal as part of its strategic vision to manage
funds for the betterment of members of the family of Freemasonry. The Board
looks forward to a long and productive relationship with the Rainbow Foundation
and thanks Most Worshipful Richard Wakefield Hopper for his vision and support
of this partnership.
Board Governance
During the past year, the Foundation actively worked with the Grand
Lodge staff and in conjunction with the major constitutional boards and
committees to improve the Board governance process by adopting the Carver
Policy Governance Model. Trustees attended training in the concept and process
as well as working directly with Miriam Carver to establish Ends and Means
policies for the Board. The Carver model requires the Board of Trustees, with the
President acting as Chief Governance Officer, to focus on the strategic planning
process and to define explicit goals and expectations to be accomplished in line
with the Foundation’s reason for existence. These policies are then used by the
Executive Vice President, as the Chief Executive Officer, to frame an execution

288

Proceedings of the

plan that accomplishes the expectations within the policies constraints. The Board
found this model to be closely aligned with the current operating approach of the
Board and it was adopted for implementation. Ends and Means policies were
drafted, reviewed and approved. The Board wishes to commend Mrs. Carver
and Brad Colby, Director of Administration and Board Governance, for their
facilitization and guidance throughout the training and policies creation process.
Looking Forward to 2013
With the new governance model firmly in place, the Foundation is
prepared to increase its efforts to make a profound impact in public education.
The Board anticipates forming new Public Schools Advisory Councils in at least
two regions, Alameda/Contra Costa counties and the Sacramento area. This
will increase the number of lodges and brethren actively participating in their
communities by helping to bring Raising a Reader and Investment in Success to a
larger population of students. The Foundation also looks forward to working with
the Executive Committee to continue to raise awareness and funding for Raising
a Reader.
The Foundation’s long term objective of doubling its financial resources
by the end of the decade was given lower priority in 2012 to allow establishment
of the funding pipeline for Raising a Reader. In 2013, the Board will again
begin to define a campaign to achieve this objective by the Foundation’s 50th
anniversary in 2019. With increased resources, we will be able to substantially
increase our presence and impact in our communities and fulfill our vision of
making a profound difference in students’ lives and in our society.

Most Worshipful Grand Master and members of the Grand Lodge:
I am pleased to make the annual report of the Board of Trustees of the
California Masonic Memorial Temple.
The CMMT owns this magnificent edifice and derives tax-exempt
revenue by leasing space to the Grand Lodge of California whose offices are
on the third floor; to the Nob Hill Masonic Center that operates the garage; the
telecommunications facility on the roof and to other third parties, primarily Live
Nation, who lease space in the building. We also receive tax-exempt contributions
from candidates who are initiated into our California lodges. In spite of the
continued low return on investments this year, the CMMT experienced a healthy
cash flow. This Board was most prudent in the expenses for operating and
maintaining this building and we look to an increase in building use in order to
fund necessary improvements in the future.
Our efforts continue to be devoted to implementing our vision to keep
your facility viable for the future and competitive in the ever changing market
in which we operate. In this regard a considerable amount of time has been
spent this year by your CMMT Board to develop new, and review existing board
governance policies
The legal challenges impeding our plans to optimize the utilization of this
building, enabling us to meet our current and future operating needs, and provide
the means for the increasing costs of maintenance, repair, and restoration have
been vanquished. Approval for the current use of the building has been granted
and the required EIR Report will soon be completed. With patience the result will
be to create the auditorium into the premiere performance venue in San Francisco,
make the California Room a viable and welcome respite while transforming the
Exhibit Hall and kitchen, all while maintaining our beautiful War Memorial for all
time; still serve the needs for our Annual Communication and Grand Lodge while
maintaining a positive relationship with our neighbors on Nob Hill.
Our agreement with Live Nation guarantees tenancy for three more
years with the likely probability of a many year extension. This contract results in
significant revenue to CMMT as well as the Nob Hill Masonic Center, all for the
betterment of Freemasonry in California.
We have increased our capacity of telecommunication space on the roof
which in turn increases our long-term lease income.

Report of the Board of Directors

of the Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc. is unique among the various Masonicentity boards in California in that it is our only for profit, income tax paying entity
responsible for overseeing the efficient and profitable operations of the garage
located at the top of Nob Hill. One of our most important responsibilities is to
ensure payment of a dividend to Grand Lodge at the end of each fiscal year which
in turn helps fund the many ways the Masons of California make a profound
difference in the lives of our members and in society.
To ensure the efficient and safe management of our garage we have
extended our ACE Parking Agreement. ACE is one of the City’s most-recognized
garage operators and they have managed the day-to-day operations of the facility
well. With their help and with an event parking guarantee from Live Nation
for calendar year 2012 and 2013, we now can generate strong event parking
revenue along with greatly improved monthly and daily parking revenue. With
our Conditional Use Permit (CUP) unanimously approved by the San Francisco
Planning Commission and Board of Supervisors, the building may now continue
to operate legally with planned events that will help close out the year ending
October 31, 2012 significantly ahead of last year.
We have also completed an agreement with ZIP cars to use eighteen
parking spaces in our garage which ensures a steady revenue stream and makes
our location a significant hub for this innovative program sharing cars as needed
for people throughout San Francisco.
Two years ago we completed an extensive automation project, installing
pay stations at key positions in the garage to provide convenient and secure 24hour access for patrons, including guests at many of the nearby hotels on Nob
Hill. This automation has allowed us to realize significant labor savings. We have
also explored the Carver Board Governance model and are considering how to
improve our board operations by introducing a policy governance approach. This
year we have had several workshops and a retreat to focus our board on our long
term strategic objectives as opposed to our day to day operations.

Report of the Committee
on Finance

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F & A.M. of California:
The California Masonic Code, Section 406.035 E, requires the Committee
on Finance to review all of the proposed Recommendations and Resolutions to
be considered at the Annual Communication and to report on the financial impact
these items may have on the Grand Lodge budget.
Earlier this year, the committee reviewed the Grand Master’s Carry-Over
Resolutions and New Resolutions as provided by the Grand Secretary. On June
20, we finalized our report on the cost impact of each item. The Grand Secretary
on July 16 posted the report, with the legislation, to the lodges.
Only one resolution was found to have any financial impact on the Grand
Lodge, and in as much as our written report has been distributed, I will report on
it now and not later during the session.
Carry-Over Resolution No. 11-15: Allows Grand Lodge to use the
Same Auditor for More Than Five Consecutive Years: The recent Audit RFQ has
resulted in a significant reduction in audit costs proposed by our current auditor,
Moss Adams. Failure to pass this Resolution would require us to change out
auditor; this would result in the loss of a potential $44,000 in savings across all
entities covered by the audit and $12,500 in lost savings to Grand Lodge.
Again, in the view of the Committee on Finance, none of the other
legislation will have a financial impact on the Grand Lodge budget.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California
The Institute for Masonic Studies continues to provide high quality
Masonic education events, materials and resources to the Masons of California and
the public who study and appreciate the significant contributions the fraternity has
made throughout history. The members of the institute appreciate the confidence
and faith reposed in them by the Most Worshipful Frank Loui, Grand Master, and
the many brethren who have supported the activities of the IMS this past year.
12th Annual California Masonic Symposium
The symposium introduced a new format in 2012 with speakers
presenting twice,- once on Saturday, June 30, at the San Francisco Scottish Rite
Masonic Center with 181 in attendance, and then on Sunday, July 1, at the Pasadena
Scottish Rite with 256 in attendance. Each day’s program was identical. As in the
past, the symposium was sponsored jointly by the Grand Lodge of California, the
California Masonic Foundation, and the Institute for Masonic Studies. The topic,
The Emergence of Speculative Masonry, generated increased interest and the new
format attracted a record number of 437 attendees. The format will be retained
in 2013.
The symposium included five presentations of papers. During the
morning session the papers presented included:
•

The Emergence of Speculative Masonry: An Overview by Most
Worshipful R. Stephen Doan, Past Grand Master of Masons in California

•

Gentlemen Entrants in Scottish 17th Century Lodges: Motivations,
Processes and Consequences by Dr. and Worshipful A. Trevor Stewart,
the Henry Wilson Coil Lecturer for the symposium, a Past Master of
Quatuor Coronati Lodge No. 2076 (the Premiere Lodge of Research),
and the United Grand Lodge of England’s 2004 Prestonian Lecturer.

•

We Are Speculative Only: The Development of Speculative Freemasonry
in Organizational Identity and Legend by Worshipful Shawn E. Eyer,
Past Master of Academia Lodge No. 847, the editor of Philalethes:
The Journal of Masonic Research & Letters and Ahiman: A review of
Masonic Culture & Tradition.

The attendees then divided into tiled and untiled sessions for
the afternoon.

Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum
Oversight of the Grand Lodge’s library and museum remains an
important part of the mission of the Institute for Masonic Studies. The library,
named for the celebrated Masonic scholar and California Mason, Henry Coil, is
a repository of the history and material culture of Freemasonry in California. The
operation of the library and museum is managed by the Grand Secretary and his
staff, primarily Worshipful Adam Kendall, Collections Manager. Their efforts to
preserve, restore, and exhibit the holdings of the library and museum, make it one
of the leading institutions of its kind in the United States.
This past year, the library and museum acquired a new artifact—the ruby
and diamond encrusted 33° gold jewel that belonged to both Charles Frederick
Crocker, President of Crocker Bank, and William Henry Crocker, Vice President
of the Southern Pacific Railroad. The acquisition was made possible by a donation
from the San Francisco Scottish Rite Bodies and California Lodge No. 1. The
jewel and other artifacts from the lives of the Crockers will be on display during
the Annual Communication.
The library and museum again took part in the annual San Francisco
History Expo sponsored by the San Francisco History Society and held at the Old
Mint. More than 2,800 visitors viewed exhibits from thirty-three San Francisco
historical and cultural organizations. The Henry Wilson Coil exhibit featured
trowels and other Masonic implements used in the ceremonial cornerstone laying
of the 1876 San Francisco City Hall and Law Courts, UCSF, and the California
Masonic Memorial Temple.
The institute would like to again acknowledge Worshipful Adam
Kendall’s work for the preservation and exhibition of the rich Masonic heritage
in the possession of the Grand Lodge as well as for his research and scholarship
on California Masonic history. Using the historical archives of the Grand Lodge,
Worshipful Kendall has written and presented papers which have produced

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

301

significant recognition and appreciation for the Grand Lodge of California, the
Institute for Masonic Studies, and the Henry Wilson Coil Library and Museum.
Further, the Institute would like to recognize Brother Kendall who was elected and
is serving as the Vice President of the Masonic Library and Museum Association.
Basic Candidate Education Program
The institute is conducting a revision and reformation of the Basic
Candidate Education program of the Grand Lodge. The new program will be
an enhanced and enriched online education experience for Entered Apprentices,
Fellow Crafts, and new Master Masons and will include opportunities to practice
for mastery and reflect upon the teachings of each degree. Outstanding artwork,
video, and online links will be added to the readings to provide more depth and
breadth in the study of the three degrees of Masonry.
The UCLA Project: Advancing the Study
and Understanding of Freemasonry
Since 2009, the Grand Lodge of California has partnered with the UCLA
History Department and Distinguished Professor of History, Dr. Margaret Jacob,
to lift the “veil of secrecy” that surrounds and obscures Freemasonry’s place in
history. Over the past four years, four undergraduate courses have been developed
and five scholars have been supported in their research, scholarship, and teaching.
These scholars continue to advance the study and understanding of Freemasonry
and its proper place in developing and continuing civil society. This past year,
Dr. Maria Eugenia Vazquez Semadini, received the sought after position of postdoctoral fellow supported by the partnership.
In December 2011, the Grand Lodge of California and the UCLA History
Department teamed to present an international conference on Freemasonry in

Report of the Committee
on Jurisprudence
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. of California:
The Committee on Jurisprudence serves as the legal adviser to the
Grand Master and the legal adviser to the Grand Lodge when in session. The
Committee reviews proposed resolutions and recommendations to be considered
at the next Annual Communication and prepares any necessary legislation to carry
out the intent of the proponents. At the Annual Communication, it comments
on the legality of the Grand Master’s decisions and dispensations and on the
legal effect of the proposed recommendations and resolutions. After the Annual
Communication, it prepares the changes to the California Masonic Code to reflect
the legislation which was adopted.
In the Committee’s view, those of Grand Master Loui’s decisions
and dispensations coming to its attention were legal and within his discretion.
In the Committee’s view, the legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the
Grand Lodge website on July 16th of this year is sufficient to carry out the
intent of the proponents, and the legislation contained in Grand Master Loui’s
recommendations which he will present in his message is sufficient to carry out
his intent. We believe that each piece of this legislation has the legal effect set
forth in it.
The legislation posted by the Grand Secretary to the Grand Lodge website
on July 18th of this year and the legislation contained in Grand Master Loui’s
recommendations require no separate motion because they are automatically
before this Annual Communication. The presiding officer will announce the vote
required for the passage of each item before discussion begins. Any legislation
which does not amend the California Masonic Code or the Ritual requires a simple
majority only for adoption. Any amendment to the California Masonic Code or
the Ritual must be adopted by a five-sixths affirmative vote. If the amendment
receives a simple majority but less than a five-sixths affirmative vote, it carries
over to the next Annual Communication when only a two-thirds affirmative vote
is required for adoption.
We thank the Grand Master for the opportunity which he has given us to
serve this year.

Mark K. Ameli
Jeffrey L. Bear

Respectfully submitted,
R. Stephen Doan, PGM, Chairman
David M. Ferreria, Vice Chairman

Report of the Committee on
Trial Review

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The Committee on Trial Review has carefully examined the records of
all trials held during the past Masonic year. All Committee votes were unanimous
except where otherwise noted.
In each of the following matters, the Committee finds there was
compliance with the procedural requirements of the California Masonic Code,
that the findings were supported by the evidence and that the penalties fixed
were appropriate.
1.

In Trial Number 2611 the Accused, who was Junior Warden of his Lodge,
pled no contest to a charge of financial mis-management and refusing
to obey the Master’s authority as a result of misusing money from the
lodge refreshment fund. The Accused later re-paid the money and it may
have been more of a case of just not returning the funds to the lodge in
a timely manner. The Trial Master investigated the charges, found the
Accused guilty and fixed the penalty at suspension for six months.

2.

In Trial Number 2620 the accused used a false name on his application
because he had for some time been using a false name to protect his
lack of legal immigration status in this country. He fully admitted
the offense to the Trial Master and indeed it was he who brought the
offense to the Grand Lodge’s attention. Upon investigation, the Trial
Master determined that the charges were true and found him guilty of
unmasonic conduct but found a number of mitigating factors including
the fact that he did not falsify his name to obtain any personal financial
benefit nor did his background demonstrate in any other particular any
conduct or trait which would exclude him from the fraternity but only
because he wanted to become a Mason, both his brother and son belong
to his lodge, he was the one who brought the falsification to light and
all of the brothers present at a stated meeting indicated they wished him
to remain as a member of his lodge. The Trial Master found that while
there was clearly some fraud involved in what he did it did not arise out
of an “inherently evil motive” and that there was no “material” harm to
Masonry hence did not constitute moral turpitude to the extent that it
would justify an expulsion. He therefore fixed the penalty at reprimand.

3.

In Trial Number 2621 the accused was charged with striking a brother
Mason during a tiled meeting, refusing to obey an order of the Master
to sit down and stop talking during a tiled meeting and of resigning as a
member of the State Bar of California after admitting he misappropriated

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

305

money from clients and committed other acts involving dishonesty in
violation of the California Business and Professions Code as it pertains
to Attorneys and of the California Code of Professional Responsibility.
Two other charges were withdrawn prior to trial. The Accused pled
not guilty and was tried by Commissioners who found him guilty and
found the offenses to constitute un-Masonic conduct. The Trial Master
determined that the appropriate penalty for the offenses occurring during
the tiled meeting would be reprimand but fixed the penalty as to the State
Bar charges and resignation at expulsion.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for
adoption the following Resolution:
“Resolved that in Trial Numbers 2611, 2620 and 2621 the
findings and penalties affixed are affirmed.”
4.

In Trial Number 2006 one member of the Committee recused himself
from consideration of the matter. The Accused pled not guilty and trial
was by Commission which found that he had started a fight with another
brother, hitting him in the face and that a civil suit against the Accused
and the residential park where he lived was later settled by payment
of $45,000 to the injured brother; the Accused was also involved in
continuous, deliberate and malicious acts against a neighbor in a Masonic
community in which the Accused lived, including operating a noisy
mosquito abatement machine 24 hours a day which was later abated by a
Superior Court order which the Accused further violated by destroying a
hedge on the neighbor’s property, continually coming on to the property
in violation of the order, kicking down a barrier constructed by the
neighbor and violently hurling pieces of it against their residence and
continually confronting and harassing the neighbor, at one point telling
her he was not “welcome here” (she is of East Indian ancestry); the Trial
Master also found that the Accused and his supporters had harassed and
intimidated witnesses to the point that some were afraid to appear at the
trial; at the time of trial the Accused showed absolutely no remorse for
any of his behavior. The Trial Master fixed the penalty at expulsion.
This matter was reported on by the Committee at last year’s Grand Lodge
and the Committee recommended affirmance of the findings and penalty
and this Grand Lodge voted to follow the Committee’s recommendation.
Following that vote it was determined that the decision of the Trial Master
had not been received by the Grand Secretary in time for the Accused to
avail himself of his right under the California Masonic Code to submit to
the Committee any newly discovered evidence which he would like the

306

Proceedings of the
Committee to consider. In consultation with the Committee the Grand
Master determined to set aside the vote of Grand Lodge at last year’s

of documents to the Committee which the Committee, after review, has
determined does not comply with the requirements of the Code in that it
does not present any newly discovered evidence and further does not in
any way argue that any new evidence could not have been presented at

this Grand Lodge.
