of expulsion as affixed by the Trial Master is affirmed.”
5.

The next matter presents a convoluted substantive and procedural picture
and therefore requires careful attention to the following:
In Trial Number 2609 the Accused pled not guilty and trial was by
Commission which came to a decision on the following specifications:
on Specification #1 which charged that the Accused had spread false
rumors about another brother that he was having sexual relations with
another brother’s aunt and mother the Commission found the Accused
guilty of Unmasonic Conduct and the Trial Master fixed the penalty
at expulsion; on Specification #2 which charged the Accused with
spreading rumors that a brother’s wife had once been a “whore” and
that her prior husband had been her “pimp” the Commission found the
Accused guilty of Unmasonic conduct which the Trial Master fixed the
penalty at expulsion; on Specification #3 which charged that the Accused
had defamed another brother and cheated him the Commission found the
Accused Not Guilty; on Specification #4 which charged that the Accused
had spread false rumors about another brother’s adult daughter by stating
that a third brother was “seeing” her and implied that he was sleeping
with her the Commission found the Accused Guilty and the Trial Master
fixed the penalty at expulsion; on Specification #5 which charged that
the Accused falsely accused another brother of embezzling lodge funds
the Commission found the Accused not guilty; on Specification #6 which
repeated the charges in Specification #2 that another brother’s wife had
been a prostitute the Commission found the Accused Guilty and the
Trial Master fixed the penalty at suspension for one year; Specification
#7 was dismissed; on Specification #8 which appears to repeat the

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

307

charges in Specification #5 and charged that the Accused had accused
another brother of embezzlement of lodge funds the Commission
found the Accused Guilty of unmasonic conduct and the Trial Master
fixed the penalty at expulsion; on Specification #9 which charged the
presentation of an unworthy candidate the Accused was found not guilty;
on Specification #10 which charge the Accused with accusing another
brother of selling stolen merchandise the Accused was found Guilty and
the Trial Master fixed the penalty at expulsion; and on Specification #11
which charged the slander of another brother by alleging he was an FBI
informant and a “snitch” the Accused was found not guilty.
The Committee makes the following procedural recommendations
to this Grand Lodge: First, Specifications #2 and #6 appear to be the
same allegation, that the Accused claimed that a brother’s wife was a
prostitute in a prior life. The Accused was expelled on Specification #2
and suspended on Specification #6. The Committee recommends that
these charges be consolidated into one charge as it would be improper to
convict the Accused on the same set of facts twice.
Specifications #5 and #8 both charge that the Accused claimed another
brother was embezzling lodge funds. The Commission found him not
guilty on Specification #5 and guilty on Specification #8. The facts
presented to the Commission were that the secretary of the lodge would
be given the cash donations collected at lodge dinners and he would often
reimburse himself from the collected funds for expenditures he made
on behalf of the lodge instead of giving all the funds to the Treasurer
as required by the Code. He would report what he had done at Stated
Meetings. The Accused admitted speaking to others about the process
but claimed it was in the context of seeking compliance with the Code
and attempting to correct an improper procedure.
The Committee recommends that due to the conflicting verdicts on
these two Specifications and the nature of the evidence that the equities
be balanced and that the two Specifications be consolidated and that
a verdict of not guilty be entered as to the consolidated count. This
recommendation is, again, based on the inconsistent verdicts and on the
lack of “substantial evidence” to support the guilty finding.
Assuming this Grand Lodge accepts the Committee’s recommendation
the status of this matter is as follows; the Commission found the
Accused not guilty on Specifications #5, 9, and 11 and Specification #7
was dismissed. The Accused will therefore remain convicted on Counts
1,2,4,6 and 10. The Committee is of the opinion that the findings of
the Commission on those counts is supported by substantial evidence
and therefore recommends that those findings be adopted by this
Grand Lodge.

308

Proceedings of the
All of the counts which the Committee is recommending that this
Grand Lodge affirm involve defamatory comments, that is, in this case
slander, the uttering of a false defamatory statement. The issue then
becomes whether or not the ultimate penalty imposed, that of expulsion,
is appropriate in light of the Committee’s recommendations. Before
considering that issue the Committee’s report will address certain
legal issues raised by the Accused in an appellate brief submitted to
the Committee.
a)

The Accused claims that the Commission was invalidly constituted
because not all of the Commissioners were “disinterested” in that one
or more belonged to an Accuser’s lodge. The Code requires that a
commissioner may not belong to the Accused’s lodge. The Accuser’s
lodge is not mentioned. This issue was raised at the trial and the Trial
Master found that there was no evidence that the Trial Master or any
of the Commissioner’s would be prejudiced against the Accused. The
Committee agrees.

b) The Accused claims the trial record is incomplete. The record was
prepared in accordance with the Code and the Accused consented to the
procedure beforehand. This amounts to a waiver of any irregularities in
the procedure which, in any event, the Committee finds do not exist.
c)

The Accused claims there was improper contact between some of the
Accusers and the Commissioners during the trial but the Accused has
been unable to show any prejudice from any contact which may have
occurred such as an attempt to influence the Commissioners. Likewise
the claim that one of the Commissioners slept during parts of the trial is
not supported because the Accused made no objection during the trial
and the Trial Master, during trial, had noted the Commissioner with his
eyes closed but determined he was not sleeping.

d) The Accused claims that one of the Accusers intimidated a witness into
not testifying. The non-testifying witness says he was going to testify as
to the Accused’s honesty, integrity and fairness. The Committee finds
no prejudice in that the evidence would have been cumulative in any
event. Several witnesses testified as character witnesses for the Accused,
including a Past Grand Master.
e)

The Accused claims that the charges were motivated by lodge politics
and not the truth of the charges. While the Committee observes that there
clearly is no love lost between the Accusers and the Accused it is of
the opinion that the motive for the filing of the charges is irrelevant.
The issue here is whether or not the charges are true - not the motive in
bringing them.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California
f)

309

The Accused claims that one of the Accusers was not a Mason in good
standing when the charges were filed. Whether he was or not, the charges
he brought in Specification #3 were also found in a charging document
brought by another of the Accusers and the Accused does not challenge
his standing. The charges in Specification #4 were initially unique to
the accusations brought by the challenged Accuser but during the pretrial proceedings the Trial Master re-drafted the specifications to such an
extent that this charge became subsumed by the others.

g) Additionally, accusers other than the suspect Accuser were witnesses
to the conduct. Also, had the lodge Junior Warden been notified of the
accusations he would have been duty bound to act as an accuser. In sum,
the Committee finds that if there was any error is was not substantial.
The last claim raised by the Accused in support of his appeal also brings
the Committee to the crux of its recommendation, that is, that the penalty
is imposed is disproportionate to the offenses found to be true and
therefore contrary to the Masonic Code. In essence, the Accused claims
that the penalty of expulsion is not appropriate.
The Accused’s reasoning is as follows: The CMC declares that in order
to expel a Mason the Trial Master must find that the conduct involved
moral turpitude or involved the conviction of a crime constituting a
violation of the moral law. In Grand Master Adamson’s Decision #2,
adopted by this Grand Lodge, it is decreed that libel does not constitute
moral turpitude. The offenses found to be true here constitute slander, a
form of defamatory conduct. The difference between slander and libel
is that libel is a written defamation and slander is an oral defamation. In
the law libel is considered to be more serious than slander because of its
more permanent nature. It is logically compelling, therefore, that if libel
does not constitute moral turpitude slander likewise does not.
The Code also declares that in the absence of aggravating or mitigating
circumstances the penalty for this type of conduct should be suspension.
The Trial Master felt that multiple offenses, the Accused’s use of his
position in Masonry to intimidate other brothers and to cause fear of
retaliation by him constituted sufficient aggravating factors to warrant
expulsion. The Committee respectfully disagrees. The fear of retaliation
was because of the Accused’s purported position and his connections in
California freemasonry. The Committee feels that this is not a proper
aggravating factor as it requires speculation as to the effect of those
connections and the multiple offenses, offensive as they were, still do
not constitute moral turpitude under the Grand Master’s decision.

310

Proceedings of the
The Committee therefore agrees with the Accused that the penalty
imposed was disproportionate and improper under the Code because the
offenses do not constitute moral turpitude and the requisite aggravating
circumstances are not present. In making this recommendation the
Committee does not diminish the Accused’s conduct which did serious
damage to his brethren, to his Lodge and ultimately to this Grand Lodge
- - not to mention his own reputation in the Masonic community. As
a result of the Accused’s conduct members were lost to freemasonry,
Eastern Star and DeMolay and those losses will probably never
be recovered.
The Committee therefore recommends that the specifications in this
matter be reversed and consolidated as outlined in this report and that
the penalty imposed be modified to that of suspension for an indefinite
period so that the brothers of the Accused’s lodge can determine for
themselves if he has taken the necessary steps to reform his negative
pattern of conduct.
The Committee also desires to go on record in this matter concerning
the performance of the Trial Master. Resolution 12-19, which relates to
this matter, opines that the Trial Master was inexperienced and made a
number of errors in the trial. The Trial Master in this case was assigned
a trial consisting of four sets of charges which were convoluted and
filled with irrelevant material. It is the opinion of the Committee that he
did an exemplary job of ferreting through the irrelevancies and limiting
the issues in the trial to what was relevant. While the Committee has
recommended a reversal of the penalty it has also found that no errors
of such a nature as to cause a reversal of the other findings in the trial
occurred and is of the opinion that the Trial Master did a competent and
thorough job with a difficult case and did so in a judicious manner.

The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for
adoption the following Resolution:
“Resolved, that in Trial Number 2609 the committee’s
recommendations as to the reversal and consolidation of the
charges be adopted and the penalty of expulsion be modified to
that of indefinite suspension.”
6.

In Trial Number 2623 the Accused was present at a Third Degree conferral
celebration at the home of another brother from the Lodge. Alcoholic
beverages were consumed and the Accused became intoxicated and was
accused of starting a fight with several of the brethren present, afflicting

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

311

personal violence upon one brother and using abusive and threatening
language against a female present at the celebration. The Accused pled
not guilty and trial was had before a Trial Master only. The Accused
testified and denied he had struck the other brother. He was found guilty
of striking a brother Mason in the face and threatening another brother
with a sharp instrument, slamming his head against a concrete wall and
threatening to “cut him up”. Two counts involving threatening language
against a female were dismissed. In mitigation the Trial Master found
that the parties involved had all been friends for many years and had
served in the U.S. Navy together and that a lot of alcohol had been
consumed by all of them over a several hour period. He fixed the penalty
at indefinite suspension.
Following the trial the prosecutor and the accused’s lawyer contacted
the Committee and expressed their concern that the witnesses against
the Accused had made substantially conflicting statements about the
specifics of what occurred during the evening in question and that the
Accusation, filed some two years after the events, was filed in retaliation
for the Accused exercising his right of blackball shortly before the filing
of the Accusations.. The Trial Master was consulted and he agreed that
because of the confusion in the evidence and the other mitigating factors
a modification of the penalty to suspension for one year would not be
inappropriate. All agreed that a return to the lodge level for trial would
not be of any benefit.
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for
adoption the following Resolution:
“Resolved, that in Trial Number 2623 the findings be affirmed
and that the penalty of indefinite suspension be modified to
suspension for one year.”
For informational purposes, in Trial Number 2612 the Accused, Junior
Warden of his Lodge, was accused of removing a back cube from the ballot box.
At a pre-trial conference it was agreed that in return for a withdrawal of the
charges the Accused would demit from the Lodge. The Trial Master approved of
the agreement.
Two requests for restoration after expulsion have been referred to the
Committee for evaluation. They both involve the same incident. During the period
of 2003 and 2004 a Lodge’s Senior Warden embezzled in excess of $20,000 from
his Lodge; he admitted to another brother that he had embezzled money and asked
for help. The brother notified Catalino Alvarado, the sitting master, and Alvarado

312

Proceedings of the

told the reporting brother to audit the hall association account. An audit committee
comprised of 5 brothers was formed to audit the hall association funds but they
did not perform the audit as directed.
The embezzling brother subsequently signed a promissory note to repay
the funds and the audit committee all conspired and agreed to not report the
embezzlement to the lodge because he was their friend and they wanted him to be
installed as Master.
The embezzlement finally came to light and in December, 2005,
charges of unmasonic conduct were brought against the embezzling brother,
against Alvarado in Trial Matter Number 0528, against Dioscoro Puspos, one
of the auditors, in Trial Matter Number 0530 and the other 4 members of the
audit committee. A Masonic Trial was held on May 30 and May 31, 2006. The
embezzling brother did not appear and was expelled. The 5 members of the audit
committee and Alvarado were suspended.
Both Alvarado and Puspos admitted the following:
1.

They knew the theft had occurred and who had embezzled the funds.

2.

Neither of them notified the Lodge’s membership of the theft.

3.

They claimed to have participated in the hall association audit when in
fact they had not.

4.

They concealed the theft after the embezzler signed a promissory note
to repay the funds.

5.

They did not consider the embezzlement a crime because he had signed
the promissory note.

6.

They wanted the embezzler to be installed as Worshipful Master in
November 2003 and that was why they did not confirm the theft.

On the recommendation of this Committee, their suspensions were
upgraded to expulsion by Grand Lodge in October of 2006.
At the March 1, 2012, at a Stated Meeting of the Lodge the membership
present voted upon a resolution requesting the Restoration of Mr. Alvarado and
Mr. Puspos to the rights and privileges of Masonry in California. The results of
the balloting for Alvarado were: Affirmative 33 - Negative 2. The results of the
balloting for Puspois were: Affirmative 33 - Negative 1 - Abstentions -1. These
requests for restoration of Mr. Alvarado and Mr. Puspos follow.

Grand Lodge F. & A.M. of California

313

Last year at our annual communication, Mr. Alvarado and Mr. Puspos
filed a similar request. Following an investigation by the Committee we reported
to Grand Lodge as follows:
“The proponents of the request for the restoration of Mr. Alvarado note
that he has, since his expulsion, been active in fund raising for the Lodge,
active in supporting Job’s Daughters, has led a blameless life in the 5 years
since he was expelled, has expressed remorse for his involvement in the
cover-up of the theft and that he will never become involved in similar
conduct again. Two members of the Lodge committee investigating the
request for restoration submitted favorable comments, noting that Mr.
Alvarado continues to support the Lodge and youth groups and is now
vice president of the Tagudinian Association which assists in town school
projects and that if restored he will bring harmony and good fellowship
to the Lodge.
As to Mr. Puspos they note that he has similarly expressed remorse and
now recognizes the seriousness of the offense and would not do it again.”
The committee nevertheless recommended denial of the applications.
On receiving the current restoration requests the Committee again
performed its own independent investigation and was able to confirm that,
despite the denial last year, these two gentlemen have continued to support
the Masonic fraternity and specifically the Masonic youth groups in their area
with the same exuberance as before. Specifically, we interviewed the Chairman
of the lodge investigating committee and the District Inspector who both
recommended restoration.
Based on all of the foregoing information and while still recognizing
the seriousness of the offenses which caused the expulsions in their first place,
the Committee is now of the opinion that the time has come. These two former
brothers are amply demonstrated that they are truly sorry for their offenses and
have repeatedly demonstrated that they are capable of being good and faithful
Masons and, most importantly, the Committee is of the opinion that the likelihood
of their recidivism is very low. Accordingly,
The Committee on Trial Review therefore submits and moves for
adoption the following Resolution:
“Resolved, that in Trial Numbers 0528 and 0530 the requests
for restoration be granted.”

Report of the Committee on
Youth Orders
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The Youth Orders Committees proudly continues the work of supporting
our Masonic youth orders—DeMolay International, Job’s Daughters International
and the International Order of the Rainbow for Girls.
Youth Orders Initiatives
The youth orders are an important part of our fraternity’s strategic plan
and remain a priority as our lodges extend themselves beyond the lodge walls and
take a more prominent role in their communities. To assist lodges with information
about the youth orders and to provide an opportunity for individual masons to
volunteer as advisors and chaperones, the website, masons4youth.org, remains a
valuable resource. It is a source of information regarding each of the youth orders,
the requirements for participating as an adult supporter, and an online form that
notifies the state leadership of each order of a Mason’s desire to volunteer.
This year the committee was proud to have an issue of the California
Freemason magazine devoted to the youth orders. Articles in the April/May 2012
publication told the story of commitment by General Douglas Mac Arthur Lodge
No. 853 in Sacramento, one of the newest lodges in California, to the creation
of a new DeMolay chapter. The relationship has strengthened both fraternities.
The magazine also highlights the DeMolay and Masonic careers of two young
leaders, Ben Turconi and Maxwell Shoemaker both of whom have served as
International Master Councilor, and credit their association with DeMolay and
Masonry for changing their lives. And Job’s Daughter, Megan Goudy who was
Miss California Job’s Daughters in 2012, and Rainbow Girl, Jade Ho who is a
Past Worthy Advisor of Concord Assembly No. 15, share how their respective
youth orders are building character and confidence in young women.
Recognizing that leadership is critical to the success of lodges and the
youth orders, a special breakout session was featured at this year’s Master and
Wardens Retreats. The program provided lodge leaders information about each
of the youth orders and how their lodges may positively support existing youth
programs and create new assemblies, bethels and chapters in their communities.
The sessions generated enthusiasm and interest among many Masters
and Wardens.

316

Proceedings of the
Youth Orders Adult Volunteer Trainings

Supporting the adult volunteers working with DeMolay, Job’s Daughters
and Rainbow for Girls remains a priority for the committee. On June 16, 2012 the
committee offered for the Youth Order Adult Volunteer Training at the Masonic
Homes in Union City. The training was led by Larry Newman, originator of the
Masonic Model Student Assistance Program. The session focused on helping
the adults identify the features and benefits of the youth orders to help with
membership recruitment, how to develop more effective relations with parents,
and maximizing opportunities for the creation of developmental assets for young
members. A second offering of the training will be provided in the south on
November 3, 2012 at the DeMolay Center in Anaheim, California.

following brothers who were recommended to receive the Grand Master’s Youth

RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
The Grand Lodge of California recognizes all of the Grand Lodges in the United States
published in the 2013 List of Lodges Masonic, which includes all 50 states and the District
of Columbia. In addition, the Grand Lodge of California recognizes a number of Prince
Hall Grand Lodges and foreign Grand Lodges around the world. The Grand Lodge of
California recognizes some, but not all, of the foreign Grand Lodges in the 2013 List of
Lodges Masonic as well as a number of foreign Grand Lodges that are not listed therein.
For clarity, the foreign Grand Lodges that are recognized by the Grand Lodge of California
are listed below alphabetically by country. For those that are published in the 2013 List of
Lodges Masonic, the corresponding page number is provided in parenthesis. Recognized
Grand Lodges that are not published in the 2013 List of Lodges Masonic are marked with
an asterisk. The Grand Secretary of the Grand Lodge of California is responsible for all
correspondence with these Grand Lodges and the Lodges under their jurisdiction. Please
contact his office for assistance.

PRINCE HALL GRAND LODGES
The Grand Lodge of California has mutual recognition with a number of Prince Hall Grand
Lodges in the United States. In addition, the Grand Lodge of California has extended an
offer of recognition to a number of Prince Hall Grand Lodges throughout the country
where mutual recognition does not yet exist.
The Grand Lodge of California maintains mutual recognition with following Prince Hall
Grand Lodges. Some of these Grand Lodges are published in the List of Lodges Masonic
so the same markings follow the name of the Grand Lodge to indicate whether or not the
Grand Lodge is published in the List of Lodges Masonic, and if so, the 2011 edition page
number is provided. The terms of recognition are the same with each Prince Hall Grand
Lodge and are consistent with the agreement of mutual recognition between the Grand
Lodge of California and the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc. In essence, dual
membership in Lodges under the two jurisdictions is not allowed. Visitation may be had
between members of Lodges of both jurisdictions. For these purposes, visitation means
visiting tiled meetings.
CALIFORNIA: ALASKA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Alaska and Its Jurisdiction, Inc.
(20); Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc. (27); COLORADO (WYOMING &
UTAH): Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Colorado, Wyoming, and Utah*; DISTRICT OF
COLUMBIA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia* (includes Lodges
in Maryland); MASSACHUSETTS (MAINE): Prince Hall Grand Lodge Jurisdiction of
Massachusetts* (includes Lodges in New Hampshire and Maine); MISSOURI: Prince
Hall Grand Lodge of Missouri and Jurisdiction*; NEBRASKA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge
of Nebraska and Its Jurisdiction*; NEVADA: The Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand
Lodge of Nevada and Jurisdiction, Inc.*NEW MEXICO: Prince Hall Grand Lodge
of the State of New Mexico, Inc.*; OREGON: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Oregon*;
PENNSYLVANIA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge Jurisdiction of Pennsylvania* (includes
Lodges in Ohio); TEXAS: Prince Hall Grand Lodge Jurisdiction of Texas*.
The Grand Lodge of California has extended an offer of mutual recognition with the
following Prince Hall Grand Lodges, but mutual recognition has not yet been established.
Visitation between our members and members of Lodges under the jurisdiction of these
Grand Lodges can not yet be made. When mutual recognition is established, the Grand
Secretary will notify our Lodges in writing.
ARIZONA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Arizona and Its Jurisdiction*; CONNECTICUT:
Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Connecticut, Inc. (30); HAWAII: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of
Hawaii and Its Jurisdiction*; ILLINOIS: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Illinois INDIANA:
Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Indiana, Inc.*; IOWA: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Iowa
and Jurisdiction*; KANSAS: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Kansas and Its Jurisdiction*;
MARYLAND: Prince Hall Grand Lodge of Maryland; MICHIGAN: Prince Hall Grand

REPORT OF INDEPENDENT AUDITORS
To the Audit Committee
The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California

We have audited the accompanying consolidated statements of financial position of The Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the “Grand Lodge”) as of October 31, 2012, and
the related consolidated statements of activities and changes in net assets and cash flows for the year then
ended. These consolidated financial statements are the responsibility of the management of the Grand Lodge.
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the consolidated financial statements based on our audit. The
prior year summarized comparative information has been derived from the Grand Lodge’s 2011 consolidated
financial statements and, in our report dated March 16, 2012, we expressed an unqualified opinion on those
consolidated financial statements.

We conducted our audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of
America. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the consolidated financial statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes
consideration of internal control over financial reporting as a basis for designing audit procedures that are
appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the
Grand Lodge’s internal controls over financial reporting. Accordingly, we express no such opinion. An audit
includes examining, on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the consolidated
financial statements, assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management,
as well as evaluating the overall consolidated financial statement presentation. We believe that our audit
provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.

In our opinion, the above referenced consolidated financial statements present fairly, in all material respects,
the consolidated financial position of the Grand Lodge as of October 31, 2012, and the results of the
consolidated activities and changes in net assets, and cash flows for the year then ended in conformity with
accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America.
Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the consolidated financial statements as a
whole. The accompanying consolidating supplementary schedules are presented for purposes of additional
analysis and are not a required part of the basic consolidated financial statements. Such information is the
responsibility of management and was derived from and relates directly to the underlying accounting and other
records used to prepare the consolidated financial statements. The information has been subjected to the
auditing procedures applied in the audit of the consolidated financial statements and certain additional
procedures, including comparing and reconciling such information directly to the underlying accounting and
other records used to prepare the consolidated financial statements or to the consolidated financial statements
themselves, and other additional procedures in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the
United States of America. In our opinion, the information is fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the
consolidated financial statements as a whole.
The accompanying supplemental schedules of fraternal expenses, program appropriations, and general and
administrative expenses are presented for purposes of additional analysis and are not a required part of the
basic consolidated financial statements. These schedules are the responsibility of the management of the Grand
Lodge. We did not audit or apply limited procedures to such information and we do not express an opinion or
any form of assurance on them.
San Francisco, California
March 22, 2013

NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

NOTE 1 – SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
History and organization – The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the “Grand
Lodge”) is a nonprofit, unincorporated fraternal organization and governed by a constitution and ordinances setting forth its
jurisdiction and authority. The jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge includes all lodges and Masons within the state of California, and
members of lodges of California, wherever residing.
The Grand Lodge provides general and administrative services to its related entities: the Masonic Homes of California (the
“Masonic Homes”); the California Masonic Memorial Temple (the “Temple”); and the California Masonic Foundation (the
“Foundation”); (collectively, the “Masonic Entities”). These services are reimbursed by the related entities.

On February 15, 2007, the Temple transferred operation of the auditorium and garage to a new entity, Nob Hill Masonic Center, Inc.
(the “Nob Hill”), an entity created for this purpose. The Nob Hill is a subsidiary of the Grand Lodge. Accordingly, the financial
statements of the Nob Hill have been consolidated in the financial statements of the Grand Lodge.
On October 30, 2008, the Temple transferred the operation of the auditorium from the Nob Hill to Live Nation, not an affiliate.

Principles of consolidation – The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of the Grand Lodge and its subsidiary,
the Nob Hill. All significant inter-company accounts and transactions have been eliminated.

Summarized financial information – The consolidated financial statements include certain prior year summarized comparative
information in total but not by net asset class. Such information does not include sufficient information to constitute a presentation
in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America. Accordingly, such information should
be read in conjunction with the Grand Lodge’s consolidated financial statements as of October 31, 2011, and for the year then
ended, from which the summarized information was derived.

Net assets classifications – The accompanying consolidated financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the
standards set forth in Statements of Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”)
958-605 “Revenue Recognition”, ASC 958-205 “Presentation of Financial Statements” and the guidelines set forth in the industry
audit and accounting guide “Not-for-Profit Entities” issued by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. Under these
guidelines, contributions of cash and other assets are classified as one of the following three categories:
Unrestricted – Unrestricted net assets represent resources that are not subject to donor-imposed stipulations and are
available to support all activities of the Grand Lodge, including the Grand Lodge Endowment Fund (the “Endowment
Fund”). The Endowment Fund was established at the Grand Lodge’s October 1993 Annual Communication. If, in any fiscal
year, there is an excess of support and revenues over expenses, as defined by the Grand Lodge Executive Committee, the
excess shall be added to the Endowment Fund. For the years ended October 31, 2012 and 2011, excess of support and
revenues over expenses are $10,429 and $5,424, respectively.
Temporarily restricted – Temporarily restricted net assets represent contributions that are limited in use in accordance
with donor-imposed stipulations. These stipulations may expire with time and/or may be satisfied by the actions of the
Grand Lodge according to the intention of the donor. Upon satisfaction of such stipulations, the associated net assets are
released from temporarily restricted net assets and reported as unrestricted. If a restriction is fulfilled in the same fiscal
year in which the contribution was received, the contribution is reported as temporarily restricted support and net assets
released from restriction in that period.

Permanently restricted – Permanently restricted net assets represent contributions to be invested and held in perpetuity
as directed by the donor. For the years ended October 31, 2012 and 2011, there were no permanently restricted net
assets.

NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

Use of estimates – The preparation of consolidated financial statements in conformity with accounting principles generally
accepted in the United States of America requires management to make estimates and assumptions. These estimates and
assumptions affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities, disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the
consolidated financial statements, and the reported amounts of revenues and expenses during the reporting period. Actual results
could differ from those estimates.

Fair value of financial instruments – The carrying amounts reported in the accompanying consolidated statements of financial
position for cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, accounts payable, accrued liabilities, and related entities
receivables/payables, approximate fair value due to their short-term nature. Discussion on the fair value of financial instruments is
included in Note 2.

Cash and cash equivalents – Cash and cash equivalents consist of highly liquid investments with original maturities of three
months or less at the time of purchase, with the exception of cash and cash equivalents held as investments.
Inventory – Inventory is stated at the lower of cost or net realizable value on a first-in, first-out basis.
Prepaid expenses – Prepaid expenses consist primarily of prepaid insurance coverage.

Investments – Investments in debt and equity securities are stated at estimated fair market values based on quoted market prices.
Investments received through gifts are recorded at estimated fair market values at the dates of donation. The fair value of
alternative investments is recorded at the investment manger’s Net Asset Value (“NAV”), as the managers have the greatest insight
into the investments of their funds and the related industry and have the appropriate expertise to determine the NAV. The Grand
Lodge assesses the NAV and takes into consideration events such as suspended redemptions, restructuring, secondary sales, and
investor defaults to determine if an adjustment is necessary. Additionally, asset holdings are reviewed within the investment
manager’s audited financial statements, as are interim financial statements and fund manager communications, for the purposes of
assessing valuation. Unrealized gains or losses that result from market fluctuations are recorded in the period in which such
fluctuations occur. Realized gains or losses resulting from sales or maturities of securities are calculated on a cost basis.
Property and equipment – Property and equipment, including leasehold improvements, greater than $1,000 are recorded at cost
and are depreciated using the straight-line method over estimated useful lives of 3 to 25 years.

The Grand Lodge periodically evaluates the carrying value of its long-lived assets for impairment. The evaluations address the
estimated recoverability of the assets’ carrying value, which is principally determined based on projected undiscounted cash flows
generated by the underlying tangible assets. When the carrying value of an asset exceeds its estimated recoverability, a write-down
is recorded. No impairment was recorded during the years ended October 31, 2012 and 2011.
Other assets – Other assets consist primarily of a collection of jewelry used in lodge ceremonies.

Deferred per capita dues revenue – Deferred per capita dues revenue consists of dues received in the current year for the
subsequent fiscal year. These amounts are recognized as revenue using the straight-line method over the period to which they
relate.

Assets held in trust for future lodge – Assets held for Covina Lodge consists of the assets remaining as a result of closing the
Masonic Lodge located in Covina. Upon closure of the Covina Lodge during October 2011, the remaining cash was deposited into
the Grand Lodge bank accounts and these funds were used to pay expenditures remaining on Covina Lodge’s behalf. Additionally,
in 2012, the Covina Masonic Temple was sold and the proceeds are being held by the Grand Lodge until a new lodge is constituted
in Covina.

Revenue recognition – Contributions are recognized as revenue when received or unconditionally promised. Non-cash donations
are recognized at fair market value at the time of the donation. Dues are recognized as revenue ratably over the period to which
they relate.

Concentration of credit risk – Financial instruments potentially subjecting the Grand Lodge to concentrations of credit risk
consist primarily of bank demand deposits in excess of Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”) insurance thresholds, cash
held in money market accounts in excess of the amounts insured by the U.S. Treasury insurance for money market funds, and
various debt and equity investments in excess of Securities Investor Protection Corporation (“SIPC”) insurance. Demand deposits
are placed with a local financial institution, and management has not experienced any loss related to these demand deposits in the
past. Investment securities are exposed to various risks, such as interest rate, market, and credit risk. It is at least reasonably
possible, given the level of risk associated with investment securities, that changes in the near term could materially affect the
amount reported in the consolidated statements. The risk associated with the investments is mitigated through diversification.
Income tax status – The Grand Lodge has been granted tax-exempt status for both federal income and California franchise tax
purposes; while Nob Hill, a subsidiary of the Grand Lodge, is subject to federal income and California franchise tax.
As of October 31, 2012 and 2011, the Grand Lodge had no unrecognized tax positions or uncertain tax positions requiring accrual.
Therefore, no provision for income taxes has been provided in the consolidated financial statements.

New accounting pronouncements – In September 2009, the FASB issued ASU 2010-06, “Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures
(Topic 820): Improving Disclosures about Fair Value Measurements”. This guidance adds new requirements for disclosures about
transfers in and out of Level 1 and Level 2 measurements and the reasons for the transfers; and a gross presentation activity within
the Level 3 roll forward, presenting separately information about purchases, sales, issuances, and settlements. The Grand Lodge
adopted this guidance in 2011 (see Note 2).

In May 2011, the FASB issued ASU 2011-04, “Fair Value Measurement (Topic 820), Amendments to Achieve Common Fair Value
Measurement and Disclosure Requirements in U.S. GAAP and IFRSs” (“ASU 2011-04”), which amended ASC Topic 820, Fair Value
Measurement (“ASC Topic 820”), to change the wording used to describe many of the requirements in U.S. GAAP for measuring fair
value and for disclosing information about fair value measurements. The adoption of ASU 2011-04 is effective for the Grand Lodge
beginning November 1, 2012. The Grand Lodge is currently evaluating the impact of ASU 2011-04 on the consolidated financial
statements.
Reclassification – Certain accounts in prior year consolidated financial statements have been reclassified for comparative
purposes to conform with the presentation in the current year consolidated financial statements.

ASC 820 “Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures” defines fair value as the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to
transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. ASC 820 also establishes a fair
value hierarchy which requires an entity to maximize the use of observable inputs and minimize the use of unobservable inputs
when measuring fair value. The standard describes three levels of inputs that may be used to measure fair value:
Level 1
Level 2

Level 3

Quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.

Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices, such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities; quoted
prices in active markets that are not active; or other inputs that are observable or can be corroborated by
observable market data for substantially the full term of the assets or liabilities; or net asset value per share
(or its equivalent) with the ability to redeem the investments in the near term.

Unobservable inputs that are supported by little or no market activity and that are significant to the fair
value of the assets or liabilities.

Following is a description of the valuation methodologies used for instruments measured at fair value on a recurring basis and
recognized in the accompanying consolidated financial statements, as well as the general classification of such instruments
pursuant to the valuation hierarchy:

Investments – Where quoted market prices are available in an active market, securities are classified within Level 1 of
the valuation hierarchy. Level 1 securities include exchange traded equities. If quoted market prices are not available,
then fair values are estimated by using pricing models, quoted prices of securities with identical characteristics or
discounted cash flows. In certain cases where Level 1 or Level 2 inputs are not available, securities are classified within
Level 3 of the hierarchy and include certain real estate investments, managed futures, and other less liquid securities.

Managed futures (“Man and Robeco”) – This category invests in funds that are engaged primarily in the speculative trading of
futures and forward contracts related to interest rates, foreign currencies, equity prices or commodity prices. The fair values of the
investments in this category have been estimated using the net asset value of the Grand Lodge’s ownership interest in partner’s
capital. . The investment managers in this fund have the ability to suspend withdrawals in situations when the Fund suspends the
calculation of net asset value of the Fund. For this reason, Management has classified this as a Level 3 investment even though the
redemption notice period is 5-10 days.
Real estate (“UBS TPF”) – This category invests in an actively managed core portfolio of equity real estate that seeks to provide
attractive returns while limiting downside risk and has both relative and real return objectives. Its relative performance objective
is to outperform the NFI-ODCE index over any given three- to five-year period. The Fund’s real return performance objective is to
achieve at least a 5% real rate of return (i.e., inflation-adjusted return), before advisory fees, over any given three- to five-year
period. The fair values of the investments in this category have been estimated using the net asset value per share of the
investments.

NOTE 7 – RETIREMENT PLANS
Defined benefit plan – Masonic Homes, the Grand Lodge, and the Temple participate in a defined benefit pension plan (the “Plan”)
that covers all employees. The allocation of Grand Lodge and Nob Hill employees represent 16.33% of the Plan. The Grand Lodge is
the sponsoring employer of the Plan.

Plan termination – The Plan was frozen effective March 31, 2007, with the intent to eventually terminate the Plan. The cost of the
Plan termination has not been determined as of October 31, 2012. As a result of freezing the plan, participants no longer accrue
benefits based on future service. Plan assets will be shared among eligible plan participants in the event of a termination in the
following priority order:

employees who were eligible to retire at least three years before plan termination.) The benefit paid would be the

Explanation of investment strategies and policies – In July 2012, the Plan Fiduciaries delegated the responsibilities for the
management of the California Masonic Retirement Plan assets to Hewitt EnnisKnupp (“HEK”). HEK utilizes the Delegated Solutions
framework to employ liability-hedging assets (fixed income) and return seeking assets (equities) in the appropriate ratio to allow
for the improvement of the funded ratio of the retirement plan. HEK executes and monitors the Plan’s strategy in accordance to the
Investment Policy Statement for the California Masonic Retirement Plan dated July 17, 2012. Based on long-term goals and desired
risk levels, the glide path (liability-hedging assets vs. return seeking assets) target allocations are adjusted if the Plan’s funded
status changes. The allocations will be rebalanced back to within the corresponding range, with a general expectation that
rebalancing will occur toward the target allocation.

Capital market assumption methodology – In determining the long-term rate of return for plan assets, the Grand Lodge studies
historical markets and long-term historical relationships between equities and fixed income, consistent with the widely accepted
capital market principle that assets with higher volatility generate a greater return over the long-run. Current market factors such
as inflation and interest rates are evaluated before long-term capital market assumptions are determined.

Management has established an expected long-term rate of return on assets (“ELTRA”) of 7.00%, which reflects the historical
support for operation of 4.00% plus a 3.00% factor representing inflation. Future return may not be as strong which will require
management to review their operation’s support policies.

NOTE 8 – CONTINGENCIES
In the ordinary course of business, the Grand Lodge is a party to claims and legal actions. After consulting with legal counsel, the
Grand Lodge’s management is of the opinion that any liability that may ultimately be incurred as a result of claims or legal actions
will not have a material effect on the consolidated financial position or consolidated results of operations of the Grand Lodge.
NOTE 9 – UPMIFA DISCLOSURES
Board interpretation of law
Interpretation of Relevant Law UPMIFA enacted by California, FMV preservation – The Board of Trustees of the Grand Lodge has
interpreted the California Prudent Management of Institutional Funds Act (“CPMIFA”) as requiring the preservation of the fair
value of the original gift as of the gift date of the donor-restricted endowment funds absent explicit donor stipulations to the
contrary. As a result of this interpretation, the Grand Lodge classifies as permanently restricted net assets (a) the original value of
gifts donated to the permanent endowment, (b) the original value of subsequent gifts to the permanent endowment, and
(c) accumulations to the permanent endowment made in accordance with the direction of the applicable donor gift instrument at
the time the accumulation is added to the fund. The remaining portion of the donor-restricted endowment fund that is not
classified in permanently restricted net assets is classified as unrestricted or temporarily restricted net assets until those amounts
are appropriated for expenditure by the Grand Lodge in a manner consistent with the standard of prudence prescribed by CPMIFA.
In accordance with CPMIFA, the Grand Lodge considers the following factors in making a determination to appropriate or
accumulate donor-restricted endowment funds:
a.
b.
c.
d.
e.
f.
g.

The duration and preservation of the fund
The purposes of the Grand Lodge and the donor-restricted endowment fund
General economic conditions
The possible effect of inflation and deflation
The expected total return from income and the appreciation of investments
Other resources of the Grand Lodge
The investment policies of the Grand Lodge

Spending policy, investing policy, and strategy

Return objectives and risk parameters – The Grand Lodge has adopted investment and spending policies for endowment assets that
attempt to provide a predictable stream of funding to programs supported by its endowment while seeking to maintain the
purchasing power of the endowment assets. Endowment assets include those assets of donor-restricted funds that the Grand Lodge
must hold in perpetuity or for a donor-specified period(s) as well as board-designated funds. Under this policy, as approved by the
Board of Trustees, the endowment assets are invested in a manner that is intended to produce results that exceed the price and
yield results of various market benchmarks appropriate to the investment classes utilized while assuming a moderate level of
investment risk. The Grand Lodge expects its endowment funds, over time, to provide an average rate of return of approximately
7.0%-7.5% annually. Actual returns in any given year may vary from this amount.
Strategies employed for achieving objectives – To satisfy its long-term rate-of-return objectives, the Grand Lodge relies on a total
return strategy in which investment returns are achieved through both capital appreciation (realized and unrealized) and current
yield (interest and dividends). The Grand Lodge targets a diversified asset allocation that places a greater emphasis on equitybased investments to achieve its long-term return objectives within prudent risk constraints.

NOTES TO CONSOLIDATED FINANCIAL STATEMENTS

Spending policy and how the investment objectives relate to the spending policy – For 2011/2012, the Grand Lodge has a policy of
appropriating for distribution 4.50% of its endowment fund’s average fair value over the prior twenty quarters through the
calendar year-end preceding the fiscal year in which the distribution is planned. In establishing this policy, the Grand Lodge
considered the long-term expected return on its endowment. Accordingly, over the long term, the Grand Lodge expects the current
spending policy to allow its endowment to grow at an average of 3% annually. This is consistent with the Grand Lodge’s objective
to maintain the purchasing power of the endowment assets held in perpetuity or for a specified term as well as to provide
additional real growth through new gifts and investment return.

NOTE 10 – SUBSEQUENT EVENTS
Subsequent events are events or transactions that occur after the consolidated financial position date but before consolidated
financial statements are issued. The Grand Lodge recognizes in the consolidated financial statements the effects of all subsequent
events that provide additional evidence about conditions that existed at the date of the consolidated financial position, including
the estimates inherent in the process of preparing the consolidated financial statements. The Grand Lodge’s consolidated financial
statements do not recognize subsequent events that provide evidence about conditions that did not exist at the date of the
consolidated financial position but arose after the consolidated financial position date and before consolidated financial statements
are available to be issued.

The Grand Lodge has evaluated subsequent events through March 22, 2013 which is the date the consolidated financial statements
are available to be issued.

REPORT OF INDEPENDENT AUDITORS
To the Audit Committee
Masonic Homes of California and Subsidiaries

We have audited the accompanying consolidated statements of financial position of Masonic Homes of
California and Subsidiaries (collectively the “Organization”) as of October 31, 2012, and the related consolidated
statements of activities and changes in net assets and cash flows for the year then ended. These consolidated
financial statements are the responsibility of the management of Masonic Homes of California and Subsidiaries.
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the consolidated financial statements based on our audit. The
prior year summarized comparative information has been derived from the Organization’s 2011 consolidated
financial statements and, in our report dated February 24, 2012, we expressed an unqualified opinion on those
consolidated financial statements.

We conducted our audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of
America. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audits to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the consolidated financial statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes
consideration of internal control over financial reporting as a basis for designing audit procedures that are
appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the
Organization’s internal control over financial reporting. Accordingly, we express no such opinion. An audit also
includes examining, on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the consolidated
financial statements, assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates made by management,
as well as evaluating the overall consolidated financial statement presentation. We believe that our audit
provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.
In our opinion, the consolidated financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material respects,
the financial position of Masonic Homes of California and Subsidiaries as of October 31, 2012, and the changes
in its net assets and its cash flows for the year then ended in conformity with accounting principles generally
accepted in the United States of America.

Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the consolidated financial statements as a
whole. The accompanying consolidating supplementary schedules are presented for purposes of additional
analysis and are not a required part of the basic consolidated financial statements. Such information is the
responsibility of management and was derived from and relates directly to the underlying accounting and other
records used to prepare the consolidated financial statements. The information has been subjected to the
auditing procedures applied in the audit of the consolidated financial statements and certain additional
procedures, including comparing and reconciling such information directly to the underlying accounting and
other records used to prepare the consolidated financial statements or to the consolidated financial statements
themselves, and other additional procedures in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the
United States of America. In our opinion, the information is fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the
consolidated financial statements as a whole.

The accompanying supplemental schedule of program expenses and supporting services expenses are
presented for purposes of additional analysis and are not a required part of the basic consolidated financial
statements. These schedules are the responsibility of the Organization’s management. We did not audit or apply
limited procedures to such information and we do not express an opinion or any form of assurance on them.
San Francisco, California
February 26, 2013

REPORT OF INDEPENDENT AUDITORS
Board of Trustees
California Masonic Foundation

We have audited the accompanying consolidated statement of financial position of California Masonic
Foundation and its supporting entity (the “Organization”), as of October 31, 2012, and the related consolidated
statements of activities and changes in net assets, and cash flows for the year then ended. These financial
statements are the responsibility of the management of California Masonic Foundation. Our responsibility is to
express an opinion on the consolidated financial statements based on our audit. The prior year summarized
comparative information has been derived from the Organization’s consolidated financial statements for the
year ended October 31, 2011; and, in our report dated March 16, 2012, we expressed an unqualified opinion on
those consolidated financial statements.
We conducted our audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of
America. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the consolidated financial statements are free of material misstatement. An audit includes
consideration of internal control over financial reporting as a basis for designing audit procedures that are
appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the
Organization’s internal control over financial reporting. Accordingly, we express no such opinion. An audit
includes examining, on a test basis, evidence supporting the amounts and disclosures in the consolidated
financial statements. An audit also includes assessing the accounting principles used and significant estimates
made by management, as well as evaluating the overall consolidated financial statement presentation. We
believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinion.
In our opinion the above referenced consolidated financial statements present fairly, in all material respects, the
financial position of California Masonic Foundation and its supporting entity as of October 31, 2012, and the
consolidated results of their activities and changes in net assets, and their cash flows for the year then ended in
conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America.

Our audit was conducted for the purpose of forming an opinion on the consolidated financial statements as a
whole. The accompanying consolidating supplementary schedules are presented for purposes of additional
analysis and are not a required part of the basic consolidated financial statements. Such information is the
responsibility of management and was derived from and relates directly to the underlying accounting and other
records used to prepare the consolidated financial statements. The information has been subjected to the
auditing procedures applied in the audit of the consolidated financial statements and certain additional
procedures, including comparing and reconciling such information directly to the underlying accounting and
other records used to prepare the consolidated financial statements or to the consolidated financial statements
themselves, and other additional procedures in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the
United States of America. In our opinion, the information is fairly stated in all material respects in relation to the
consolidated financial statements as a whole.

The accompanying combining statements of financial position, excluding Temple and combining statements of
activities, excluding Temple are presented for purposes of additional analysis and are not a required part of the
basic consolidated financial statements. These schedules are the responsibility of the Organization’s
management. We did not audit or apply limited procedures to such information and we do not express an
opinion or any form of assurance on them.
San Francisco, California
March 22, 2013

NOTE 1 – SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
History and organization – The California Masonic Foundation (the “Foundation”) was established in 1968 by the Grand Lodge of
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California (the “Grand Lodge”). The Foundation was formed as a California not-for-profit
charitable corporation to further all phases of education, charity, and science. During fiscal year 2004, the Foundation notified the
Internal Revenue Service (“IRS”) requesting approval to terminate their private foundation status under section 507(b)(1)(B) of
the Internal Revenue Code and requested conversion to operate as a public charity under 509(a) of the Internal Revenue Code. In
the same period, the California Masonic Memorial Temple, Inc. (the “Temple”) placed a request with the IRS to convert from a
private foundation to a public charity supporting organization of the Foundation, as defined in section 509(a)(3) of the Internal
Revenue Code. The Foundation and Temple have both received advance rulings granting public charity status. The advance ruling
period ended June 30, 2010 and the private foundation status was terminated, making both Temple and Foundation public
charities. As a result, the Foundation effectively controls and has an economic interest in the Temple.

In July 2006, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) issued Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) 740 “Income
Taxes” which clarifies the accounting for income taxes by prescribing a minimum probability threshold that a tax position must
meet before a financial statement benefit is recognized. The minimum threshold is defined in ASC 740 as a tax position that is more
likely than not to be sustained upon examination by the applicable taxing authority, including resolution of any related appeals or
litigation processes, based on the technical merits of the position. The tax benefit to be recognized is measured as the largest
amount of benefit that is greater than fifty percent likely of being realized upon ultimate settlement.
The Foundation believes that it has appropriate support for any tax positions taken, and as such, does not have any uncertain tax
positions that are material to the consolidated financial statements.

The Temple is a California not-for-profit corporation. The Temple owns the California Masonic Memorial Temple, a facility that is
comprised of an auditorium, exhibit hall, a parking garage, and office space located in San Francisco, California. The Restated
Articles of Incorporation for the Temple provide that income, less operating expenses and reserves, is to be transferred to the
Foundation. The amount and proportions of such distributions are at the sole discretion of the Board of Trustees. For the years
ended October 31, 2012 and 2011, no such transfers were made.
As of February 15, 2007, the Temple transferred operations of the auditorium and garage to a new entity, Nob Hill Masonic Center,
Inc. (“Nob Hill”), an entity created for this purpose. The new entity is a subsidiary of the Grand Lodge.

On October 30, 2008, the Temple signed a 10-year lease agreement with Live Nation. Under the agreement, Live Nation is
committed to pay Temple a base rent of $83,333 per month, subject to annual increase, for the lease of Temple’s auditorium,
Exhibition Hall, California, and conference rooms. The lease commencement date was January 1, 2009 while the payments started
in July 2009. Live Nation could opt out of the lease if done so by June 30, 2009.
In June of 2009, Amendment one was executed extending the Live Nation opt out date to December 31, 2009. In December 2009,
Amendment two was executed extending the Live Nation opt out date to May 31, 2010 which was extended through a
memorandum for an additional 30 days to June 30, 2010. In June of 2010, Amendment three was executed extending the Live
Nation opt out date to December 31, 2010. In addition, Amendment three committed Temple to contribute $285,000 toward capital
improvements in the building.
In December of 2010, Amendment four was executed extending the Live Nation opt out date to April 1, 2011. Amendment Four also
extended the lease term by five years to December 31, 2026. Amendment Four also modified the rent schedule where Live Nation
on April 1, 2011 would begin paying Temple rent at an annual rate of $600,000. The rent will increase annually until it caps in 2018
at $850,000 per year. Amendment four also increased the capital contribution requirement of the Temple from $285,000 to
$1,500,000.

In March 2011, Amendment five was executed extending the Live Nation opt out date to April 1, 2014. Amendment five extended
the lease term to March 31, 2028. This amendment modified the rent schedule where Live Nation would pay Temple the total
amount of $285,000 for the period April 1, 2011 through December 31, 2011 and $480,000 for calendar years 2012 and 2013.
Beyond calendar year 2013, the rent will increase incrementally through March 31, 2019 to a maximum annual rent of $875,500.
Thereafter through March 31, 2028, rent will increase by 3% per year. Amendment five also established a minimum annual parking
revenue guarantee of $300,000 per year for 2012 and 2013.
Principles of consolidation – The consolidated financial statements include the accounts of California Masonic Foundation and
California Masonic Memorial Temple, Inc. (collectively, the “Organization”). All significant inter-company accounts and transactions
have been eliminated.

Comparative information – The consolidated financial statements include certain prior-year summarized comparative
information in total but not by net asset class. Such information does not include sufficient detail to constitute a presentation in
conformity with generally accepted accounting principles. Accordingly, such information should be read in conjunction with the
Organization’s consolidated financial statements for the year ended October 31, 2011, from which the summarized information
was derived.
Reclassification – Certain accounts in the prior year consolidated financial statements have been reclassified for comparative
purposes to conform to the presentation in the current period consolidated financial statements.

Net asset classifications – The accompanying consolidated financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the
ASC 958-605 “Revenue Recognition” and ASC 958-205 “Presentation of Financial Statements” and the guidelines set forth in the
industry audit and accounting guide “Not-for-Profit Organizations” issued by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants
(“AICPA”). Under these guidelines, contributions of cash and other assets are classified as one of the following three categories:
Unrestricted – Unrestricted net assets are not subject to donor-imposed restrictions and are available for support of the
Organization’s programs and supporting services.

Temporarily restricted – Temporarily restricted net assets represent contributions whose use by the Organization is
limited by donor-imposed restrictions. The restrictions can be fulfilled by incurring expenses satisfying the restricted
purposes and/or expire with the passage of time.
Permanently restricted – Permanently restricted net assets represent contributions restricted by donors for investment in
perpetuity. These permanently restricted net assets consist of original corpus.

Use of estimates – The preparation of consolidated financial statements in conformity with accounting principles generally
accepted in the United States of America requires management to make estimates and assumptions. These estimates and
assumptions affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities, disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the
consolidated financial statements, and the reported amounts of revenues and expenses during the reporting period. Actual results
could differ from those estimates.
Fair value of financial instruments – The carrying amounts reported in the accompanying consolidated statements of financial
position for cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, accounts payable, accrued liabilities, and related entities
receivables/payables, approximate fair value due to their short-term nature. Discussion on the fair value of financial instruments is
included in Note 2.

Cash and cash equivalents – Cash and cash equivalents consist of highly liquid investments with original maturities of three
months or less at the time of purchase, with the exception of cash and cash equivalents held in the endowment fund as investments
or whose use is restricted.

Investments – Investments in debt and equity securities are stated at estimated fair values based on quoted market prices.
Investments received through gifts are recorded at estimated fair values at the dates of donation. The fair value of alternative
investments is recorded at the investment manager’s Net Asset Value (“NAV”), as the managers have the greatest insight into the
investments of their funds and the related industry, and have the appropriate expertise to determine the NAV. The Organization
assesses the NAV and takes into consideration events such as suspended redemptions, restructuring, secondary sales, and investor
defaults to determine if an adjustment is necessary. Additionally, asset holdings are reviewed within investment manager’s audited
financial statements, as are interim financial statements and fund manager communications, for the purposes of assessing
valuation. Unrealized gains or losses that result from market fluctuations are recorded in the period in which such fluctuations
occur. Realized gains or losses resulting from sales or maturities of securities are calculated on a cost basis.
Property and equipment – Property and equipment are carried at cost and are depreciated on the straight-line method over the
following estimated useful lives:
Buildings and improvements
Equipment
Furniture and fixtures

5 - 50 years
3 - 5 years
5 - 20 years

The Organization evaluates prominent events or changes in circumstances affecting capital assets to determine whether
impairment of a capital asset has occurred. Impairment losses on capital assets are measured using the method that best reflects
the diminished service utility of the capital asset.
Advanced deposits – Advanced deposits consist primarily of unearned revenue from various third party entities.

Contributions – The Organization records contributions in accordance with ASC 958-605 “Revenue Recognition.” Unconditional
promises to give cash and other assets to the Organization are reported at estimated fair value at the date the promise is received.
Conditional promises to give and indications to give are reported at fair value at the date the condition is fulfilled and the gift is
received, respectively. The gifts are reported as either temporarily or permanently restricted support if they are received with
donor stipulations that limit the use of the donated assets. When a donor restriction expires, that is, when a stipulated time
restriction ends and/or purpose restriction is accomplished, temporarily restricted net assets are reclassified as unrestricted net
assets.

Collection of books and non-valuable contributions – The Foundation library contains a book collection of approximately
10,000 volumes. The collection includes approximately 8,500 works on Masonic and related philosophic topics and nearly 1,500
non-Masonic volumes, including historical, religious, scientific, political, and biographical works. Fewer than 50 works in the
collection could be considered rare. The Foundation museum collection contains donated items from the membership of The
Masonic Fraternity in California and elsewhere. Artifacts in the collection include works of art, Masonic regalia, and numerous
historical pieces. The Foundation does not recognize books and non-valuable contributions in its consolidated financial statements.
The Foundation does not recognize these assets as contributions, as they are protected and preserved, held for public exhibition,
and subject to an organizational policy that requires proceeds from the sale of collection items to be used to acquire other items for
collections. Accessions and de-accessions of books and non-valuable contributions during 2012 and 2011 were not significant.
Concentration of risk – Financial instruments potentially subjecting the Foundation to concentrations of credit risk consist
primarily of bank demand deposits in excess of Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”) insurance thresholds, cash held in
money market accounts in excess of the amounts insured by the U.S. Treasury insurance for money market funds, and various debt
and equity investments in excess of Securities Investor Protection Corporation (“SIPC”) insurance. Demand deposits are placed
with a local financial institution, and management has not experienced any loss related to these demand deposits in the past.
Investment securities are exposed to various risks, such as interest rate, market, and credit risk. It is at least reasonably possible,
given the level of risk associated with investment securities, that changes in the near term could materially affect the amount
reported in the consolidated financial statements. The risk associated with the investments is mitigated through diversification.

New accounting pronouncements – In September 2009, the FASB issued ASU 2010-06, “Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures
(Topic 820): Improving Disclosures about Fair Value Measurements.” This guidance adds new requirements for disclosures about
transfers in and out of Level 1 and Level 2 measurements and the reasons for the transfers; and a gross presentation activity within
the Level 3 roll forward, presenting separately information about purchases, sales, issuances, and settlements. The Organization
adopted this guidance in 2011 (see Note 2).

Alternative Investments

These funds are comprised of Real Estate and Managed Futures. The Organization’s Investment Policy states the Organization
believes the capital markets are “mean-reverting” by nature. Therefore they adhere to long-term asset allocation strategies and
periodic, regular rebalancing. The Organization believes market timing is ineffective as a long-term investment strategy and will
remain fully invested in all long-term mandates.

ASC 820 “Fair Value Measurements and Disclosures” defines fair value as the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to
transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. ASC 820 also establishes a fair
value hierarchy which requires an entity to maximize the use of observable inputs and minimize the use of unobservable inputs
when measuring fair value. The standard describes three levels of inputs that may be used to measure fair value:
Level 1
Level 2

Level 3
Page 8

Quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.

Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices, such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities; quoted
prices in active markets that are not active; or other inputs that are observable or can be corroborated by
observable market data for substantially the full term of the assets or liabilities.
Unobservable inputs that are supported by little or no market activity and that are significant to the fair
value of the assets or liabilities.

Following is a description of the valuation methodologies used for instruments measured at fair value on a recurring basis and
recognized in the accompanying financial statements, as well as the general classification of such instruments pursuant to the
valuation hierarchy:
Available-for-sale securities – Where quoted market prices are available in an active market, securities are classified
within Level 1 of the valuation hierarchy. Level 1 securities include exchange traded equities. If quoted market prices are
not available, then fair values are estimated by using pricing models, quoted prices of securities with identical
characteristics or discounted cash flows. In certain cases where Level 1 or Level 2 inputs are not available, securities are
classified within Level 3 of the hierarchy and include certain real estate investments, managed futures, and other less
liquid securities.
